G4A_COUNTING_001.questionText: How many whole numbers are there from 15 to 42, counting both 15 and 42?
hints: When you count from one number up to another and both ends are included, think about whether subtracting alone counts every number.
Find 42 − 15 first. Then ask yourself whether the starting number 15 has been counted yet.
A similar problem: from 6 to 10 the numbers are 6, 7, 8, 9, 10. Subtracting gives 10 − 6 = 4, and adding 1 for the starting number gives 5 numbers.

stepByStep.text: Subtract the smaller number from the larger one.
This counts the jumps. Add 1 so that the starting number 15 is counted too.
There are 28 whole numbers from 15 to 42.

misconceptions.A: This is 42 − 15, which counts the jumps between the numbers. Add 1 more so that 15 itself is counted.
misconceptions.B: Well done! 42 − 15 = 27, and one more for the starting number gives 28.
misconceptions.C: This adds 2 after subtracting. Only one extra is needed, for the starting number.
misconceptions.D: This leaves out both 15 and 42. The question asks you to count both of them.

G4A_COUNTING_002.questionText: Meera stands in a queue at the school canteen. She is 7th from the front and 5th from the back. How many children are in the queue?
hints: A position from the front and a position from the back both count the same child. Think about what happens if you simply add them.
There are 6 children in front of Meera. Work out how many are behind her, then count Meera once.
A similar problem: Raju is 3rd from the front and 4th from the back. In front of him are 2 children, behind him are 3, and Raju makes 2 + 3 + 1 = 6 children.

stepByStep.text: Count the children in front of Meera and behind her.
Add them, and add Meera herself once.
There are 11 children in the queue.

misconceptions.A: This is 7 + 5, which counts Meera twice. Take 1 away so she is counted only once.
misconceptions.B: This adds 1 to 7 + 5. Meera has already been counted twice, so 1 must be taken away instead.
misconceptions.C: Great thinking! 6 in front, 4 behind, and Meera herself make 11.
misconceptions.D: This counts the 6 in front and the 4 behind but leaves out Meera. Remember to count her once.

G4A_COUNTING_003.questionText: A straight fence is 40 metres long. A post stands every 5 metres, with a post at each end. How many posts are there?
hints: Posts stand at the ends of the gaps. In a straight line with a post at both ends, compare the number of posts with the number of gaps.
First find how many 5-metre gaps fit into 40 metres.
A similar problem: a 12-metre fence with a post every 4 metres has 12 ÷ 4 = 3 gaps. The posts stand at 0, 4, 8 and 12 metres, so there are 4 posts.

stepByStep.text: Find the number of gaps between posts.
A straight line of gaps has one more post than gaps.
There are 9 posts.

misconceptions.A: You got it! 8 gaps need 9 posts, because there is a post at both ends.
misconceptions.B: This is the number of gaps, 40 ÷ 5. The post at the very start still needs to be counted.
misconceptions.C: This takes 1 away from the 8 gaps. With a post at each end, there is one more post than gaps.
misconceptions.D: This adds 2 to the number of gaps. Only one extra post is needed.

G4A_COUNTING_004.questionText: How many 2-digit numbers end in the digit 5?
hints: Think about which digits are allowed in the tens place of a 2-digit number.
Start listing them: 15, 25, 35, and keep going until the last 2-digit number that ends in 5.
A similar problem: the 2-digit numbers smaller than 60 that end in 2 are 12, 22, 32, 42 and 52. The tens digit runs from 1 to 5, so there are 5 numbers.

stepByStep.text: The ones digit is fixed as 5. The tens digit can be 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 or 9.
There are 9 such numbers.

misconceptions.A: This counts 5 itself (or 05) as well. The number 5 has only one digit, so it is not a 2-digit number.
misconceptions.B: This looks like the ending digit, not the count. Try listing the numbers: 15, 25, 35 and so on.
misconceptions.C: One number has been missed. Check that 55 and 95 are both in your list.
misconceptions.D: Excellent! The tens digit can be any of 1 to 9, so there are 9 numbers.

G4A_COUNTING_005.questionText: Riya has 3 different tops and 2 different skirts. An outfit is one top worn with one skirt. How many different outfits can she make?
hints: Every top can be paired with every skirt. Think about how many pairs each top makes.
Take the first top. How many outfits can it make with the 2 skirts? Then do the same for the other tops.
A similar problem: with 4 caps and 2 scarves, each cap can go with 2 scarves, so there are 4 × 2 = 8 pairs.

stepByStep.text: Each top can be worn with either of the 2 skirts, so each top gives 2 outfits.
There are 3 tops.
Riya can make 6 different outfits.

misconceptions.A: This adds 3 + 2. Each top goes with every skirt, so the numbers are multiplied.
misconceptions.B: Great job! Each of the 3 tops makes 2 outfits, so 3 × 2 = 6.
misconceptions.C: This is 3 × 3. There are only 2 skirts for each top, so it is 3 × 2.
misconceptions.D: This counts only the tops. Each top makes 2 different outfits, one for each skirt.

G4A_COUNTING_006.questionText: How many even numbers are there from 1 to 30?
hints: Even and odd numbers take turns as you count. Think about what share of the numbers are even.
The even numbers start 2, 4, 6. Find the last even number in the range and see which place it holds in the list.
A similar problem: from 1 to 10 the even numbers are 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. Every second number is even, so there are 10 ÷ 2 = 5 of them.

stepByStep.text: From 1 to 30, every second number is even: 2, 4, 6, and so on up to 30.
Half of the 30 numbers are even.
There are 15 even numbers from 1 to 30.

misconceptions.A: Well done! Every second number is even, and 30 ÷ 2 = 15.
misconceptions.B: This leaves out one even number. Check that 30 itself is counted, because 30 is even.
misconceptions.C: This counts one too many. Zero is not in the range 1 to 30, so the list starts at 2.
misconceptions.D: This is how many numbers there are altogether. Only every second one is even.

G4A_COUNTING_007.questionText: A carpenter cuts a long wooden plank into 6 pieces. He cuts one piece at a time. How many cuts does he make?
hints: Think about what one cut does to the number of pieces.
Before any cut there is 1 piece. After the first cut there are 2 pieces. Keep going until there are 6.
A similar problem: to cut a ribbon into 3 pieces, the first cut makes 2 pieces and the second cut makes 3 pieces. So 2 cuts are needed.

stepByStep.text: The plank starts as 1 piece. Every cut adds 1 more piece.
To reach 6 pieces, 5 more pieces are needed.
The carpenter makes 5 cuts.

misconceptions.A: This matches the number of pieces. The plank is already 1 piece before any cut, so one cut fewer is needed.
misconceptions.B: This adds 1 to the number of pieces. Cuts are one fewer than pieces, not one more.
misconceptions.C: You got it! Each cut adds one piece, so 5 cuts turn 1 piece into 6.
misconceptions.D: This doubles the pieces. Try it with a paper strip: each cut makes just one extra piece.

G4A_COUNTING_008.questionText: How many different 2-digit numbers can you make using only the digits 3 and 8? A digit may be used twice in a number.
hints: Think about the choices for the tens place and the choices for the ones place.
Write the numbers that start with 3 first. Then write the ones that start with 8.
A similar problem: with the digits 1, 2 and 5 and repeats allowed, there are 3 choices for the tens place and 3 for the ones place, so 3 × 3 = 9 numbers.

stepByStep.text: The tens digit can be 3 or 8, and the ones digit can be 3 or 8.
That gives 2 choices for each place.
The numbers are 33, 38, 83 and 88, so 4 numbers can be made.

misconceptions.A: This counts only 38 and 83. A digit may be used twice, so 33 and 88 count too.
misconceptions.B: One number has been missed. Check your list for 33, 38, 83 and 88.
misconceptions.C: This is more than can be made. With 2 choices for each of the 2 places there are 2 × 2 numbers.
misconceptions.D: Excellent! 33, 38, 83 and 88 make 4 numbers.

G4A_COUNTING_009.questionText: The pages of a small story book are numbered from 1 to 25. How many digits are printed in all to number the pages?
hints: Some page numbers have one digit and some have two. Count the two groups separately.
Pages 1 to 9 use one digit each. Work out how many pages are left from 10 to 25.
A similar problem: for pages 1 to 12, pages 1 to 9 use 9 digits. Pages 10, 11 and 12 are 3 pages using 2 digits each, which is 6 digits. In all, 9 + 6 = 15 digits.

stepByStep.text: Pages 1 to 9 have one digit each.
Pages 10 to 25 are 16 pages with two digits each.
Add the two groups.
In all, 41 digits are printed.

misconceptions.A: Great job! 9 digits for pages 1 to 9 and 32 digits for pages 10 to 25 make 41.
misconceptions.B: This gives two digits to every page. Pages 1 to 9 have only one digit each.
misconceptions.C: This is the number of pages, not the number of digits. Pages from 10 onwards use two digits each.
misconceptions.D: This is 9 + 25. Count only the pages from 10 to 25 as two-digit pages: there are 16 of them, and each uses 2 digits.

G4A_COUNTING_010.questionText: How many 2-digit numbers have digits that add up to 7?
hints: Work in an organised way: choose the tens digit first, and the ones digit is then decided.
Start with tens digit 1. The ones digit must be 6, giving 16. Now try tens digit 2, and carry on.
A similar problem: 2-digit numbers with digits adding to 4 are 13, 22, 31 and 40. The tens digit runs from 1 to 4, so there are 4 numbers.

stepByStep.text: The tens digit can be 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 or 7. It cannot be 0.
For each tens digit there is exactly one ones digit that makes the total 7.
The numbers are 16, 25, 34, 43, 52, 61 and 70.
There are 7 such numbers.

misconceptions.A: One number has been left out. Remember 70, because 7 + 0 = 7.
misconceptions.B: This also counts 07. That is just 7, which has only one digit.
misconceptions.C: Well done! 16, 25, 34, 43, 52, 61 and 70 are the 7 numbers.
misconceptions.D: This doubles the count. Each tens digit from 1 to 7 gives just one number.

G4A_COUNTING_011.questionText: Kiran writes all the numbers from 1 to 40 in her notebook. How many times does she write the digit 3?
hints: A digit can appear in the ones place or in the tens place. Count each place separately.
First list the numbers that have 3 in the ones place: 3, 13, and so on. Then look at the numbers that have 3 in the tens place.

A similar problem: from 1 to 30, the digit 2 is in the ones place in 2, 12 and 22, which is 3 times. It is in the tens place in 20 to 29, which is 10 times. In all it is written 13 times, and 22 is counted twice because it has two 2s.

stepByStep.text: In the ones place, 3 appears in 3, 13, 23 and 33.
In the tens place, 3 appears in 30, 31, 32, and so on up to 39.
Add the two counts. The number 33 has two 3s, so it is rightly counted in both.
She writes the digit 3 a total of 14 times.

misconceptions.A: This counts only the ones place. The numbers 30 to 39 each have a 3 in the tens place too.
misconceptions.B: This counts 33 only once. It has two 3s, and the question asks how many times the digit is written.
misconceptions.C: This counts only the tens place. The numbers 3, 13, 23 and 33 also have a 3 in the ones place.
misconceptions.D: Excellent! 4 times in the ones place and 10 times in the tens place make 14.

G4A_COUNTING_012.questionText: 30 children stand in a line for the morning assembly. Arjun is 12th from the front. What is his position from the back?
hints: Find how many children stand behind him. His place from the back is one more than that.
Arjun is 12th from the front, so take 12 away from 30 to find how many children are behind him.
A similar problem: in a line of 10 children, Sita is 4th from the front. Behind her are 10 − 4 = 6 children, so she is 7th from the back.

stepByStep.text: Find how many children are behind Arjun.
Counting from the back, those 18 children come first and Arjun is next.
Arjun is 19th from the back.

misconceptions.A: This is the number of children behind Arjun. He comes just after them, so his position is one more.
misconceptions.B: Great job! 18 children are behind him, so Arjun is 19th from the back.
misconceptions.C: This adds 2 to the 18 children behind him. Only Arjun himself needs to be added, which is 1.
misconceptions.D: This adds 30 and 12. A position in the line cannot be bigger than the number of children.

G4A_COUNTING_013.questionText: A square garden has sides of 12 metres. Posts are fixed all around its edge, one at every corner and one every 3 metres along each side. How many posts are needed?
hints: The posts go all the way around and come back to the start. In a closed loop, compare the number of posts with the number of gaps.
Find the distance all the way around the garden first. Then see how many 3-metre gaps fit into it.
A similar problem: a square of side 6 metres with a post every 2 metres has a distance around of 24 metres. That is 24 ÷ 2 = 12 gaps, and going around a loop needs exactly 12 posts.

stepByStep.text: Find the distance around the garden.
Find the number of 3-metre gaps.
Around a closed loop the last gap ends at the first post, so the number of posts equals the number of gaps.
16 posts are needed.

misconceptions.A: This counts 5 posts on each of the 4 sides. Each corner post then gets counted twice, once for each side it joins.
misconceptions.B: This adds 1 to the 16 gaps, as for a straight fence. Around a loop the last post is the first post again.
misconceptions.C: Excellent thinking! 48 metres around gives 16 gaps, and a loop needs 16 posts.
misconceptions.D: This counts only the 3 posts in the middle of each side. The 4 corner posts must be added.

G4A_COUNTING_014.questionText: Anu, Binu and Charu stand in a row for a photo. In how many different orders can they stand?
hints: Think place by place: who can stand first, then who can stand next, then who is left.
Suppose Anu stands first. Write the orders the other two can stand in. Then let Binu stand first, and then Charu.
A similar problem: two friends, Raj and Sam, can stand as Raj then Sam, or Sam then Raj. There are 2 choices for the first place and 1 for the second, so 2 × 1 = 2 orders.

stepByStep.text: Any of the 3 children can stand first.
Once the first is chosen, 2 children are left for the second place, and then 1 for the last place.
Multiply the choices.
They can stand in 6 different orders.

misconceptions.A: This is 3 × 3. After one child takes the first place, only 2 are left for the next place.
misconceptions.B: This counts only who stands first. For each first child, the other two can stand in 2 ways.
misconceptions.C: Some orders have been missed. List them by first child: each child can be first in 2 orders.
misconceptions.D: Well done! 3 choices, then 2, then 1 give 3 × 2 × 1 = 6 orders.

G4A_COUNTING_015.questionText: A window has 4 small square panes, arranged as 2 rows of 2. Counting squares of every size, how many squares can you see in the window?
hints: Squares can be of different sizes. Count the small ones, then look for bigger squares made by joining small ones.
Count the small panes first. Then ask whether all four panes together make a square.
A similar problem: a single square pane has just 1 square. A row of 2 panes has 2 small squares and no bigger square, because the two together make a long rectangle. So it has 2 squares.

stepByStep.text: There are 4 small square panes.
The whole window, made of all 4 panes, is 1 big square.
Add them.
There are 5 squares in the window.

misconceptions.A: You got it! 4 small squares and 1 big square make 5.
misconceptions.B: This counts only the small panes. The whole window is a square too.
misconceptions.C: This counts one square too many. Two panes side by side make a rectangle, not a square.
misconceptions.D: This counts the pairs of panes as squares. Two panes joined together are longer than they are tall, so they are rectangles.

G4A_COUNTING_016.questionText: 16 players enter a knockout badminton tournament. In every match the loser goes out and the winner plays on. How many matches are played to find the champion?
hints: Each match sends exactly one player out. Think about how many players must go out before one champion is left.
Count round by round: 16 players play 8 matches in the first round, leaving 8 players. Carry on until one player is left.
A similar problem: with 4 players, the first round has 2 matches and the final is 1 match. That is 2 + 1 = 3 matches, and 3 players have gone out.

stepByStep.text: Count the matches in each round.
Another way to see it: each match sends one player out, and 15 players must go out to leave 1 champion.
15 matches are played.

misconceptions.A: This is only the first round. The 8 winners must keep playing until one champion is left.
misconceptions.B: This matches the number of players. The champion never loses, so there is one match fewer.
misconceptions.C: Great thinking! 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 15 matches, one for each player who goes out.
misconceptions.D: This is the number of rounds. Each round has several matches, so add up the matches in all the rounds.

G4A_COUNTING_017.questionText: How many 2-digit numbers are multiples of 7?
hints: Find the smallest and the largest 2-digit multiples, then count how many multiples lie from one to the other.
The first multiple of 7 with two digits is 14, which is 7 × 2. Find the largest multiple of 7 that is below 100.
A similar problem: the 2-digit multiples of 20 are 20, 40, 60 and 80. They are 20 × 1 up to 20 × 4, so there are 4 of them.

stepByStep.text: The smallest 2-digit multiple of 7 is 14.
The largest 2-digit multiple of 7 is 98.
Count the multipliers from 2 to 14.
There are 13 two-digit multiples of 7.

misconceptions.A: This counts all multiples of 7 up to 98, including 7 itself. The number 7 has only one digit.
misconceptions.B: Well done! The multiples run from 7 × 2 to 7 × 14, which is 13 numbers.
misconceptions.C: This takes away one too many. From 7 × 2 to 7 × 14 there are 14 − 2 + 1 multipliers.
misconceptions.D: This counts too many. 7 × 15 = 105 has three digits, and 7 × 1 = 7 has one digit.

G4A_COUNTING_018.questionText: Sunita walks up from the 1st floor to the 4th floor and climbs 48 steps. Every floor has the same number of steps. How many steps would she climb from the 1st floor to the 7th floor?
hints: Going from one floor to another, count the flights of stairs climbed, not the floor numbers.
From the 1st floor to the 4th floor Sunita climbs 3 flights of stairs. Use this to find the steps in one flight.
A similar problem: going from the 1st floor to the 3rd floor is 2 flights. If that is 20 steps, each flight has 10 steps. From the 1st floor to the 5th floor is 4 flights, which is 40 steps.

stepByStep.text: From the 1st to the 4th floor there are 3 flights of stairs.
Find the steps in one flight.
From the 1st to the 7th floor there are 6 flights.
She would climb 96 steps.

misconceptions.A: This divides 48 by 4 and multiplies by 7. Starting on the 1st floor, reaching the 4th floor takes only 3 flights.
misconceptions.B: This uses 16 steps per flight, which is right, but counts 7 flights. From the 1st floor to the 7th there are 6 flights.
misconceptions.C: This uses 6 flights, which is right, but divides 48 by 4. The 48 steps are shared among 3 flights.
misconceptions.D: Excellent! Each flight has 16 steps, and 6 flights make 96 steps.

G4A_COUNTING_019.questionText: An ice-cream shop has 4 flavours: mango, chocolate, vanilla and strawberry. Rohan picks 2 different flavours for his cup. How many different pairs of flavours can he choose?
hints: A pair is the same whichever flavour is named first. List the pairs in an organised way so that none is repeated.
Start with mango and pair it with each of the other three. Then move to chocolate, pairing it only with flavours not used with it before.
A similar problem: from 3 fruits, apple, banana and cherry, the pairs are apple-banana, apple-cherry and banana-cherry. That is 2 + 1 = 3 pairs.

stepByStep.text: Mango can pair with chocolate, vanilla or strawberry: 3 pairs.
Chocolate can pair with vanilla or strawberry: 2 new pairs. Vanilla can pair with strawberry: 1 new pair.
Add the pairs.
Rohan can choose 6 different pairs.

misconceptions.A: You got it! 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 pairs.
misconceptions.B: This is 4 × 3, which counts mango with chocolate and chocolate with mango as two pairs. In a cup they are the same pair, so halve it.
misconceptions.C: This is 4 × 2. Try listing the pairs: mango goes with 3 others, chocolate with 2 new ones, vanilla with 1 new one.
misconceptions.D: This is the number of flavours. Each pair uses two flavours, so list the pairs to count them.

G4A_COUNTING_020.questionText: Using each of the digits 2, 0 and 5 exactly once, how many 3-digit numbers can be made?
hints: Look carefully at the hundreds place. One of these digits cannot go there.
A 3-digit number cannot begin with 0. So the hundreds digit is 2 or 5. List the numbers that begin with 2 first.
A similar problem: with the digits 0 and 7 used once each, 07 is just 7, so the only 2-digit number is 70. That is 1 number, not 2.

stepByStep.text: The hundreds digit can be 2 or 5, but not 0.
Starting with 2: 205 and 250. Starting with 5: 502 and 520.
Count them.
4 three-digit numbers can be made.

misconceptions.A: This is 3 × 2 × 1, which also counts 025 and 052. Those begin with 0, so they are really 2-digit numbers.
misconceptions.B: One number has been missed. For each of the two possible hundreds digits there are 2 numbers.
misconceptions.C: Well done! 205, 250, 502 and 520 are the 4 numbers.
misconceptions.D: This counts the choices for the hundreds place only. Each choice gives 2 different numbers.

G4A_COUNTING_021.questionText: A big triangle has two straight lines drawn from its top corner down to its base. These lines split it into 3 small triangles side by side. Counting triangles of every size, how many triangles are there in the figure?
hints: Count the small triangles first, then triangles made by joining neighbouring small ones.
There are 3 small triangles. Next, count the triangles made of 2 small triangles that are next to each other.
A similar problem: one line from the top corner to the base splits a triangle into 2 small triangles. Together with the big one, that makes 2 + 1 = 3 triangles.

stepByStep.text: There are 3 small triangles.
Two neighbouring small triangles together make a bigger triangle. This can be done in 2 ways: left with middle, and middle with right.
All three together make the 1 big triangle.
Add them all.
There are 6 triangles in the figure.

misconceptions.A: This counts only the small triangles. Neighbouring ones join to make bigger triangles too.
misconceptions.B: Great job! 3 small, 2 made of two parts, and 1 big one make 6.
misconceptions.C: One triangle has been missed. Check the two-part triangles: left with middle, and middle with right.
misconceptions.D: This counts the small triangles and the big one. Two neighbouring small triangles also make a triangle.

G4A_COUNTING_022.questionText: In a ticket queue at the railway station, Ravi is 8th from the front and Sana is 15th from the front. How many people stand between them?
hints: The people between them hold the positions after Ravi and before Sana. Neither Ravi nor Sana is counted.
List the positions between them, starting 9th, 10th, and stopping just before the 15th.
A similar problem: between the 3rd and the 6th person stand the 4th and the 5th. Subtracting gives 6 − 3 = 3, and taking 1 away gives 2 people.

stepByStep.text: The people between them are at positions 9, 10, 11, 12, 13 and 14.
A quick way: subtract the positions and take away 1.
6 people stand between them.

misconceptions.A: This is 15 − 8, which counts Sana as well. Take 1 away so that only the people in between are counted.
misconceptions.B: This adds the two positions. To find who is between them, look at the positions from 9th to 14th.
misconceptions.C: This counts both Ravi and Sana along with the people between them. Count only positions 9 to 14.
misconceptions.D: Excellent! Positions 9 to 14 hold 6 people.

G4A_COUNTING_023.questionText: How many numbers from 100 to 200, counting both 100 and 200, end in the digit 0?
hints: Numbers ending in 0 come once in every ten numbers. Be careful with both ends of the range.
List them: 100, 110, 120, and keep going. Check whether 200 belongs in your list.
A similar problem: from 10 to 50, the numbers ending in 0 are 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50. There are 4 jumps of ten, and 4 + 1 = 5 numbers.

stepByStep.text: From 100 to 200 there are 10 jumps of ten, and one more for the starting number.
There are 11 such numbers.

misconceptions.A: Well done! Ten jumps of ten from 100 to 200 give 11 numbers.
misconceptions.B: This counts the jumps of ten. Both 100 and 200 are in the range, so there is one more number than jumps.
misconceptions.C: This leaves out both 100 and 200. The question says to count both.
misconceptions.D: This counts too many. Only one number in every ten ends in 0.

G4A_COUNTING_024.questionText: The pages of a book are numbered starting from 1. In all, 129 digits were printed for the page numbers. How many pages does the book have?
hints: Work backwards. Take away the digits used by the one-digit pages, then see how many two-digit pages the remaining digits can number.
Pages 1 to 9 use 9 digits. Subtract these from 129 to find the digits left for pages with two digits.
A similar problem: a booklet uses 29 digits. Pages 1 to 9 use 9, leaving 20 digits. That numbers 20 ÷ 2 = 10 two-digit pages, so the booklet has 9 + 10 = 19 pages.

stepByStep.text: Pages 1 to 9 use 9 digits. Find the digits left.
Each page from 10 onwards uses 2 digits.
Add the one-digit pages and the two-digit pages.
The book has 69 pages.

misconceptions.A: This halves 129 as if every page used two digits. Pages 1 to 9 use only one digit each.
misconceptions.B: Excellent! 9 one-digit pages and 60 two-digit pages make 69 pages.
misconceptions.C: This is the number of two-digit pages only. The 9 one-digit pages must be added.
misconceptions.D: This adds 10 one-digit pages. The one-digit pages are 1 to 9, which is 9 pages.

G4A_COUNTING_025.questionText: How many 2-digit numbers have a tens digit that is bigger than the ones digit? For example, 72 is such a number but 27 is not.
hints: Work in an organised way: fix the tens digit and count the ones digits that are smaller than it. Look for a pattern.
With tens digit 1, the only smaller ones digit is 0, giving 10. With tens digit 2, the ones digit can be 0 or 1. Carry on up to tens digit 9.
A similar problem: among numbers from 10 to 39, tens digit 1 gives 1 number (10), tens digit 2 gives 2 numbers (20, 21) and tens digit 3 gives 3 numbers (30, 31, 32). That is 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 numbers.

stepByStep.text: Tens digit 1 gives 1 number (10). Tens digit 2 gives 2 numbers (20, 21). Tens digit 3 gives 3 numbers, and so on.
Tens digit 9 gives 9 numbers (90 to 98).
Add the counts.
There are 45 such numbers.

misconceptions.A: This leaves out the numbers with ones digit 0, such as 10, 20 and 30. Zero is smaller than every tens digit.
misconceptions.B: This adds 1 + 2 + 3 up to 10. The largest tens digit is 9, so the adding stops at 9.
misconceptions.C: Great thinking! 1 + 2 + 3 + ... + 9 = 45.
misconceptions.D: This only removes the 9 numbers with equal digits, like 11 and 22. Numbers such as 27, where the tens digit is smaller, must also be left out.

G4A_COUNTING_026.questionText: How many 3-digit numbers have digits that add up to 4?
hints: Work in an organised way: fix the hundreds digit, then count the ways the other two digits can make up the rest.
Start with hundreds digit 1. The other two digits must add up to 3. List these numbers, then move on to hundreds digit 2.
A similar problem: 3-digit numbers with digits adding to 2 are 101, 110 and 200. Hundreds digit 1 gives 2 numbers and hundreds digit 2 gives 1 number, so there are 3.

stepByStep.text: Hundreds digit 1: the other digits add to 3, giving 103, 112, 121 and 130. That is 4 numbers.
Hundreds digit 2: 202, 211 and 220. That is 3 numbers.
Hundreds digit 3: 301 and 310. Hundreds digit 4: 400. That is 2 numbers and 1 number.
Add the counts.
There are 10 such numbers.

misconceptions.A: One number has been missed. Check for 400, where the digits are 4, 0 and 0.
misconceptions.B: This also counts numbers like 013 and 004 that begin with 0. Those are not 3-digit numbers.
misconceptions.C: This only arranges the digits 1, 0 and 3. Other sets of digits also add up to 4, such as 1, 1, 2 and 2, 2, 0.
misconceptions.D: Well done! 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10 numbers.

G4A_COUNTING_027.questionText: A square board is divided into 9 small squares, in 3 rows of 3. Counting squares of every size, how many squares are there on the board?
hints: Squares come in different sizes. Count each size separately: the smallest, the middle size, and the largest.
There are 9 small squares. Now count the squares that are 2 small squares wide and 2 tall. One sits in each corner of the board.
A similar problem: a board with 2 rows of 2 has 4 small squares and 1 big square, so 4 + 1 = 5 squares.

stepByStep.text: There are 9 small squares.
Squares that are 2 wide and 2 tall: one fits in each corner of the board, so there are 4.
The whole board is 1 large square.
Add all the sizes.
There are 14 squares on the board.

misconceptions.A: You got it! 9 small, 4 middle-sized and 1 large make 14.
misconceptions.B: This counts only the small squares. Bigger squares are made by joining small ones.
misconceptions.C: This counts the small squares and the whole board. There are also 4 squares that are 2 wide and 2 tall.
misconceptions.D: This leaves out the whole board, which is the largest square of all.

G4A_COUNTING_028.questionText: Four small squares are joined in a single row to make a long strip. Counting rectangles of every size, with the small squares counted too, how many rectangles are there in the strip?
hints: A rectangle in the strip is made of 1, 2, 3 or 4 neighbouring squares. Count each length separately.
There are 4 rectangles made of 1 square. Next, count the rectangles made of 2 neighbouring squares: first with second, second with third, and so on.
A similar problem: a strip of 3 squares has 3 rectangles of one square, 2 of two squares and 1 of three squares. That is 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 rectangles.

stepByStep.text: Rectangles made of 1 square: 4.
Rectangles made of 2 neighbouring squares: 3. Made of 3 neighbouring squares: 2.
The whole strip of 4 squares: 1.
Add them.
There are 10 rectangles in the strip.

misconceptions.A: This counts the single squares and the pairs. Rectangles made of 3 squares and the whole strip count too.
misconceptions.B: Excellent! 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10 rectangles.
misconceptions.C: This counts only the small squares. Neighbouring squares join to make longer rectangles.
misconceptions.D: This leaves out the whole strip, which is the longest rectangle.

G4A_COUNTING_029.questionText: At a birthday party, every child gave one card to every other child. In all, 30 cards were given. How many children were at the party?
hints: Each child gives a card to everyone except themselves. So the total is the number of children times one less than that number.
Try a small party: with 3 children, each gives 2 cards. Work out the total for 4 children, then 5, and keep going until you reach 30.
A similar problem: if 12 cards were given, try 4 children. Each gives 3 cards, and 4 × 3 = 12. So there were 4 children.

stepByStep.text: If there are some children, each one gives a card to all the others, which is one fewer than the number of children.
Look for two numbers next to each other that multiply to 30.
So 6 children each gave 5 cards.
There were 6 children at the party.

misconceptions.A: This is the number of cards each child gave. The number of children is one more than that.
misconceptions.B: This halves 30, as for handshakes. A card goes one way only, so every card is counted just once.
misconceptions.C: Well done! 6 children giving 5 cards each makes 30 cards.
misconceptions.D: With 10 children, each would give 9 cards, making 90 cards. Look for two neighbouring numbers that multiply to 30.

G4A_COUNTING_030.questionText: Using the digits 0, 1, 2 and 3, with no digit repeated in a number, how many 3-digit even numbers can be made?
hints: Two places need care: the ones place must make the number even, and the hundreds place cannot be 0. Split into cases by the last digit.
An even number here ends in 0 or 2. First count the numbers that end in 0. The other two places are filled from 1, 2 and 3.
A similar problem: 2-digit even numbers from the digits 0, 3 and 4 with no repeats. Ending in 0: 30 and 40. Ending in 4: only 34, because 04 is not a 2-digit number. That is 2 + 1 = 3 numbers.

stepByStep.text: Ending in 0: the hundreds digit has 3 choices (1, 2 or 3) and the tens digit then has 2 choices.
Ending in 2: the hundreds digit can only be 1 or 3, and the tens digit then has 2 choices.
Add the two cases.
10 such numbers can be made.

misconceptions.A: This allows 0 in the hundreds place for numbers ending in 2, such as 012 and 032. Those are not 3-digit numbers.
misconceptions.B: Some numbers ending in 2 have been missed. They are 102, 132, 302 and 312.
misconceptions.C: This is the count of all 3-digit numbers that can be made. Only those ending in 0 or 2 are even.
misconceptions.D: Great job! 6 numbers end in 0 and 4 end in 2, making 10.

G4A_COUNTING_031.questionText: A temple bell takes 6 seconds to ring 4 times, measured from the first ring to the last ring. The rings are evenly spaced. How many seconds does it take to ring 10 times?
hints: The time is spent in the gaps between the rings, not on the rings themselves. Count the gaps.
Between 4 rings there are 3 gaps. Use this to find how long one gap lasts.
A similar problem: a bell takes 8 seconds to ring 3 times. That is 2 gaps, so each gap is 4 seconds. Ringing 6 times has 5 gaps, which takes 5 × 4 = 20 seconds.

stepByStep.text: 4 rings have 3 gaps between them. Find the length of one gap.
10 rings have 9 gaps between them.
Multiply the gaps by the length of each gap.
It takes 18 seconds to ring 10 times.

misconceptions.A: This divides 6 seconds by 4 rings. The time is taken by the 3 gaps between the rings, so each gap is 2 seconds.
misconceptions.B: Excellent thinking! 9 gaps of 2 seconds each take 18 seconds.
misconceptions.C: This uses 2 seconds per gap, which is right, but counts 10 gaps. Between 10 rings there are only 9 gaps.
misconceptions.D: This doubles the 6 seconds. Count the gaps instead: 4 rings have 3 gaps and 10 rings have 9 gaps.

G4A_COUNTING_032.questionText: Children stand in a row. Tara is 9th from the left and Uma is 6th from the right. They swap places, and now Tara is 15th from the left. How many children are in the row?
hints: After the swap, Tara stands exactly where Uma stood. So you know one spot's position from both ends.
Uma's old spot is 6th from the right. After the swap Tara is in that spot, and it is 15th from the left. Use both positions for this one spot.
A similar problem: a spot is 4th from the left and 3rd from the right. There are 3 children to its left and 2 to its right, so the row has 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 children.

stepByStep.text: After swapping, Tara stands in Uma's old spot. That spot is 15th from the left and 6th from the right.
Add the two positions and take away 1, because the spot is counted twice.
There are 20 children in the row.

misconceptions.A: This adds 15 and 6 but counts the child in that spot twice. Take 1 away.
misconceptions.B: This is Tara's new position from the left. There are still 5 more children to her right.
misconceptions.C: Well done! The same spot is 15th from the left and 6th from the right, so 15 + 6 − 1 = 20.
misconceptions.D: This adds Tara's old and new positions, 9 and 15. Use the two positions of the same spot instead: 15th from the left and 6th from the right.

G4A_COUNTING_033.questionText: Aman writes all the numbers from 1 to 100. How many times does he write the digit 1?
hints: Count place by place: how often the digit is in the ones place, in the tens place, and in the hundreds place.
In the ones place the digit 1 appears in 1, 11, 21, and so on up to 91. Count these first, then look at the tens place.
A similar problem: from 1 to 50, the digit 4 is in the ones place 5 times (4, 14, 24, 34, 44) and in the tens place 10 times (40 to 49). That makes 15 times.

stepByStep.text: Tens place: 10, 11, 12, and so on up to 19.
Hundreds place: only in 100.
Add them.
Aman writes the digit 1 a total of 21 times.

misconceptions.A: Great job! 10 in the ones place, 10 in the tens place and 1 in the number 100 make 21.
misconceptions.B: This leaves out the 1 in 100. The number 100 is in the list too.
misconceptions.C: This counts 11 only once and leaves out 100. The number 11 has two 1s, and both are written.
misconceptions.D: This counts only the ones place and the 1 in 100. The numbers 10 to 19 each have a 1 in the tens place as well.

G4A_COUNTING_034.questionText: How many numbers from 1 to 60 can be divided exactly by 2 or by 3, or by both?
hints: Some numbers can be divided by both 2 and 3. If you count the two groups and add, those numbers get counted twice.
Count the multiples of 2 up to 60, and the multiples of 3 up to 60. Then find how many numbers are in both lists.
A similar problem: from 1 to 12 there are 6 multiples of 2 and 4 multiples of 3. The numbers 6 and 12 are in both lists. So the count is 6 + 4 − 2 = 8.

stepByStep.text: Count the multiples of 2 and the multiples of 3.
Numbers in both lists are the multiples of 6.
Add the two lists and take away the numbers counted twice.
There are 40 such numbers.

misconceptions.A: This adds 30 and 20, which counts the multiples of 6 twice. Take away those 10 numbers.
misconceptions.B: This counts only the multiples of 2. Odd multiples of 3, such as 3, 9 and 15, belong too.
misconceptions.C: This is how many numbers are divisible by both 2 and 3. The question also wants numbers divisible by just one of them.
misconceptions.D: Excellent! 30 + 20 − 10 = 40.

G4A_COUNTING_035.questionText: A flag has 3 stripes in a row. Each stripe is painted red, green or blue. Stripes that touch each other must be different colours. How many different flags can be made?
hints: Choose the colours stripe by stripe. Read the rule with care: only stripes that touch must differ.
The first stripe can be any of the 3 colours. The second stripe must differ from the first. Think about how many colours the third stripe can take.
A similar problem: a flag with 2 stripes and 3 colours, where the stripes must differ. The first stripe has 3 choices and the second has 2, so there are 3 × 2 = 6 flags.

stepByStep.text: The first stripe can be any of 3 colours.
The second stripe touches the first, so it has 2 choices.
The third stripe touches only the second, so it also has 2 choices. It may match the first stripe.
Multiply the choices.
12 different flags can be made.

misconceptions.A: You got it! 3 × 2 × 2 = 12 flags.
misconceptions.B: This makes all three stripes different. The first and third stripes do not touch, so they may be the same colour.
misconceptions.C: This is 3 × 3 × 3, which lets touching stripes share a colour. The second and third stripes each have only 2 choices.
misconceptions.D: This is 3 × 3. Count the choices for each stripe in turn: 3, then 2, then 2.

G4A_PUZZLES_001.questionText:
In this magic square, every row, every column and both diagonals add up to the same total.
Row 1: 9, 2, 7
Row 2: 4, 6, 8
Row 3: 5, ?, 3
Which number is missing?
hints: In a magic square every line has the same total. Find that total from a line with no number missing.
Add the numbers in Row 1 to find the magic total. Then see what Row 3 still needs.
A similar problem: a magic square has rows 8, 1, 6 and 3, 5, 7 and 4, ?, 2. Row 1 adds to 15. Row 3 has 4 + 2 = 6, so the missing number is 15 − 6 = 9.

stepByStep.text: Find the magic total from Row 1.
Row 3 must also add up to 18.
The missing number is 10.

misconceptions.A: With 9, Row 3 would add up to 17, one short of the magic total of 18.
misconceptions.B: Great job! 5 + 10 + 3 = 18, the same as every other line.
misconceptions.C: With 11, Row 3 would add up to 19, one more than the magic total of 18.
misconceptions.D: With 8, Row 3 would add up to only 16. Find the total of Row 1 first, then see what Row 3 needs.

G4A_PUZZLES_002.questionText: I am a 2-digit number. My tens digit is 4. My two digits add up to 11. Which number am I?
hints: Use one clue at a time. The first clue fixes one digit, and the second clue gives the other.
The tens digit is 4. What must the ones digit be so that the two digits add up to 11?
A similar problem: a 2-digit number has tens digit 3 and its digits add up to 8. The ones digit is 8 − 3 = 5, so the number is 35.

stepByStep.text: The tens digit is 4.
Find the ones digit.
The number is 47.

misconceptions.A: Well done! The tens digit is 4 and 4 + 7 = 11.
misconceptions.B: The digits do add up to 11, but here 4 is the ones digit. The clue says 4 is the tens digit.
misconceptions.C: This joins the tens digit 4 with the first digit of 11. The ones digit should be 11 − 4.
misconceptions.D: These digits add up to 11, but the tens digit is 5. The clue says the tens digit is 4.

G4A_PUZZLES_003.questionText: In the sum 4P + 25 = 71, the letter P stands for one digit, so 4P is a two-digit number. Which digit is P?
hints: A missing number in an addition can be found by working backwards with subtraction.
Find the number that must be added to 25 to make 71. Its ones digit is P.
A similar problem: in 3R + 14 = 52, the first number is 52 − 14 = 38. So 3R is 38 and R is 8.

stepByStep.text: Work backwards to find the two-digit number 4P.
So 4P is 46.
P is 6.

misconceptions.A: This is the tens digit of 46. The letter P is in the ones place.
misconceptions.B: This is the ones digit of 25. Subtract 25 from 71 to find the number 4P.
misconceptions.C: You got it! 46 + 25 = 71, so P is 6.
misconceptions.D: Try it: 47 + 25 = 72, which is one too many. Subtract 25 from 71 to find 4P.

G4A_PUZZLES_004.questionText: In a picture puzzle, a star plus a star makes 14. A star plus a moon makes 10. What is the moon worth?
hints: Start with the clue that has only one kind of shape. Once you know that shape, use it in the other clue.
Two stars make 14. Find what one star is worth.
A similar problem: a sun plus a sun makes 12, so a sun is 6. A sun plus a cloud makes 8, so the cloud is 8 − 6 = 2.

stepByStep.text: Two equal stars make 14, so find one star.
A star plus a moon makes 10.
The moon is worth 3.

misconceptions.A: This is what the star is worth. Use it in the second clue to find the moon.
misconceptions.B: This is 14 − 10. First halve 14 to find the star, then take the star away from 10.
misconceptions.C: This halves 10, as if the star and the moon were equal. The star is worth 7, so the moon is 10 − 7.
misconceptions.D: Excellent! The star is 7, and 7 + 3 = 10.

G4A_PUZZLES_005.questionText: Amit is taller than Bina. Bina is taller than Chetan. Divya is shorter than Chetan. Who is the tallest of the four?
hints: Put the children in order of height, using one clue at a time.
Write the names in a line from tallest to shortest. Start with Amit and Bina, then fit Chetan in.
A similar problem: Ria is taller than Sam, and Sam is taller than Tia. From tallest to shortest the order is Ria, Sam, Tia, so Ria is the tallest.

stepByStep.text: Amit is taller than Bina, and Bina is taller than Chetan. So the order is Amit, Bina, Chetan.
Divya is shorter than Chetan, so she comes last: Amit, Bina, Chetan, Divya.
The tallest is Amit.

misconceptions.A: Bina is taller than Chetan, but the first clue says Amit is taller than Bina.
misconceptions.B: Chetan is taller than Divya only. Bina and Amit are both taller than Chetan.
misconceptions.C: Well done! From tallest to shortest the order is Amit, Bina, Chetan, Divya.
misconceptions.D: Divya is shorter than Chetan, so she is the shortest of the four.

G4A_PUZZLES_006.questionText: In a magic square, every row adds up to 21. One row has the numbers 4 and 11 and one missing number. What is the missing number?
hints: The three numbers in the row must add up to the magic total. Two of them are known.
Add 4 and 11. Then find how much more is needed to reach 21.
A similar problem: a row must add up to 15 and has 2 and 9. Those make 11, so the missing number is 15 − 11 = 4.

stepByStep.text: Add the two numbers you know.
Find what is needed to reach 21.
The missing number is 6.

misconceptions.A: Great job! 4 + 11 + 6 = 21.
misconceptions.B: With 7 the row would add up to 22. Check the subtraction 21 − 15.
misconceptions.C: This is 4 + 11, the total of the two known numbers. Take it away from 21 to find the missing one.
misconceptions.D: This adds all three numbers, 4 + 11 + 21. The 21 is the total of the row, so subtract instead.

G4A_PUZZLES_007.questionText: Two signs are missing: 8 __ 4 __ 2 = 10. Which two signs, in this order, make it true?
hints: Try each pair of signs in turn and work out the answer it gives.
The answer 10 is a little more than 8. Think about which first sign makes 8 bigger, and what the second sign must then do.
A similar problem: for 9 __ 3 __ 2 = 8, the answer is a little less than 9, so try minus first: 9 − 3 = 6. Then 6 must become 8, so add 2. The signs there are minus, then plus.

stepByStep.text: Try plus first.
Now 12 must become 10, so subtract 2.
The signs are plus, then minus.

misconceptions.A: This gives 8 − 4 + 2 = 6, which is less than 10.
misconceptions.B: This gives 8 + 4 + 2 = 14, which is more than 10.
misconceptions.C: This gives 8 × 4 − 2 = 30, which is far more than 10.
misconceptions.D: You got it! 8 + 4 − 2 = 10.

G4A_PUZZLES_008.questionText: A palindrome number reads the same forwards and backwards, like 353. Which of these is a palindrome number?
hints: Read each number from right to left and compare it with the number read from left to right.
In a 4-digit palindrome, the first digit matches the last digit and the second digit matches the third. Check each number for this.
A similar problem: 4004 read backwards is 4004, so it is a palindrome. 4040 read backwards is 0404, so it is not.

stepByStep.text: Write each number backwards: 1212 becomes 2121, 1122 becomes 2211, and 2121 becomes 1212. These all change.
1221 written backwards is still 1221.
The palindrome number is 1221.

misconceptions.A: Read backwards, this becomes 2121, which is a different number.
misconceptions.B: Excellent! The first and last digits match, and the two middle digits match.
misconceptions.C: Read backwards, this becomes 2211, which is a different number.
misconceptions.D: Read backwards, this becomes 1212, which is a different number.

G4A_PUZZLES_009.questionText:
In this magic square, every row, every column and both diagonals add up to the same total.
Row 1: 16, 2, P
Row 2: 6, Q, 14
Row 3: 8, 18, 4
What is P + Q?
hints: Find the magic total from a line that has no letter in it. Then use it on the lines that have a letter.
Row 3 has no letter. Add its numbers to find the magic total, then look at Row 1.
A similar problem: a magic square has rows 8, 1, R and 3, S, 7 and 4, 9, 2. Row 3 adds to 15. So R = 15 − 8 − 1 = 6 and S = 15 − 3 − 7 = 5, and R + S = 11.

stepByStep.text: Find the magic total from Row 3.
Use Row 1 to find P.
Use Row 2 to find Q.
Add P and Q.

misconceptions.A: This is double P. Find Q from Row 2 as well: it is 30 − 6 − 14.
misconceptions.B: This is the magic total of each line. The question asks for P + Q.
misconceptions.C: This is double Q. Find P from Row 1 as well: it is 30 − 16 − 2.
misconceptions.D: Well done! P is 12 and Q is 10, so P + Q = 22.

G4A_PUZZLES_010.questionText: In the sum 3P + P8 = 82, the letter P stands for the same digit both times. 3P and P8 are two-digit numbers. Which digit is P?
hints: Look at the ones column first. The ones digits must add up to a number that ends in the ones digit of the answer.
In the ones column, P + 8 must end in 2. Which digit added to 8 gives a number ending in 2?
A similar problem: in 1R + R6 = 49, the ones column says R + 6 must end in 9, so R is 3. Check the whole sum: 13 + 36 = 49. It is true, so R is 3.

stepByStep.text: In the ones column, P + 8 must end in 2. Since 4 + 8 = 12, P could be 4.
Check the whole sum with P as 4.
The sum is true, so P is 4.

misconceptions.A: Great thinking! 34 + 48 = 82.
misconceptions.B: Try it: 35 + 58 = 93, which is more than 82. Look at the ones column: P + 8 must end in 2.
misconceptions.C: Try it: 33 + 38 = 71, which is less than 82. Look at the ones column: P + 8 must end in 2.
misconceptions.D: This is 8 − 2 from the ones column. The ones digits are added, so P + 8 must end in 2.

G4A_PUZZLES_011.questionText: P and Q are digits. The two-digit numbers PQ and QP add up to 77, and P is 1 more than Q. What is the number PQ?
hints: When a two-digit number is added to its reverse, each column adds the same two digits. Find what the two digits add up to.
In the ones column, Q + P must give 7. Now find two digits that add up to 7 where one is 1 more than the other.
A similar problem: RS + SR = 99 and R is 1 more than S. The digits add up to 9, so they are 5 and 4. R is the bigger one, so RS is 54.

stepByStep.text: In each column the digits P and Q are added, and the total is 77, so P + Q = 7.
Two digits that add up to 7 and differ by 1 are 4 and 3.
P is the bigger digit, so P is 4 and Q is 3.
Check the sum.
The number PQ is 43.

misconceptions.A: These are the right digits, but here the first digit is smaller. P is 1 more than Q, so P must be 4.
misconceptions.B: Excellent! 43 + 34 = 77, and 4 is 1 more than 3.
misconceptions.C: 52 + 25 = 77, but 5 is 3 more than 2. P should be just 1 more than Q.
misconceptions.D: 61 + 16 = 77, but 6 is 5 more than 1. P should be just 1 more than Q.

G4A_PUZZLES_012.questionText: I think of a number. I double it and then add 3. The answer is 17. What number did I think of?
hints: Work backwards from the answer, undoing each step in the opposite order.
The last thing done was adding 3. Undo that first by taking 3 away from 17.
A similar problem: I double a number and add 5 to get 25. Undo the adding: 25 − 5 = 20. Undo the doubling: 20 ÷ 2 = 10. The number was 10.

stepByStep.text: Undo the adding of 3.
Undo the doubling.
Check.
The number was 7.

misconceptions.A: This adds 3 to 17 and then halves. To undo adding 3, take 3 away.
misconceptions.B: This undoes the adding but stops there. The doubling must be undone too, by halving 14.
misconceptions.C: Well done! 7 doubled is 14, and 14 + 3 = 17.
misconceptions.D: This doubles 17 and adds 3. That repeats the steps instead of undoing them.

G4A_PUZZLES_013.questionText: Isha, Jay, Kiran and Lata each have one pet: a cat, a dog, a parrot and a rabbit. Jay has the cat. Kiran has the rabbit. Isha does not have the dog. Which pet does Lata have?
hints: Cross off the pets that are already taken, then use the last clue to decide between the pets that are left.
Jay and Kiran have the cat and the rabbit. Which two pets are left for Isha and Lata?
A similar problem: Om, Pia and Raj have a ball, a kite and a top. Om has the ball. Pia does not have the kite. So Pia has the top, and Raj has the kite.

stepByStep.text: Jay has the cat and Kiran has the rabbit, so the dog and the parrot are left for Isha and Lata.
Isha does not have the dog, so Isha has the parrot.
The only pet left for Lata is the dog.

misconceptions.A: The parrot belongs to Isha, because Isha does not have the dog and the other pets are taken.
misconceptions.B: The first clue says that Jay has the cat.
misconceptions.C: The second clue says that Kiran has the rabbit.
misconceptions.D: Great thinking! The dog and the parrot were left, Isha took the parrot, so Lata has the dog.

G4A_PUZZLES_014.questionText: I am a 2-digit number less than 50. I am a multiple of 7. My digits add up to 6. Which number am I?
hints: Use the clue that leaves the fewest numbers first, list them, then test each with the other clue.
List the 2-digit multiples of 7 that are less than 50. Then add the digits of each one.
A similar problem: a 2-digit multiple of 9 less than 40 whose digits differ by 5. The multiples are 18, 27 and 36. Only 27 has digits that differ by 5, so the number is 27.

stepByStep.text: The 2-digit multiples of 7 below 50 are 14, 21, 28, 35, 42 and 49.
Their digit totals are 5, 3, 10, 8, 6 and 13.
Only one has digits adding up to 6. The number is 42.

misconceptions.A: You got it! 42 = 7 × 6, and 4 + 2 = 6.
misconceptions.B: The digits add up to 6, but 24 is not a multiple of 7. Try the same digits the other way round.
misconceptions.C: 35 is a multiple of 7, but its digits add up to 8.
misconceptions.D: The digits add up to 6, but 33 is not in the table of 7.

G4A_PUZZLES_015.questionText: A pencil and an eraser together cost ₹12. Two pencils and an eraser together cost ₹19. How much does the eraser cost?
hints: Compare the two purchases. Look at what the second one has that the first one does not.
The second purchase has exactly one more pencil than the first. Find how much more it costs.
A similar problem: a pen and a cap cost ₹10, and two pens and a cap cost ₹16. The extra pen costs 16 − 10 = ₹6, so the cap costs 10 − 6 = ₹4.

stepByStep.text: The second purchase has one extra pencil. Find its cost.
A pencil and an eraser cost ₹12 together.
The eraser costs ₹5.

misconceptions.A: This is the cost of the pencil. Take it away from ₹12 to find the eraser.
misconceptions.B: Well done! The pencil costs ₹7, so the eraser costs 12 − 7 = ₹5.
misconceptions.C: This halves ₹12, as if the pencil and the eraser cost the same. The extra pencil in the second purchase shows a pencil costs ₹7.
misconceptions.D: The pencil costs ₹7. Check the subtraction 12 − 7 once more.

G4A_PUZZLES_016.questionText: The three-digit number 2R5 is multiplied by 3 and the answer is 735. R stands for one digit. Which digit is R?
hints: A multiplication can be undone by division. Find the whole number first, then read off the hidden digit.
Divide 735 by 3 to find the number 2R5.
A similar problem: 1R4 × 2 = 368. Dividing, 368 ÷ 2 = 184, so 1R4 is 184 and R is 8.

stepByStep.text: Undo the multiplication.
So 2R5 is 245, and R is the tens digit.
R is 4.

misconceptions.A: This is the tens digit of 735, the answer. R is the tens digit of the number being multiplied, which is 735 ÷ 3.
misconceptions.B: This is the ones digit of 245. R is in the tens place.
misconceptions.C: Excellent! 245 × 3 = 735, so R is 4.
misconceptions.D: This is the hundreds digit of 245. R is in the tens place.

G4A_PUZZLES_017.questionText: Five children ran a race. Dev finished after Farah but before Esha. Hari finished between Dev and Esha. Gita finished last. Who came second?
hints: Draw five blanks for the five places and fit the children in, one clue at a time.
Start with the first clue: Farah is ahead of Dev, and Dev is ahead of Esha. Then find where Hari fits.
A similar problem: in a race of three, Mina finished before Nitu, and Omar finished before Mina. The order is Omar, Mina, Nitu, so Mina came second.

stepByStep.text: From the first clue, the order is Farah, then Dev, then Esha.
Hari is between Dev and Esha: Farah, Dev, Hari, Esha.
Gita is last: Farah, Dev, Hari, Esha, Gita.
The child who came second is Dev.

misconceptions.A: Farah finished ahead of Dev and everyone else, so Farah came first.
misconceptions.B: Hari finished after Dev, so Hari came third.
misconceptions.C: Esha finished after Dev and Hari, so Esha came fourth.
misconceptions.D: Great job! The order is Farah, Dev, Hari, Esha, Gita.

G4A_PUZZLES_018.questionText: On a dice, the dots on opposite faces always add up to 7. Neha can see three faces showing 1, 2 and 3. What is the total of the dots on the three faces she cannot see?
hints: Each face Neha can see has a hidden face opposite it. Use the rule for opposite faces.
The face opposite 1 must make 7 with it. Find that face, then do the same for 2 and 3.
A similar problem: if the faces seen are 2, 4 and 6, the hidden faces are 7 − 2 = 5, 7 − 4 = 3 and 7 − 6 = 1. Their total is 5 + 3 + 1 = 9.

stepByStep.text: Find the face opposite each face she can see.
Add the hidden faces.
The hidden faces total 15.

misconceptions.A: This takes 3 away from 21, the total of all six faces. Take away the dots Neha can see, which are 1 + 2 + 3.
misconceptions.B: Well done! The hidden faces are 6, 5 and 4, and 6 + 5 + 4 = 15.
misconceptions.C: This is the total of the faces Neha can see. The hidden faces are the ones opposite them.
misconceptions.D: This is the total of all six faces. Take away the faces Neha can see.

G4A_PUZZLES_019.questionText:
In this magic square, every row, every column and both diagonals add up to the same total. Some boxes are blank.
Row 1: P, 16, 9
Row 2: blank, 11, blank
Row 3: 13, blank, Q
What is the value of Q?
hints: Look for a line of three boxes that has no blank and no letter. It may be a diagonal. That line gives the magic total.
The diagonal from the top right corner to the bottom left corner is 9, 11, 13. Add these to find the magic total, then use Row 1 to find P.
A similar problem: Row 1 is R, 7, 6. Row 2 is blank, 5, blank. Row 3 is 4, blank, S. The diagonal 6, 5, 4 gives a total of 15. So R = 15 − 7 − 6 = 2, and the other diagonal gives S = 15 − 2 − 5 = 8.

stepByStep.text: The diagonal 9, 11, 13 is complete. Find the magic total.
Use Row 1 to find P.
The other diagonal is P, 11, Q. Use it to find Q.
Q is 14.

misconceptions.A: This is the value of P. Use the diagonal P, 11, Q to find Q.
misconceptions.B: Excellent thinking! The total is 33, P is 8, and 8 + 11 + 14 = 33.
misconceptions.C: This is the number in the first box of Row 2. Q comes from the diagonal P, 11, Q.
misconceptions.D: This is the number in the middle box of Row 3. Q comes from the diagonal P, 11, Q.

G4A_PUZZLES_020.questionText: A two-digit number ending in 3 is multiplied by a two-digit number ending in 4. Which of these can be the product?
hints: You cannot find the exact numbers, so test each choice instead. Check its last digit, and check whether its size is possible.
The last digit of the product comes from 3 × 4. Which choices end in the right digit? Then think about the smallest and largest products possible.

A similar problem: a two-digit number ending in 2 times a two-digit number ending in 6 must end in 2, because 2 × 6 = 12. The smallest such product is 12 × 16 = 192 and the largest is 92 × 96 = 8832. So 1472 is possible (it is 32 × 46), but 9992 is too big.

stepByStep.text: Find the last digit of the product.
So the product ends in 2. This rules out 1037.
Find the smallest and largest possible products.
172 is smaller than 182 and 9872 is bigger than 8742, so neither is possible.
The one left is possible.
The product can be 1032.

misconceptions.A: This ends in 7, which comes from adding 3 and 4. In a product the last digit comes from 3 × 4 = 12, so it must be 2.
misconceptions.B: This ends in 2, but it is too big. The largest possible product is 93 × 94 = 8742.
misconceptions.C: Great thinking! It ends in 2 and lies between 182 and 8742. In fact 43 × 24 = 1032.
misconceptions.D: This ends in 2, but it is too small. The smallest possible product is 13 × 14 = 182.

G4A_PUZZLES_021.questionText: In the sum P + P + P = QP, the letters P and Q stand for two different digits, and QP is a two-digit number. What is P + Q?
hints: Look at the ones digit. Three times the digit P gives a number that ends in P again. Very few digits can do that.
Test the digits one by one: 3 × 1 = 3, 3 × 2 = 6, and so on. Look for a two-digit answer whose ones digit is the digit you started with.
A similar problem: R + R + R + R + R + R = 2R, where 2R is a two-digit number that starts with 2. Six times R must end in R and lie in the twenties. Since 6 × 4 = 24, R is 4.

stepByStep.text: Three times P must end in the digit P and must be a two-digit number.
Testing the digits, only 5 works.
So P is 5 and QP is 15, which makes Q equal to 1.
Add the two digits.

misconceptions.A: This is P alone. The sum 5 + 5 + 5 = 15 shows that Q is 1, so add it on.
misconceptions.B: This is the two-digit number QP. The question asks for the digits P and Q added together.
misconceptions.C: P is 5, and 5 + 5 + 5 = 15, so Q is 1 and not 2.
misconceptions.D: Excellent! 5 + 5 + 5 = 15, so P is 5, Q is 1, and 5 + 1 = 6.

G4A_PUZZLES_022.questionText: I am a 3-digit number. My hundreds digit is double my ones digit. My tens digit equals my hundreds digit plus my ones digit. My three digits add up to 12. Which number am I?
hints: Every digit can be described using the ones digit. Try small values for the ones digit and see which one fits all the clues.
If the ones digit is 1, the hundreds digit is 2 and the tens digit is 2 + 1 = 3. Do these digits add up to 12? If not, try ones digit 2.

A similar problem: the hundreds digit is three times the ones digit, the tens digit is their total, and the digits add up to 8. With ones digit 1, the hundreds digit is 3 and the tens digit is 4. Since 3 + 4 + 1 = 8, the number is 341.

stepByStep.text: Try ones digit 1: hundreds digit 2, tens digit 3. The digits add up to 6, which is too small.
Try ones digit 2: hundreds digit 4, tens digit 6.
All the clues fit.
The number is 462.

misconceptions.A: Well done! 4 is double 2, 6 = 4 + 2, and 4 + 6 + 2 = 12.
misconceptions.B: These are the right digits in reverse order. The hundreds digit must be double the ones digit, so 4 goes in the hundreds place.
misconceptions.C: Here the hundreds digit 6 is three times the ones digit 2. It should be double, and the tens digit should be the total of the other two.
misconceptions.D: This fits the first two clues, but its digits add up to only 6. They must add up to 12.

G4A_PUZZLES_023.questionText: A farmer has hens and goats. Together they have 10 heads and 28 legs. How many goats does the farmer have?
hints: Each animal has one head, so you know how many animals there are. Suppose they were all hens and see how many legs are missing.
There are 10 animals. If all 10 were hens, how many legs would there be? Compare that with 28.
A similar problem: 5 heads and 14 legs. If all 5 were hens there would be 10 legs. The 4 extra legs come from goats, which have 2 more legs each, so there are 4 ÷ 2 = 2 goats.

stepByStep.text: There are 10 animals. Suppose all were hens with 2 legs each.
Find the extra legs.
Each goat has 2 more legs than a hen.
Check with 4 goats and 6 hens.
The farmer has 4 goats.

misconceptions.A: This is the number of hens. The question asks for the goats.
misconceptions.B: You got it! 4 goats and 6 hens have 16 + 12 = 28 legs and 10 heads.
misconceptions.C: This divides 28 legs by 4, as if every animal were a goat. There would then be only 7 heads, not 10.
misconceptions.D: This divides 28 legs by 2, as if every animal were a hen. There are only 10 animals in all.

G4A_PUZZLES_024.questionText: The digits of a 2-digit number add up to 9. When the two digits swap places, the new number is 27 more than the first number. What is the first number?
hints: List the 2-digit numbers that fit the first clue. Then test each one with the second clue.
Numbers whose digits add up to 9 are 18, 27, and so on. The swapped number is bigger, so the first number has the smaller digit in the tens place. Test each by swapping and subtracting.
A similar problem: the digits add up to 7 and the swapped number is 9 more. Test 16: 61 − 16 = 45. Test 25: 52 − 25 = 27. Test 34: 43 − 34 = 9. So the number is 34.

stepByStep.text: Numbers with digits adding up to 9 and a smaller tens digit are 18, 27, 36 and 45.
Swap the digits of each and subtract.
Only one of them grows by 27 when its digits swap.
The first number is 36.

misconceptions.A: This is the number after the swap. The first number is the smaller one, with the digits the other way round.
misconceptions.B: This is how much bigger the new number is. Testing 27 itself gives 72 − 27 = 45, which is not the right gap.
misconceptions.C: Excellent! 63 − 36 = 27, and 3 + 6 = 9.
misconceptions.D: Swapping gives 54, which is only 9 more than 45. The new number must be 27 more.

G4A_PUZZLES_025.questionText: A laddoo is hidden in one of three boxes. Each box has a label. The label on Box 1 says: The laddoo is in this box. The label on Box 2 says: The laddoo is not in this box. The label on Box 3 says: The laddoo is not in Box 1. Only one of the three labels is true. Where is the laddoo?
hints: Suppose the laddoo is in one box, and count how many labels would then be true. Do this for each box in turn.
Suppose the laddoo is in Box 1. Is the label on Box 1 true? Is the label on Box 2 true? Count the true labels and compare with what the question says.

A similar problem: a coin is in one of two tins, and you are told that both labels are untrue. The label on Tin 1 says: The coin is in Tin 2. The label on Tin 2 says: The coin is in this tin. If the coin were in Tin 2, both labels would be true. If it is in Tin 1, both labels are untrue, just as you were told. So the coin is in Tin 1.

stepByStep.text: If the laddoo is in Box 1: the labels on Box 1 and Box 2 are both true. That is two true labels, so this does not fit.
If the laddoo is in Box 3: the labels on Box 2 and Box 3 are both true. That is two true labels again.
If the laddoo is in Box 2: the label on Box 1 is untrue, the label on Box 2 is untrue, and the label on Box 3 is true. Exactly one label is true.
The laddoo is in Box 2.

misconceptions.A: If the laddoo were in Box 1, the labels on Box 1 and Box 2 would both be true. Only one label may be true.
misconceptions.B: If the laddoo were in Box 3, the labels on Box 2 and Box 3 would both be true. Only one label may be true.
misconceptions.C: It can be worked out by testing each box in turn and counting the true labels. Only one box leaves exactly one true label.
misconceptions.D: Great thinking! With the laddoo in Box 2, only the label on Box 3 is true.

hints: The square of a number is the number multiplied by itself.
Here you need 12 × 12. Try splitting it into 12 × 10 and 12 × 2.
Example: the square of 11 is 11 × 11. 11 × 10 = 110 and 11 × 1 = 11, so 110 + 11 = 121.

stepByStep.text: The square of 12 means 12 multiplied by itself.
120 + 24 = 144, so the square of 12 is 144.

misconceptions.A: Yes! 12 × 12 = 144, the number multiplied by itself.
misconceptions.B: 24 comes from 12 × 2 or 12 + 12. Squaring means multiplying the number by itself: 12 × 12.
misconceptions.C: 104 comes from adding 10 × 10 and 2 × 2, which leaves out part of the multiplication. Work out 12 × 10 and 12 × 2, then add.
misconceptions.D: 122 looks like 12 with a 2 written after it. The square means 12 multiplied by itself.

G4A_SQUARES_002.questionText: Which of these numbers is a perfect square?
hints: A perfect square is what you get when a whole number is multiplied by itself. Run through the squares you know.
Try the squares near these numbers: 6 × 6, 7 × 7, 8 × 8 and 9 × 9. Does any of them match a number in the list?
Example: among 30, 36, 40 and 42, only 36 is a perfect square, because 6 × 6 = 36.

stepByStep.text: List the squares near these numbers: 6 × 6 = 36, 7 × 7 = 49, 8 × 8 = 64 and 9 × 9 = 81.
48, 56 and 72 are not in that list.
64 is 8 × 8, so the perfect square is 64.

misconceptions.A: 48 is 6 × 8, two different numbers. A perfect square needs the same number twice, like 8 × 8.
misconceptions.B: Well spotted! 8 × 8 = 64, so 64 is a perfect square.
misconceptions.C: 56 is 7 × 8, which is in the times tables but uses two different numbers. Look for a number times itself.
misconceptions.D: 72 is 8 × 9, two different numbers. A perfect square is a number times itself.

G4A_SQUARES_003.questionText: A square carrom board is marked with 81 small squares, in equal rows and columns. How many small squares are there in each row?
hints: When the rows and columns are equal, the total is a number multiplied by itself. You are looking for that number.
Ask yourself: which number times itself makes 81? Try 8 × 8 and 9 × 9.
Example: 49 tiles laid in equal rows and columns have 7 in each row, because 7 × 7 = 49.

stepByStep.text: Equal rows and columns means the number in each row, multiplied by itself, is 81.
8 × 8 = 64 is too small, and 9 × 9 = 81 fits.
So there are 9 small squares in each row.

misconceptions.A: 27 comes from 81 ÷ 3. The board does not have 3 rows; it has as many rows as there are squares in each row.
misconceptions.B: 18 is 9 doubled. You found the key number 9, and there is no need to double it: 9 × 9 is already 81.
misconceptions.C: Right! 9 × 9 = 81, so each row has 9 small squares.
misconceptions.D: 8 × 8 = 64, which is fewer than 81. Try the next number up.

G4A_SQUARES_004.questionText: A number ends in the digit 7. Which digit does its square end in?
hints: The last digit of a square depends only on the last digit of the number being squared.
So you only need to work out 7 × 7 and look at its last digit.
Example: a number ending in 4, such as 14 or 24, has a square ending in 6, because 4 × 4 = 16.

stepByStep.text: Only the last digit matters, so look at 7 × 7.
7 × 7 = 49, which ends in 9.
Check with 17: 17 × 17 = 289, which also ends in 9. So the square ends in 9.

misconceptions.A: The last digit does not simply stay the same. Multiply 7 × 7 and look at the last digit of the result.
misconceptions.B: 4 is the last digit of 7 + 7 = 14. Squaring means 7 × 7, not 7 + 7.
misconceptions.C: Squares end in 1 when the number ends in 1 or 9. For a number ending in 7, work out 7 × 7.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 7 × 7 = 49, so the square of any number ending in 7 ends in 9.

G4A_SQUARES_005.questionText: What is the next perfect square after 49?
hints: Perfect squares come from squaring the counting numbers in order: 1 × 1, 2 × 2, 3 × 3 and so on.
First find which number is squared to give 49. Then square the next counting number.
Example: 25 is 5 × 5, so the next perfect square after 25 is 6 × 6 = 36.

stepByStep.text: The next counting number after 7 is 8.
8 × 8 = 64, so the next perfect square after 49 is 64.

misconceptions.A: Right! 49 is 7 × 7, and the next one is 8 × 8 = 64.
misconceptions.B: 56 is 7 × 8, or 49 + 7. For the next square both numbers go up: 8 × 8.
misconceptions.C: 50 is the next counting number after 49, but it is not a number times itself. Square the number after 7.
misconceptions.D: 81 is 9 × 9, which skips one. The square that comes straight after 7 × 7 is 8 × 8.

G4A_SQUARES_006.questionText: Ravi plants mango saplings in a square field: 11 rows with 11 saplings in each row. How many saplings does he plant?
hints: Rows of equal size are counted by multiplying the number of rows by the number in each row.
Here you need 11 × 11. Try 11 × 10 first, then add one more 11.
Example: 13 rows with 13 plants in each row have 13 × 13 plants. 13 × 10 = 130 and 13 × 3 = 39, so 130 + 39 = 169.

stepByStep.text: Saplings = rows × saplings in each row.
So Ravi plants 121 saplings.

misconceptions.A: 22 is 11 + 11. With 11 rows of 11, you add 11 eleven times, which is 11 × 11.
misconceptions.B: Well done! 11 rows of 11 make 11 × 11 = 121 saplings.
misconceptions.C: 111 is close, but check the adding: 11 × 10 = 110, then one more 11 gives 121.
misconceptions.D: 44 counts 11 along each of the four sides. The saplings fill the whole field, so multiply 11 × 11.

hints: The small 2 means the number is multiplied by itself. Square each number first, then add.
Work out 5 × 5 and 3 × 3 separately.
Example: 4² + 2² is 16 + 4 = 20.

stepByStep.text: 5² means 5 × 5, which is 25.
3² means 3 × 3, which is 9.

misconceptions.A: 64 is 5 + 3 squared together. Here each number is squared on its own first, then the two squares are added.
misconceptions.B: 16 comes from 5 × 2 and 3 × 2. The small 2 means times itself, not times 2.
misconceptions.D: 28 is 25 + 3: the 5 was squared but the 3 was not. Square the 3 as well.

hints: To square a number that ends in zero, square the front digit and remember that each zero appears twice.
30 × 30 is 3 × 3 with two zeros placed after it.
Example: the square of 20 is 20 × 20. 2 × 2 = 4, and then two zeros give 400.

stepByStep.text: The square of 30 is 30 × 30.
One zero from each 30 gives two zeros, so 30 × 30 = 900.

misconceptions.A: 60 is 30 + 30, or 30 × 2. The square is 30 × 30.
misconceptions.B: 90 has only one zero. Each 30 brings its own zero, so there are two: 900.
misconceptions.C: 9000 has one zero too many. 30 × 30 is 3 × 3 with two zeros: 900.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 3 × 3 = 9, and two zeros make 900.

G4A_SQUARES_009.questionText: What is the greatest two-digit perfect square?
hints: List the perfect squares in order and look for the last one that still has two digits.
Try 9 × 9 and 10 × 10. Which of them has two digits?
Example: the greatest one-digit perfect square is 9, because 3 × 3 = 9 and the next one, 4 × 4 = 16, has two digits.

stepByStep.text: 9 × 9 = 81, which has two digits.
10 × 10 = 100, which has three digits.
So the greatest two-digit perfect square is 81.

misconceptions.A: Right! 9 × 9 = 81, and the next square, 100, has three digits.
misconceptions.B: 99 is the greatest two-digit number, but no whole number times itself makes 99. Look for the largest square below 100.
misconceptions.C: 64 is 8 × 8, a two-digit square, but there is a bigger one. Try 9 × 9.
misconceptions.D: 100 is 10 × 10, but it has three digits. Step back one square.

G4A_SQUARES_010.questionText: What is the smallest number that must be taken away from 30 to leave a perfect square?
hints: Taking away makes the number smaller, so look for the nearest perfect square below the number.
Which perfect square is just below 30? Try 5 × 5 and 6 × 6.
Example: for 70, the nearest perfect square below is 8 × 8 = 64, so 70 − 64 = 6 must be taken away.

stepByStep.text: 5 × 5 = 25 is below 30, and 6 × 6 = 36 is above 30.
The nearest perfect square below 30 is 25.
30 − 25 = 5, so 5 must be taken away.

misconceptions.A: 6 is what you would add to reach 36. The question asks what to take away, so look below 30.
misconceptions.C: 30 − 14 = 16 is a perfect square, but a smaller number also does the job. Use the square closest to 30.
misconceptions.D: 30 − 21 = 9 is a perfect square, but you can take away much less. Use the square just below 30.

G4A_SQUARES_011.questionText: Which of these numbers is the square of an odd number?
hints: Find which number was squared to make each one, then check whether that number is odd or even.
36 is 6 × 6 and 64 is 8 × 8. Now find the numbers for 49 and 100.
Example: among 16, 25 and 144, the square of an odd number is 25, because 25 is 5 × 5 and 5 is odd.

stepByStep.text: 36 is 6 × 6, 64 is 8 × 8 and 100 is 10 × 10. The numbers 6, 8 and 10 are even.
49 is 7 × 7, and 7 is odd.
So the square of an odd number is 49.

misconceptions.A: 36 is 6 × 6, and 6 is even. An odd number times itself gives an odd result.
misconceptions.B: 64 is 8 × 8, and 8 is even. An odd number times itself gives an odd result.
misconceptions.C: Right! 49 is 7 × 7, and 7 is odd.
misconceptions.D: 100 is 10 × 10, and 10 is even. Try the only odd number in the list.

G4A_SQUARES_012.questionText: What is the difference between the square of 6 and the number 6 itself?
hints: First find the square. Then the word difference tells you to subtract.
Work out 6 × 6 first.
Example: for 5, the square is 5 × 5 = 25, and the difference is 25 − 5 = 20.

stepByStep.text: The square of 6 is 6 × 6 = 36.
Difference means subtract: 36 − 6 = 30.
So the difference is 30.

misconceptions.A: 6 comes from using 6 × 2 = 12 as the square. The square of 6 is 6 × 6 = 36.
misconceptions.B: 42 is 36 + 6. Difference means subtract, not add.
misconceptions.C: 36 is the square of 6. One more step: take away 6.

G4A_SQUARES_013.questionText: How many perfect squares are there between 50 and 150?
hints: List the perfect squares in order and pick out the ones that lie between the two numbers.
The first square above 50 is 8 × 8 = 64. Keep going with 9 × 9, 10 × 10 and so on, until you pass 150.
Example: between 10 and 40 the perfect squares are 16, 25 and 36, so there are 3 of them.

stepByStep.text: 7 × 7 = 49 is just below 50, so start from 8 × 8 = 64.
13 × 13 = 169 is more than 150, so stop there.
The squares are 64, 81, 100, 121 and 144, so there are 5.

misconceptions.A: Right! 64, 81, 100, 121 and 144 make 5 perfect squares.
misconceptions.B: One has been missed. Check each square from 8 × 8 up to 12 × 12.
misconceptions.C: That is one too many. 49 is below 50 and 169 is above 150, so neither counts.
misconceptions.D: 100 is 150 − 50, the gap between the two numbers. Count only the perfect squares in that gap.

G4A_SQUARES_014.questionText: Which of these digits can never be the last digit of a perfect square?
hints: The last digit of a square depends only on the last digit of the number squared, so there are just ten cases to check.
Square each digit from 0 to 9 and write down the last digit each time: 0, 1, 4, 9, and so on.
Example: can a perfect square end in 3? The squares of 0 to 9 end in 0, 1, 4, 9, 6, 5, 6, 9, 4 and 1. There is no 3, so a perfect square never ends in 3.

stepByStep.text: Their last digits are 0, 1, 4, 9, 6, 5, 6, 9, 4 and 1.
4, 5 and 6 are in this list, but 7 is not.
So a perfect square can never end in 7.

misconceptions.A: 4 is possible: 2 × 2 = 4 and 8 × 8 = 64. Look for a digit that never appears at the end of a square.
misconceptions.B: Right! No digit times itself ends in 7, so no perfect square ends in 7.
misconceptions.C: 5 is possible: 5 × 5 = 25. Check the other digits.
misconceptions.D: 6 is possible: 4 × 4 = 16 and 6 × 6 = 36. Check the other digits.

hints: Square each number first, then subtract. Do not subtract first.
Work out 10 × 10 and 6 × 6.
Example: 7² − 3² is 49 − 9 = 40.

stepByStep.text: 10² means 10 × 10, which is 100.
6² means 6 × 6, which is 36.

misconceptions.A: 16 comes from subtracting first, 10 − 6 = 4, and then squaring. Square each number first and then subtract.
misconceptions.B: 8 comes from 10 × 2 and 6 × 2. The small 2 means times itself, not times 2.
misconceptions.D: 136 is 100 + 36. The sign between the two squares is minus.

G4A_SQUARES_016.questionText: The sum 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 + 11 is the square of which number?
hints: Add the odd numbers, then ask which number times itself gives that total.
Add in pairs: 1 with 11, 3 with 9, and 5 with 7.
Example: 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16, and 16 is 4 × 4, so that sum is the square of 4. Notice that there were 4 odd numbers.

stepByStep.text: The total is 12 + 12 + 12 = 36.
So the sum is the square of 6.

misconceptions.A: 36 is the total itself. The question asks which number is squared to make 36.
misconceptions.B: 11 is the last number added. Find the total first, then the number whose square it is.
misconceptions.C: 5 × 5 = 25, which is the sum of only the first five odd numbers. Here there are six.
misconceptions.D: Yes! The sum is 36, which is 6 × 6. The first six odd numbers always add up to 6 × 6.

G4A_SQUARES_017.questionText: A teacher has 150 children on the playground. She makes them stand in the biggest possible square, with the same number in every row and every column. How many children are left out?
hints: The children standing in the square make a perfect square number. Find the biggest perfect square that is not more than the number of children.
Try 12 × 12 and 13 × 13. Which one is still no more than 150?
