Example: with 90 children, the biggest square is 9 × 9 = 81, so 90 − 81 = 9 children are left out.

stepByStep.text: 169 is more than 150, so the biggest square uses 144 children.
150 − 144 = 6, so 6 children are left out.

misconceptions.A: Right! 144 children make a 12 by 12 square and 6 are left out.
misconceptions.B: 12 is the number of children in each row. The question asks how many are left out: 150 − 144.
misconceptions.C: 19 is how many more children would be needed for a 13 by 13 square. With only 150, use the 12 by 12 square.
misconceptions.D: 150 − 29 = 121 is an 11 by 11 square, but a bigger square is possible. Try 12 × 12.

G4A_SQUARES_018.questionText: A gardener has 200 rose plants. He wants to plant all of them in a square, with the same number in every row and every column. What is the least number of extra plants he must buy?
hints: He is adding plants, so look for the nearest perfect square above the number he has.
Try 14 × 14 and 15 × 15. Which is the first one above 200?
Example: with 90 plants, the next perfect square is 10 × 10 = 100, so he must buy 100 − 90 = 10 more.

stepByStep.text: 14 × 14 = 196, which is less than 200, so it cannot hold all the plants.
15 × 15 = 225 is the first perfect square above 200.
225 − 200 = 25, so he must buy 25 extra plants.

misconceptions.A: 4 is 200 − 196, the plants that would be left over from a 14 by 14 square. He wants to use all the plants, so go up to the next square.
misconceptions.C: 15 is the number of plants in each row. The question asks how many extra plants: 225 − 200.
misconceptions.D: 56 more would make 256, which is 16 × 16, but a smaller square already holds all the plants. Try 15 × 15.

G4A_SQUARES_019.questionText: What is the square root of 400 added to the square root of 49?
hints: Find each square root on its own first, then add them.
Which number times itself gives 400? Think of 2 × 2 = 4 and the zeros.
Example: the square root of 900 is 30 and the square root of 16 is 4, so together they make 30 + 4 = 34.

stepByStep.text: 20 × 20 = 400, so the square root of 400 is 20.
7 × 7 = 49, so the square root of 49 is 7.
20 + 7 = 27, so the sum is 27.

misconceptions.A: 449 is 400 + 49. Find the square root of each number before adding.
misconceptions.B: 207 uses 200, which is half of 400. The square root is the number that times itself gives 400, and that is 20.
misconceptions.D: 21 × 21 = 441, which is close to 400 + 49, but the square roots must be found one at a time: 20 and 7.

G4A_SQUARES_020.questionText: 441 soldiers stand in a square, with the same number in each row and each column. Every soldier in the front row holds a flag. How many flags are there?
hints: The front row has as many soldiers as the side of the square. Find the number that times itself gives the total.
20 × 20 = 400 is a little too small. The total ends in 1, so try a number ending in 1.
Example: 169 soldiers in a square stand 13 in each row, because 13 × 13 = 169, so the front row would hold 13 flags.

stepByStep.text: The number in each row, multiplied by itself, is 441.
20 × 20 = 400 is too small, so try the next number.
The front row has 21 soldiers, so there are 21 flags.

misconceptions.A: 147 is 441 ÷ 3. The square has as many rows as soldiers in each row, so find the number that times itself gives 441.
misconceptions.B: 84 counts 21 soldiers along all four sides. Only the front row holds flags.
misconceptions.C: 20 × 20 = 400, which is 41 short. Try the next number.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 21 × 21 = 441, so the front row has 21 soldiers and 21 flags.

G4A_SQUARES_021.questionText: Which of these numbers is NOT a perfect square?
hints: Check each number: is there a whole number that, multiplied by itself, gives it?
Work out the squares from 11 × 11 to 14 × 14 and tick off the ones in the list.
Example: among 81, 90 and 100, the one that is not a perfect square is 90, since 9 × 9 = 81 and 10 × 10 = 100 and nothing falls in between.

stepByStep.text: 121, 144 and 196 are in this list.
164 falls between 144 and 169, so 164 is not a perfect square.

misconceptions.A: Right! 164 lies between 12 × 12 = 144 and 13 × 13 = 169, so it is not a perfect square.
misconceptions.B: 121 is 11 × 11, so it is a perfect square. Look for the one that matches no square.
misconceptions.C: 144 is 12 × 12, so it is a perfect square. Check the others.
misconceptions.D: 196 is 14 × 14, so it is a perfect square. Check the others.

G4A_SQUARES_022.questionText: The squares of two numbers that come one after the other are 144 and 169. What is the sum of the two numbers?
hints: Work backwards from each square to the number that was squared. Then add those numbers.
Which number times itself gives 144? Try 12.
Example: if the squares are 81 and 100, the numbers are 9 and 10, and their sum is 9 + 10 = 19.

stepByStep.text: 12 × 12 = 144, so the first number is 12.
13 × 13 = 169, so the second number is 13.
12 + 13 = 25, so the sum of the two numbers is 25.

misconceptions.A: 313 is 144 + 169, the sum of the squares. The question asks for the sum of the numbers that were squared.
misconceptions.B: Right! The numbers are 12 and 13, and 12 + 13 = 25.
misconceptions.C: 24 is 12 + 12. The second number is 13, since 13 × 13 = 169.
misconceptions.D: 26 is 13 + 13. The first number is 12, since 12 × 12 = 144.

G4A_SQUARES_023.questionText: Only one of these numbers is a perfect square. Use the last digits to find it.
hints: A perfect square can end only in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9. Any number ending in 2, 3, 7 or 8 can be ruled out straight away.
Look at the last digit of each number. Which ones end in 2, 3, 7 or 8?
Example: among 352, 361, 377 and 388, only 361 can be a perfect square, and indeed 19 × 19 = 361.

stepByStep.text: 1232 ends in 2, 1443 ends in 3 and 1687 ends in 7.
No perfect square ends in 2, 3 or 7, so these three are ruled out.
So the perfect square is 1521.

misconceptions.A: 1232 ends in 2, and no number times itself ends in 2. Look for an ending that squares can have.
misconceptions.B: 1443 ends in 3, and no perfect square ends in 3. Check the other endings.
misconceptions.C: Right! 1521 ends in 1, and 39 × 39 = 1521.
misconceptions.D: 1687 ends in 7, and no perfect square ends in 7. Check the other endings.

hints: Square each number on its own, then add the four squares.
Write the squares in a row: 1, 4, and then 3 × 3 and 4 × 4.
Example: 1² + 2² + 3² is 1 + 4 + 9 = 14.

stepByStep.text: The squares are 1, 4, 9 and 16.

misconceptions.A: 10 is 1 + 2 + 3 + 4, with nothing squared. Square each number before adding.
misconceptions.B: 20 comes from doubling each number: 2, 4, 6 and 8. Squaring means times itself.
misconceptions.C: 100 comes from adding first to get 10 and then squaring. Here each number is squared first, then the squares are added.

G4A_SQUARES_025.questionText: Tara has made a square with 64 small tiles. She wants to add tiles to make the next bigger square. How many more tiles does she need?
hints: Find the side of the square she has, make the side one tile longer, and compare the two totals.
64 is 8 × 8, so her square has 8 tiles on each side. The next bigger square has 9 tiles on each side.
Example: going from a 5 by 5 square of 25 tiles to a 6 by 6 square of 36 tiles needs 36 − 25 = 11 more tiles.

stepByStep.text: 64 is 8 × 8, so the square has 8 tiles on each side.
The next bigger square has 9 tiles on each side: 9 × 9 = 81.
81 − 64 = 17, so she needs 17 more tiles.

misconceptions.A: Right! 81 − 64 = 17. That is one extra row of 8, one extra column of 8, and 1 corner tile.
misconceptions.B: 16 covers an extra row of 8 and an extra column of 8, but the corner tile is missing. Compare 9 × 9 with 8 × 8.
misconceptions.C: 1 is how much longer each side becomes. The whole new row and column need tiles: 81 − 64.
misconceptions.D: 36 more would make 100, which is 10 × 10 and skips a square. The next square after 8 × 8 is 9 × 9.

G4A_SQUARES_026.questionText: The square of a number is 225. What is the square of the number that is 1 more?
hints: First find the number whose square is given. Then add 1 to that number and square it.
Which number times itself gives 225? It ends in 5, so try 15.
Example: if the square of a number is 100, the number is 10, and the square of 11 is 11 × 11 = 121.

stepByStep.text: 15 × 15 = 225, so the number is 15.
One more than 15 is 16.
16 × 16 = 256, so the square is 256.

misconceptions.A: 226 is 225 + 1. Add 1 to the number itself, not to its square: 15 becomes 16.
misconceptions.B: Yes! The number is 15, and 16 × 16 = 256.
misconceptions.C: 196 is 14 × 14, the square of the number that is 1 less. The question asks for 1 more.
misconceptions.D: 16 is the new number. One more step: square it.

G4A_SQUARES_027.questionText: How many perfect squares are there from 1 to 100, counting both 1 and 100?
hints: Each perfect square comes from one counting number. Count how many counting numbers have a square that is not more than the limit.
1 × 1 = 1 is the first one. Which number squared gives exactly 100?
Example: from 1 to 50 the perfect squares are 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36 and 49. They are the squares of 1 to 7, so there are 7.

stepByStep.text: So the squares of 1, 2, 3 and so on, up to 10, all lie from 1 to 100.
That makes 10 perfect squares.

misconceptions.A: One has been missed, perhaps 1 or 100. Both ends are counted here.
misconceptions.B: 50 is half of 100, but perfect squares are not every second number. Count the squares of 1 to 10.
misconceptions.C: Right! The squares of 1 to 10 give 10 perfect squares.
misconceptions.D: That is one too many. 11 × 11 = 121 is beyond 100, and 0 is not counted.

hints: Square each number, then subtract. Splitting each number around 50 makes the squaring easier.
51 × 51 is 51 × 50 and one more 51. Work that out first.

misconceptions.A: 4 comes from subtracting first, 51 − 49 = 2, and then squaring. Square each number first, then subtract.
misconceptions.B: 2 is 51 − 49 with no squaring. Each number must be squared before subtracting.
misconceptions.C: 100 is 51 + 49. That is half of a neat shortcut: multiply it by 51 − 49, which is 2.

G4A_SQUARES_029.questionText: What is the smallest number by which 48 must be divided so that the result is a perfect square?
hints: Try dividing by small numbers in order, and check each result against the perfect squares you know.
Start with 48 ÷ 2 = 24. Is 24 a perfect square? If not, try the next number.
Example: for 50, try 50 ÷ 2 = 25. Since 25 is 5 × 5, the smallest number to divide 50 by is 2.

stepByStep.text: 48 itself is not a perfect square, so dividing by 1 is no help.
48 ÷ 2 = 24, and 24 is not a perfect square.
48 ÷ 3 = 16, and 16 is 4 × 4, a perfect square.
So the smallest number to divide by is 3.

misconceptions.A: Right! 48 ÷ 3 = 16, which is 4 × 4, and no smaller number does it.
misconceptions.B: 48 ÷ 2 = 24, which is not a number times itself. Try the next number.
misconceptions.C: 48 ÷ 4 = 12, which is not a perfect square. Try a smaller number.
misconceptions.D: 48 ÷ 12 = 4 is a perfect square, but the question asks for the smallest such number. Try the small numbers first.

G4A_SQUARES_030.questionText: What is the smallest number that must be subtracted from 1000 to get a perfect square?
hints: Subtracting makes the number smaller, so find the largest perfect square below the number.
30 × 30 = 900. Now try 31 × 31 and 32 × 32 to see which is the last one below 1000.
Example: for 500, 22 × 22 = 484 is the largest perfect square below it, so 500 − 484 = 16 must be subtracted.

stepByStep.text: 1024 is more than 1000, so the largest perfect square below 1000 is 961.
1000 − 961 = 39, so 39 must be subtracted.

misconceptions.A: 24 is what you would add to reach 1024. The question asks what to subtract, so look below 1000.
misconceptions.C: 31 is the number whose square is 961. The question asks how much to subtract: 1000 − 961.
misconceptions.D: 1000 − 100 = 900 is a perfect square, but a smaller number also does the job. Try 31 × 31.

G4A_SQUARES_031.questionText: How many whole numbers lie between 15² and 16²?
hints: Work out the two squares, then count the numbers strictly between them. The two squares themselves are not counted.
15 × 15 = 225 and 16 × 16 = 256. Now count from 226 up to 255.
Example: between 3 × 3 = 9 and 4 × 4 = 16 lie 10, 11, 12, 13, 14 and 15. That is 6 numbers, one less than 16 − 9 = 7.

stepByStep.text: The gap is 256 − 225 = 31.
The numbers in between run from 226 to 255, which is one fewer than the gap.
31 − 1 = 30, so 30 whole numbers lie between them.

misconceptions.A: 1 is 16 − 15. The squares 225 and 256 are much further apart than the numbers 15 and 16.
misconceptions.B: 31 is 256 − 225. That count includes 256 itself, which is an end and not a number in between. Take 1 away.
misconceptions.C: Right! From 226 to 255 there are 30 numbers. It is always double the smaller number: 2 × 15.
misconceptions.D: 32 counts both 225 and 256. Only the numbers strictly between them are counted.

G4A_SQUARES_032.questionText: A farmer plants his young trees in a square, with the same number in each row and each column, and has 5 trees left over. To make the next bigger square he would need 20 more trees. How many trees does he have?
hints: His trees lie between two perfect squares that come one after the other. Work out how far apart those two squares are.
He is 5 above one square and 20 below the next, so the two squares are 5 + 20 = 25 apart. Which two neighbouring squares differ by 25?
Example: with 3 left over and 4 short of the next square, the squares are 3 + 4 = 7 apart. 9 and 16 differ by 7, so there are 9 + 3 = 12 trees.

stepByStep.text: The two squares are 5 + 20 = 25 apart.
He has 5 more than the smaller square, 144.
144 + 5 = 149, so he has 149 trees.

misconceptions.A: 144 trees are in the square, but 5 more are left over. Add them on.
misconceptions.B: 169 is the bigger square he cannot yet make. He is 20 short of it.
misconceptions.C: 164 takes 5 away from 169. He is 20 below 169 and 5 above 144.

G4A_SQUARES_033.questionText: Asha has two square sheets of stamps. One sheet has 9 rows of 9 stamps and the other has 12 rows of 12 stamps. She rearranges all the stamps into one big square. How many stamps are in each row of the big square?
hints: Count all the stamps first. Then find the number that, multiplied by itself, gives that total.
The first sheet has 9 × 9 stamps and the second has 12 × 12. Add the two.
Example: sheets of 3 rows of 3 and 4 rows of 4 hold 9 + 16 = 25 stamps, and 25 is 5 × 5, so the big square has 5 in each row.

stepByStep.text: 81 + 144 = 225 stamps in all.
So the big square has 15 stamps in each row.

misconceptions.B: 21 is 9 + 12. The sides cannot simply be added; add the stamps, then find the side.
misconceptions.C: 225 is the total number of stamps. The question asks how many are in each row.
misconceptions.D: 108 is 9 × 12. The two sheets are put together by adding their stamps: 81 + 144.

G4A_SQUARES_034.questionText: I am a two-digit perfect square. The sum of my two digits is 13. Which number am I?
hints: List all the two-digit perfect squares, then add the digits of each one.
The two-digit perfect squares are 16, 25, 36, 49, 64 and 81. Start adding their digits: 1 + 6 = 7, 2 + 5 = 7, and carry on.
Example: the two-digit perfect square whose digits add up to 10 is 64, because 6 + 4 = 10 and 8 × 8 = 64.

stepByStep.text: The two-digit perfect squares are 16, 25, 36, 49, 64 and 81.
Their digit sums are 7, 7, 9, 13, 10 and 9.
Only one of them has digits adding to 13: 4 + 9 = 13.
So the number is 49.

misconceptions.A: 6 + 7 = 13, but 67 is not a number times itself. Both clues must fit.
misconceptions.C: 9 + 4 = 13, but 94 is not a perfect square. Try its digits the other way round.
misconceptions.D: 64 is a perfect square, but 6 + 4 = 10, not 13. Check the other squares.

G4A_SQUARES_035.questionText: What is the smallest perfect square that can be divided exactly by both 6 and 8?
hints: The number must be in both times tables and also be a number times itself. Go through the perfect squares in order and test each one.
Squares of odd numbers cannot be divided by 8, so test the even ones: 4, 16, 36, 64, 100 and onward. Can 36 be divided by 8? Can 64 be divided by 6?
Example: the smallest perfect square that can be divided exactly by both 2 and 3 is 36, because 4, 9, 16 and 25 each miss one of them.

stepByStep.text: Test the even perfect squares in order: 4, 16, 36, 64, 100, 144.
36 ÷ 6 = 6, but 36 cannot be divided exactly by 8. 64 ÷ 8 = 8, but 64 cannot be divided exactly by 6.
4, 16 and 100 cannot be divided exactly by 6.
144 ÷ 6 = 24 and 144 ÷ 8 = 18, so the smallest such perfect square is 144.

misconceptions.A: 24 is the smallest number that both 6 and 8 divide, but it is not a perfect square. Keep looking among the squares.
misconceptions.B: 48 can be divided by 6 and by 8, but no number times itself gives 48. Test the perfect squares.
misconceptions.C: Right! 144 is 12 × 12, and both 6 and 8 divide it exactly.
misconceptions.D: 576 is 24 × 24 and can be divided by both, but it is not the smallest. Test the smaller squares first.

G4A_RATIO_001.questionText: A class has 12 boys and 18 girls. What is the ratio of boys to girls in its simplest form?
hints: Write the two numbers in the order the question names them. Then divide both by the same number until nothing more divides both.
Boys come first, so start with 12 : 18. Both numbers can be divided by 6.
Example: 15 boys and 20 girls give 15 : 20. Dividing both by 5 gives 3 : 4.

stepByStep.text: Boys to girls is 12 : 18.
Both numbers can be divided by 6: 12 ÷ 6 = 2 and 18 ÷ 6 = 3.
So the ratio in its simplest form is 2 : 3.

misconceptions.A: Right! 12 : 18 becomes 2 : 3 when both numbers are divided by 6.
misconceptions.B: 3 : 2 is girls to boys. The question asks for boys first.
misconceptions.C: 2 : 5 compares the boys with the whole class of 30. The question compares boys with girls.
misconceptions.D: 6 : 9 is the same ratio but not yet in its simplest form. Both 6 and 9 can still be divided by 3.

G4A_RATIO_002.questionText: What is the ratio 20 : 35 in its simplest form?
hints: To simplify a ratio, divide both numbers by the same number: the biggest one that divides both.
Both 20 and 35 are in the 5 times table. Divide each by 5.
Example: in 18 : 30 both numbers can be divided by 6, giving 3 : 5.

stepByStep.text: The biggest number that divides both 20 and 35 is 5.
So 20 : 35 in its simplest form is 4 : 7.

misconceptions.A: Here 20 was divided by 4 but 35 was divided by 5. Both numbers must be divided by the same number.
misconceptions.B: Yes! Dividing both numbers by 5 gives 4 : 7.
misconceptions.C: The numbers are right but the order has swapped. 20 comes first, so 4 comes first.
misconceptions.D: Only the first number was divided. Divide 35 by 5 as well.

G4A_RATIO_003.questionText: 4 notebooks cost ₹ 60. How many rupees does 1 notebook cost?
hints: When you know the cost of several equal things, divide to find the cost of one.
Share ₹ 60 equally among the 4 notebooks.
Example: if 5 pens cost ₹ 40, one pen costs 40 ÷ 5 = 8 rupees.

stepByStep.text: All 4 notebooks cost the same, so divide the total by 4.
So 1 notebook costs ₹ 15.

misconceptions.A: 240 is 60 × 4. One notebook costs less than four notebooks, so divide.
misconceptions.B: 56 is 60 − 4. Sharing a cost equally means dividing.
misconceptions.C: Right! 60 ÷ 4 = 15, so one notebook costs ₹ 15.
misconceptions.D: 64 is 60 + 4. To find the cost of one, divide the total by the number of notebooks.

G4A_RATIO_004.questionText: A bag holds 3 red balls and 5 blue balls. What is the ratio of red balls to all the balls in the bag?
hints: Read carefully what is being compared. Here one colour is compared with the whole bag, so you need the total.
First add to find all the balls in the bag.
Example: with 2 green and 7 yellow balls there are 9 balls in all, so green to all is 2 : 9.

stepByStep.text: All the balls: 3 + 5 = 8.
Red balls come first, then all the balls.
So the ratio is 3 : 8.

misconceptions.A: 3 : 5 compares red with blue. The question compares red with all the balls, so add first.
misconceptions.B: 5 : 3 is blue to red. The question asks for red to all the balls.
misconceptions.C: 5 : 8 is blue to all the balls. The question asks about the red balls.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 3 red balls out of 8 balls gives 3 : 8.

G4A_RATIO_005.questionText: Which of these ratios is equal to 2 : 3?
hints: Two ratios are equal when both numbers of one are multiplied, or divided, by the same number to get the other.
Multiply both 2 and 3 by 2, then by 3, and see which result is in the list.
Example: 1 : 4 is equal to 3 : 12, because 1 × 3 = 3 and 4 × 3 = 12.

stepByStep.text: Multiply both numbers of 2 : 3 by 3.
So 6 : 9 is equal to 2 : 3.

misconceptions.A: Right! Both 2 and 3 were multiplied by 3 to give 6 : 9.
misconceptions.B: Here 2 was multiplied by 2 but 3 was multiplied by 3. Both must be multiplied by the same number.
misconceptions.C: 3 : 2 has the same numbers in the opposite order, which makes a different ratio.
misconceptions.D: 5 : 6 comes from adding 3 to both numbers. Equal ratios come from multiplying, not adding.

G4A_RATIO_006.questionText: To make lemonade, Sana mixes 1 cup of lemon juice with 4 cups of water. If she uses 3 cups of lemon juice, how many cups of water does she need?
hints: The mix must stay the same, so whatever you multiply the juice by, multiply the water by the same number.
The juice has gone from 1 cup to 3 cups. That is 3 times as much.
Example: 1 cup of rice needs 2 cups of water, so 5 cups of rice need 5 × 2 = 10 cups of water.

stepByStep.text: The juice is 3 times as much as before.
So the water must be 3 times as much too.
4 × 3 = 12, so she needs 12 cups of water.

misconceptions.A: 7 is 4 + 3. The water is multiplied, not added to: 3 times the juice needs 3 times the water.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 3 times the juice needs 3 times the water: 4 × 3 = 12.
misconceptions.C: 15 is all the lemonade, juice and water together. The question asks only for the water.
misconceptions.D: 6 adds the 2 extra cups of juice to the water. Each cup of juice needs 4 cups of water, so multiply.

G4A_RATIO_007.questionText: A car travels 60 km in 1 hour. At the same speed, how many kilometres does it travel in 3 hours?
hints: At a steady speed, the car covers the same distance in every hour. More hours means more distance.
It covers 60 km in each hour, and there are 3 hours. Multiply.
Example: a bus that travels 40 km in 1 hour travels 40 × 4 = 160 km in 4 hours.

stepByStep.text: In 1 hour the car travels 60 km.
In 3 hours it travels 3 times as far: 60 × 3 = 180.
So it travels 180 km.

misconceptions.A: 63 is 60 + 3. Each of the 3 hours adds another 60 km, so multiply.
misconceptions.B: 20 is 60 ÷ 3. In more time the car goes further, so multiply.
misconceptions.C: Right! 60 × 3 = 180 km.
misconceptions.D: 120 km is the distance for 2 hours. Count all 3 hours.

G4A_RATIO_008.questionText: ₹ 10 buys 2 samosas. At the same price, how many samosas does ₹ 50 buy?
hints: Find how many times bigger the money is. The number of samosas grows by the same number of times.
How many tens are there in 50? Each ten buys 2 samosas.
Example: if ₹ 20 buys 3 bananas, then ₹ 80 is 4 times as much money and buys 3 × 4 = 12 bananas.

stepByStep.text: 50 ÷ 10 = 5, so ₹ 50 is 5 times as much money as ₹ 10.
The samosas are 5 times as many: 2 × 5 = 10.
So ₹ 50 buys 10 samosas.

misconceptions.A: 25 is 50 ÷ 2, as if each samosa cost ₹ 2. Each one costs ₹ 5, since ₹ 10 buys 2.
misconceptions.B: 100 is 50 × 2. ₹ 10 buys 2 samosas, and ₹ 50 is 5 lots of ₹ 10: 5 × 2.
misconceptions.C: 5 is the number of ten-rupee lots in ₹ 50. Each lot buys 2 samosas, so double it.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 5 lots of ₹ 10 buy 5 × 2 = 10 samosas.

G4A_RATIO_009.questionText: Sweets are shared between two children in the ratio 3 : 7. Into how many equal parts are the sweets divided altogether?
hints: A ratio tells you how many equal parts each person gets. The total number of parts comes from putting them together.
One child gets 3 parts and the other gets 7 parts. Put them together.
Example: sharing in the ratio 4 : 5 means 4 + 5 = 9 equal parts altogether.

stepByStep.text: The first child gets 3 parts and the second child gets 7 parts.
So the sweets are divided into 10 equal parts altogether.

misconceptions.A: Right! 3 parts and 7 parts make 10 parts.
misconceptions.B: 4 is 7 − 3, how many more parts the second child gets. For the total, add.
misconceptions.C: 21 is 3 × 7. The parts are put together by adding.
misconceptions.D: 7 is only the second child's parts. Add the first child's 3 parts too.

G4A_RATIO_010.questionText: A tailor needs 2 metres of cloth to make 1 shirt. How many shirts can he make from 14 metres of cloth?
hints: Each shirt uses up the same amount of cloth. Find how many such amounts fit into the whole cloth.
How many 2s are there in 14? Divide.
Example: if 1 kurta needs 3 metres, then 15 metres make 15 ÷ 3 = 5 kurtas.

stepByStep.text: Each shirt needs 2 metres of cloth.
So he can make 7 shirts.

misconceptions.A: 28 is 14 × 2, the cloth needed for 14 shirts. Here 14 is the cloth, so divide by 2.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 14 ÷ 2 = 7 shirts.
misconceptions.C: 12 is 14 − 2, the cloth left after one shirt. Keep taking away 2 metres for each shirt, which is the same as dividing.
misconceptions.D: 16 is 14 + 2. Each shirt uses up 2 metres, so divide 14 by 2.

G4A_RATIO_011.questionText: What is the ratio of 50 paise to ₹ 2 in its simplest form?
hints: Before writing a ratio, both amounts must be in the same unit.
Change ₹ 2 into paise. One rupee is 100 paise.
Example: 20 cm to 1 m. Since 1 m is 100 cm, the ratio is 20 : 100, and dividing both by 20 gives 1 : 5.

stepByStep.text: ₹ 2 is 200 paise.
The ratio is 50 : 200.
Divide both by 50: 50 ÷ 50 = 1 and 200 ÷ 50 = 4.
So the ratio in its simplest form is 1 : 4.

misconceptions.A: 25 : 1 comes from 50 : 2, which mixes paise with rupees. Change ₹ 2 into 200 paise first.
misconceptions.B: 1 : 2 would be 50 paise to ₹ 1. Here it is ₹ 2, which is 200 paise.
misconceptions.C: Right! 50 : 200 simplifies to 1 : 4.
misconceptions.D: 4 : 1 has the order swapped. The 50 paise comes first.

G4A_RATIO_012.questionText: A kabaddi club has 20 children. 8 of them are girls. What is the ratio of girls to boys in its simplest form?
hints: Check which two groups are being compared. You may need to work out one of them first.
Find the number of boys: 20 − 8.
Example: of 24 children, 6 are girls, so 18 are boys. Girls to boys is 6 : 18, and dividing both by 6 gives 1 : 3.

stepByStep.text: Girls to boys is 8 : 12.
Divide both by 4: 8 ÷ 4 = 2 and 12 ÷ 4 = 3.
So the ratio in its simplest form is 2 : 3.

misconceptions.A: 2 : 5 compares the girls with the whole club, 8 : 20. The question compares girls with boys.
misconceptions.B: 3 : 2 is boys to girls. Girls come first here.
misconceptions.C: 5 : 2 compares the whole club with the girls. Find the number of boys and put the girls first.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 8 girls to 12 boys simplifies to 2 : 3.

G4A_RATIO_013.questionText: 5 kg of rice costs ₹ 300. At the same price, how many rupees do 8 kg of rice cost?
hints: Find the cost of one unit first, then multiply by the number you need.
Find the cost of 1 kg: 300 ÷ 5.
Example: if 4 kg of dal costs ₹ 200, then 1 kg costs ₹ 50, and 7 kg cost 50 × 7 = 350 rupees.

stepByStep.text: 1 kg costs 300 ÷ 5 = 60 rupees.
8 kg cost 8 times as much: 60 × 8 = 480.
So 8 kg of rice cost ₹ 480.

misconceptions.A: Right! Each kg costs ₹ 60, and 60 × 8 = 480.
misconceptions.B: ₹ 60 is the cost of 1 kg. Multiply by 8 for 8 kg.
misconceptions.C: 2400 is 300 × 8. ₹ 300 is the cost of 5 kg, not 1 kg, so divide by 5 first.
misconceptions.D: 340 adds only a little for the 3 extra kg. Each kg costs ₹ 60, so 3 more kg cost ₹ 180 more.

G4A_RATIO_014.questionText: ₹ 120 is shared among Amit, Bina and Chetan in the ratio 1 : 2 : 3. How many rupees does Chetan get?
hints: Add the numbers in the ratio to find the total number of equal parts. Then find the value of one part.
The parts are 1 + 2 + 3 in all. Divide ₹ 120 by that total.
Example: ₹ 450 shared in the ratio 1 : 3 : 5 has 9 parts of ₹ 50 each, so the last person gets 5 × 50 = 250 rupees.

stepByStep.text: Total parts: 1 + 2 + 3 = 6.
One part is 120 ÷ 6 = 20 rupees.
Chetan gets 3 parts: 3 × 20 = 60.
So Chetan gets ₹ 60.

misconceptions.A: ₹ 40 is an equal share, and it is also Bina's share. Chetan has 3 of the 6 parts.
misconceptions.B: Yes! One part is ₹ 20 and Chetan has 3 parts, so he gets ₹ 60.
misconceptions.C: ₹ 20 is one part, which is Amit's share. Chetan has 3 parts.
misconceptions.D: 360 is 120 × 3. First divide ₹ 120 into 6 parts, then take 3 of them.

G4A_RATIO_015.questionText: The ratio of pencils to pens in a box is 4 : 3. There are 28 pencils. How many pencils and pens are there altogether?
hints: Use the amount you know to find the size of one part. Then use the parts to find what is asked.
The pencils are 4 parts and there are 28 of them. Find one part: 28 ÷ 4.
Example: books to copies are 5 : 2 and there are 30 books. One part is 30 ÷ 5 = 6, and there are 7 parts in all, so there are 7 × 6 = 42 things altogether.

stepByStep.text: One part is 28 ÷ 4 = 7.
Pens are 3 parts: 3 × 7 = 21.
Altogether: 28 + 21 = 49.
So there are 49 pencils and pens altogether.

misconceptions.A: 21 is the number of pens. The question asks for pencils and pens together.
misconceptions.B: 7 is the size of one part. There are 4 + 3 = 7 parts in all, so multiply.
misconceptions.C: Right! 28 pencils and 21 pens make 49.
misconceptions.D: 56 is 28 doubled. There are fewer pens than pencils: 3 parts against 4.

G4A_RATIO_016.questionText: A train covers 240 km in 4 hours. At the same speed, how many hours does it take to cover 420 km?
hints: Find how far the train goes in one hour. Then see how many such hours are needed for the new distance.
Find the distance covered in 1 hour: 240 ÷ 4.
Example: a bus covers 150 km in 3 hours, so 50 km each hour. For 450 km it takes 450 ÷ 50 = 9 hours.

stepByStep.text: In 1 hour the train covers 240 ÷ 4 = 60 km.
Time for 420 km: 420 ÷ 60 = 7.
So the train takes 7 hours.

misconceptions.A: In 8 hours the train would cover 60 × 8 = 480 km, which is too far. Divide 420 by 60.
misconceptions.B: 60 is the number of km covered each hour. Now find how many hours 420 km takes.
misconceptions.C: In 6 hours the train covers 60 × 6 = 360 km, which is short of 420 km. One more hour is needed.
misconceptions.D: Yes! The train covers 60 km each hour, and 420 ÷ 60 = 7 hours.

G4A_RATIO_017.questionText: A recipe for 6 people needs 300 grams of flour. How many grams of flour are needed for 4 people?
hints: Find the amount for one person first, then multiply by the number of people you are cooking for.
Flour for 1 person: 300 ÷ 6.
Example: a recipe for 5 people uses 400 grams of rice, so 80 grams each. For 3 people it needs 80 × 3 = 240 grams.

stepByStep.text: For 1 person: 300 ÷ 6 = 50 grams.
For 4 people: 50 × 4 = 200.
So 200 grams of flour are needed.

misconceptions.A: Right! Each person needs 50 grams, and 50 × 4 = 200 grams.
misconceptions.B: 50 grams is the flour for 1 person. Multiply by 4.
misconceptions.C: 450 grams would feed 9 people. Fewer people need less flour than 300 grams.
misconceptions.D: 1200 is 300 × 4. The 300 grams is for 6 people, so find the amount for 1 person first.

G4A_RATIO_018.questionText: 45 mangoes are shared between Kiran and Leela in the ratio 4 : 5. How many more mangoes does Leela get than Kiran?
hints: Find the size of one part. Then see how many more parts one person has than the other.
There are 4 + 5 parts in all. Divide 45 by that.
Example: 40 sweets shared in the ratio 3 : 5 make 8 parts of 5 sweets each. The second child has 2 parts more, which is 2 × 5 = 10 sweets more.

stepByStep.text: Total parts: 4 + 5 = 9.
One part is 45 ÷ 9 = 5 mangoes.
Leela has 5 parts and Kiran has 4 parts, so Leela has 1 part more.
So Leela gets 5 more mangoes.

misconceptions.A: 9 is the total number of parts. Find the size of one part, then compare the two shares.
misconceptions.B: Yes! Kiran gets 20 and Leela gets 25, so Leela gets 5 more.
misconceptions.C: 20 is Kiran's share. The question asks how many more Leela gets.
misconceptions.D: 25 is Leela's share. Take away Kiran's 20 to find how many more.

G4A_RATIO_019.questionText: On a map, 2 cm stands for 10 km. Two towns are 7 cm apart on the map. How many kilometres apart are they really?
hints: Find what 1 cm on the map stands for. Then multiply by the number of centimetres.
If 2 cm stands for 10 km, find what 1 cm stands for: 10 ÷ 2.
Example: if 3 cm stands for 12 km, then 1 cm stands for 4 km, and 5 cm stands for 4 × 5 = 20 km.

stepByStep.text: 1 cm stands for 10 ÷ 2 = 5 km.
7 cm stands for 7 × 5 = 35 km.
So the towns are really 35 km apart.

misconceptions.A: 70 is 7 × 10. But 10 km goes with 2 cm, not 1 cm. Halve it first.
misconceptions.B: 17 is 10 + 7. Each centimetre stands for the same distance, so multiply.
misconceptions.C: Right! 1 cm stands for 5 km, so 7 cm stands for 35 km.
misconceptions.D: 5 km is what 1 cm stands for. The towns are 7 cm apart, so multiply by 7.

G4A_RATIO_020.questionText: What is the ratio 18 : 24 : 30 in its simplest form?
hints: A ratio with three numbers is simplified the same way as one with two: divide all of them by the biggest number that divides every one.
18, 24 and 30 are all in the 6 times table. Divide each by 6.
Example: in 10 : 20 : 25 all three numbers can be divided by 5, giving 2 : 4 : 5.

stepByStep.text: The biggest number that divides 18, 24 and 30 is 6.
So the simplest form is 3 : 4 : 5.

misconceptions.A: All three numbers were halved, which is a good start. They can still be divided by 3.
misconceptions.B: All three numbers were divided by 3. They can still be halved.
misconceptions.C: The first two are right. Check the last one: 30 ÷ 6 = 5.
misconceptions.D: Yes! Dividing all three numbers by 6 gives 3 : 4 : 5.

G4A_RATIO_021.questionText: Which of these ratios is NOT equal to 4 : 6?
hints: Simplify each ratio, or build each one from the given ratio by multiplying or dividing both numbers by the same number.
4 : 6 in its simplest form is 2 : 3. Now simplify each ratio in the list.
Example: is 9 : 12 equal to 3 : 5? Dividing 9 and 12 by 3 gives 3 : 4, so they are not equal.

stepByStep.text: 4 : 6 simplifies to 2 : 3.
8 : 12 and 12 : 18 both simplify to 2 : 3 as well.
6 : 8 simplifies to 3 : 4, which is different.
So the ratio that is not equal to 4 : 6 is 6 : 8.

misconceptions.A: Right! 6 : 8 is made by adding 2 to each number, and adding does not keep a ratio the same.
misconceptions.B: 2 : 3 is 4 : 6 with both numbers halved, so it is equal. Look for one that does not simplify to 2 : 3.
misconceptions.C: 8 : 12 is 4 : 6 with both numbers doubled, so it is equal. Check the others.
misconceptions.D: 12 : 18 is 4 : 6 with both numbers multiplied by 3, so it is equal. Check the others.

G4A_RATIO_022.questionText: A machine fills 45 bottles in 9 minutes. At the same rate, how many bottles does it fill in 1 hour?
hints: Find how many bottles are filled in one minute. Watch the units: the question changes from minutes to an hour.
Bottles in 1 minute: 45 ÷ 9. Then remember how many minutes make 1 hour.
Example: a tap fills 24 buckets in 8 minutes, so 3 each minute. In half an hour, which is 30 minutes, it fills 3 × 30 = 90 buckets.

stepByStep.text: In 1 minute the machine fills 45 ÷ 9 = 5 bottles.
1 hour is 60 minutes.
So the machine fills 300 bottles in 1 hour.

misconceptions.A: 5 is the number of bottles filled in 1 minute. An hour has 60 minutes, so multiply.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 5 bottles each minute for 60 minutes is 300 bottles.
misconceptions.C: 405 is 45 × 9. First find the bottles in 1 minute by dividing, then multiply by 60.
misconceptions.D: 500 treats an hour as 100 minutes. An hour has 60 minutes: 5 × 60.

G4A_RATIO_023.questionText: The ratio of Arun's stamps to Bela's stamps is 3 : 5. Bela has 12 more stamps than Arun. How many stamps does Arun have?
hints: The extra stamps match the extra parts in the ratio. Use that to find the size of one part.
Bela has 5 − 3 = 2 parts more than Arun, and those 2 parts are 12 stamps.
Example: the ratio is 2 : 5 and the second person has 15 more. The 3 extra parts are 15, so one part is 5, and the first person has 2 × 5 = 10.

stepByStep.text: Bela has 5 − 3 = 2 parts more than Arun.
Those 2 parts are 12 stamps, so one part is 12 ÷ 2 = 6 stamps.
Arun has 3 parts: 3 × 6 = 18.
So Arun has 18 stamps.

misconceptions.A: 36 is 12 × 3, which treats 12 as one part. The 12 stamps are 2 parts, so one part is 6.
misconceptions.B: 30 is Bela's number of stamps, 5 parts. Arun has 3 parts.
misconceptions.C: Right! One part is 6, so Arun has 18 and Bela has 30, which is 12 more.
misconceptions.D: 48 is the two collections together. Arun has only 3 of the 8 parts.

G4A_RATIO_024.questionText: The length and breadth of a rectangular playground are in the ratio 5 : 3. The length is 40 m. What is the perimeter of the playground in metres?
hints: Use the ratio to find the missing side first. Then go all the way round the rectangle.
The length is 5 parts and measures 40 m. Find one part: 40 ÷ 5.
Example: length to breadth is 4 : 1 and the length is 20 m. One part is 5 m, so the breadth is 5 m and the perimeter is 20 + 5 + 20 + 5 = 50 m.

stepByStep.text: One part is 40 ÷ 5 = 8 m.
The breadth is 3 parts: 3 × 8 = 24 m.
One length and one breadth: 40 + 24 = 64 m.
The perimeter is twice that: 64 × 2 = 128, so the perimeter is 128 m.

misconceptions.A: 24 m is the breadth. Now go round the whole playground: two lengths and two breadths.
misconceptions.B: 64 m is one length and one breadth, only halfway round. Double it.
misconceptions.C: 960 is 40 × 24, which is the area. The perimeter is the distance all the way round.

G4A_RATIO_025.questionText: Asha's money and Bina's money are in the ratio 2 : 3. Bina's money and Chitra's money are in the ratio 3 : 4. Asha has ₹ 40. How many rupees does Chitra have?
hints: Work along the chain one link at a time: use the first ratio to find the middle person, then the second ratio to find the last.
Asha's 2 parts are ₹ 40. Find one part, then Bina's 3 parts.
Example: Pia to Qadir is 1 : 2 and Qadir to Rita is 2 : 5. If Pia has ₹ 10, then Qadir has ₹ 20, one part of the second ratio is ₹ 10, and Rita has 5 × 10 = 50 rupees.

stepByStep.text: Asha's 2 parts are ₹ 40, so one part is 40 ÷ 2 = 20 rupees.
Bina has 3 parts: 3 × 20 = 60 rupees.
In the second ratio Bina's 3 parts are ₹ 60, so one part is 60 ÷ 3 = 20 rupees.
Chitra has 4 parts: 4 × 20 = 80, so Chitra has ₹ 80.

misconceptions.A: Right! Asha has ₹ 40, Bina has ₹ 60 and Chitra has ₹ 80.
misconceptions.B: ₹ 60 is Bina's money. Use the second ratio to go on to Chitra.
misconceptions.C: 160 is 40 × 4, which treats ₹ 40 as one part. Asha's ₹ 40 is 2 parts, so one part is ₹ 20.
misconceptions.D: 120 is 40 × 3. One part is ₹ 20, not ₹ 40, and Chitra has 4 parts.

G4A_RATIO_026.questionText: A bag has 20 marbles, red and green, in the ratio 2 : 3. Then 4 more red marbles are put in. What is the new ratio of red marbles to green marbles?
hints: A ratio gives parts, not actual numbers. Find the actual numbers first, make the change, then write the new ratio.
There are 2 + 3 = 5 parts in 20 marbles. Find one part, then the number of red and of green marbles.
Example: 15 sweets, orange to lemon 2 : 3, so 6 orange and 9 lemon. Add 6 orange: now there are 12 orange and 9 lemon, which is 12 : 9, or 4 : 3.

stepByStep.text: Total parts: 2 + 3 = 5, so one part is 20 ÷ 5 = 4 marbles.
After 4 more red marbles: 8 + 4 = 12 red, and still 12 green.
12 : 12 simplifies, so the new ratio is 1 : 1.

misconceptions.A: 2 : 1 comes from adding 4 to the ratio number 2, giving 6 : 3. Add the 4 marbles to the actual number of red marbles, which is 8.
misconceptions.B: Yes! There are now 12 red and 12 green marbles, so the ratio is 1 : 1.
misconceptions.C: 3 : 2 has more red than green. After the change the two colours are equal in number.
misconceptions.D: 3 : 5 compares the red marbles with the old total of 20. Compare red with green: 12 and 12.

G4A_RATIO_027.questionText: 3 pens cost the same as 5 pencils. One pencil costs ₹ 6. How many rupees do 4 pens cost?
hints: Use the thing whose price you know to find the price of the other thing. Then find the cost of the number asked.
Find the cost of 5 pencils: 5 × 6. That is also the cost of 3 pens.
Example: 2 erasers cost the same as 6 sharpeners at ₹ 3 each, which is ₹ 18. So one eraser costs ₹ 9, and 5 erasers cost 5 × 9 = 45 rupees.

stepByStep.text: 5 pencils cost 5 × 6 = 30 rupees.
So 3 pens cost ₹ 30, and 1 pen costs 30 ÷ 3 = 10 rupees.
4 pens cost 4 × 10 = 40.
So 4 pens cost ₹ 40.

misconceptions.A: 24 is 4 × 6, the cost of 4 pencils. A pen costs more than a pencil, so find the price of one pen first.
misconceptions.B: ₹ 30 is the cost of 3 pens. The question asks for 4 pens.
misconceptions.C: Right! One pen costs ₹ 10, so 4 pens cost ₹ 40.
misconceptions.D: ₹ 10 is the cost of 1 pen. Multiply by 4.

G4A_RATIO_028.questionText: 96 sweets are shared among three children in the ratio 1 : 3 : 4. What is the difference between the largest share and the smallest share?
hints: Find the size of one part. Then compare the biggest share with the smallest by counting how many parts apart they are.
There are 1 + 3 + 4 parts in all. Divide 96 by that.
Example: 60 sweets in the ratio 1 : 2 : 3 make 6 parts of 10 sweets. The largest share is 2 parts more than the smallest, so the difference is 2 × 10 = 20.

stepByStep.text: Total parts: 1 + 3 + 4 = 8.
One part is 96 ÷ 8 = 12 sweets.
The largest share is 4 parts and the smallest is 1 part, so they are 3 parts apart.
3 × 12 = 36, so the difference is 36 sweets.

misconceptions.A: 12 is one part, the smallest share. The largest share is 4 parts, so the gap is 3 parts.
misconceptions.B: 48 is the largest share. Take away the smallest share, 12.
misconceptions.C: 24 comes from dividing 96 by 4. There are 1 + 3 + 4 = 8 parts, so one part is 12.
misconceptions.D: Yes! The shares are 12, 36 and 48, and 48 − 12 = 36.

G4A_RATIO_029.questionText: Hari walks 3 km in 45 minutes. At the same speed, how many kilometres does he walk in 2 hours?
hints: Find the time for 1 km. Change the hours into minutes so that the units match.
Time for 1 km: 45 ÷ 3 minutes. And 2 hours is 120 minutes.
Example: Mina cycles 4 km in 20 minutes, so 1 km takes 5 minutes. In 1 hour, which is 60 minutes, she cycles 60 ÷ 5 = 12 km.

stepByStep.text: 1 km takes 45 ÷ 3 = 15 minutes.
2 hours is 120 minutes.
So Hari walks 8 km in 2 hours.

misconceptions.A: Right! Each km takes 15 minutes, and 120 ÷ 15 = 8 km.
misconceptions.B: 6 km doubles the 3 km, but 2 hours is more than double 45 minutes. Two lots of 45 minutes make only 90 minutes.
misconceptions.C: 9 km would take 9 × 15 = 135 minutes, which is more than 2 hours. Divide 120 by 15.
misconceptions.D: 90 is 45 × 2, a number of minutes. The question asks for kilometres.

G4A_RATIO_030.questionText: To make green paint, a painter mixes 2 tins of blue with every 3 tins of yellow. He has 12 tins of blue and 15 tins of yellow. What is the greatest number of tins of green paint he can make?
hints: Each lot of the mix uses up some of each colour. See which colour runs out first; that colour decides how many lots can be made.
The blue is enough for 12 ÷ 2 lots. The yellow is enough for 15 ÷ 3 lots. Which is smaller?
Example: a drink needs 1 cup of syrup for every 4 cups of water. With 3 cups of syrup and 8 cups of water, the water allows only 2 lots, so the most is 2 × 5 = 10 cups of drink.

stepByStep.text: The blue is enough for 12 ÷ 2 = 6 lots. The yellow is enough for 15 ÷ 3 = 5 lots.
The yellow runs out first, so only 5 lots can be made.
Each lot is 2 + 3 = 5 tins of green paint.
5 × 5 = 25, so he can make 25 tins of green paint.

misconceptions.A: 27 is 12 + 15, all the tins together. Not all the blue can be used, because the yellow runs out first.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 5 lots of 5 tins make 25 tins, with 2 tins of blue left over.
misconceptions.C: 30 uses 6 lots, but 6 lots need 18 tins of yellow and he has only 15.
misconceptions.D: 5 is the number of lots he can mix. Each lot makes 5 tins of green paint.

G4A_AGES_001.questionText: Asha is 9 years old now. How old will she be after 6 years?
hints: As the years pass, a person's age goes up by the same number of years.
Add the 6 years to Asha's age now.
Example: Raju is 7 now. After 5 years he will be 7 + 5 = 12 years old.

stepByStep.text: Asha is 9 now.
After 6 years her age goes up by 6: 9 + 6 = 15.
So Asha will be 15 years old.

misconceptions.A: 3 is 9 − 6, her age 6 years ago. The word after means going forward in time, so add.
misconceptions.B: 54 is 9 × 6. Each year adds just 1 to her age, so add 6.
misconceptions.D: 14 is one short. Count on 6 from 9: 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15.

G4A_AGES_002.questionText: Meera is 10 years old and her father is 38 years old. How many years older than Meera is her father?
hints: The words how many years older ask for the gap between the two ages.
Subtract Meera's age from her father's age.
Example: a boy is 8 and his mother is 33. She is 33 − 8 = 25 years older.

stepByStep.text: Her father is 38 and Meera is 10.
So her father is 28 years older.

misconceptions.A: 48 is 38 + 10. To find how much older, subtract.
misconceptions.B: 18 takes away one ten too many. 38 − 10 = 28.
misconceptions.C: 38 is the father's age. The question asks how much older he is than Meera.

G4A_AGES_003.questionText: Tina is 8 years old. Her mother is 4 times as old as Tina. How old is her mother?
hints: The words times as old tell you to multiply.
Multiply Tina's age by 4.
Example: Sunil is 6 and his father is 5 times as old, so his father is 6 × 5 = 30.

stepByStep.text: Tina is 8.
Her mother is 4 times as old: 8 × 4 = 32.
So her mother is 32 years old.

misconceptions.B: 12 is 8 + 4. The words 4 times as old mean multiply by 4.
misconceptions.C: 2 is 8 ÷ 4. Her mother is older than Tina, so multiply.

G4A_AGES_004.questionText: Four years ago, Zoya was 6 years old. How old is she now?
hints: The words years ago take you into the past. Coming back to today, the age goes up.
She was 6 then, and 4 years have passed since. Add.
Example: three years ago Kabir was 9, so now he is 9 + 3 = 12.

stepByStep.text: Four years ago Zoya was 6.
Since then 4 years have passed: 6 + 4 = 10.
So Zoya is 10 years old now.

misconceptions.A: 2 is 6 − 4. She was 6 in the past, so today she is older, not younger.
misconceptions.C: 24 is 6 × 4. Each year adds 1 to her age, so add 4.
misconceptions.D: 6 was her age four years ago. Add the 4 years that have passed.

G4A_AGES_005.questionText: Dev was born in the year 2015. How old was he on his birthday in 2024?
hints: Age on a birthday is the number of years from the birth year to that year.
Subtract the birth year from 2024.
Example: someone born in 2010 turns 2021 − 2010 = 11 on the birthday in 2021.

stepByStep.text: Dev was born in 2015.
So Dev was 9 years old on his birthday in 2024.

misconceptions.A: 10 counts both 2015 and 2024. In 2015 he was just born, so count the steps between the years: 9.
misconceptions.B: 8 is one short. From 2015 to 2024 is 9 years.
misconceptions.D: 19 has an extra ten. 2015 to 2025 would be 10 years, so 2015 to 2024 is 9.

G4A_AGES_006.questionText: Rohan's father is 36 years old. Rohan is one-third as old as his father. How old is Rohan?
hints: One-third as old means the age is split into 3 equal parts and you take one of them.
Divide the father's age by 3.
Example: a mother is 40 and her son is one-quarter as old, so the son is 40 ÷ 4 = 10.

stepByStep.text: His father is 36.
One-third of 36 is 36 ÷ 3 = 12.
So Rohan is 12 years old.

misconceptions.A: 33 is 36 − 3. One-third means divide by 3.
misconceptions.B: 108 is 36 × 3. Rohan is younger than his father, so divide.
misconceptions.C: 18 is half of 36. One-third means 3 equal parts: 36 ÷ 3.

G4A_AGES_007.questionText: Anil is 3 years older than his brother Sunil today. How many years older than Sunil will Anil be after 10 years?
hints: Think about what happens to both brothers as the years go by. Do they grow older at the same pace?
Try it with ages you choose: say Sunil is 5 and Anil is 8. Find both ages after 10 years.
Example: Rita is 4 years older than Gita. If Gita is 6 and Rita is 10, then after 5 years they are 11 and 15, and Rita is still 15 − 11 = 4 years older.

stepByStep.text: Suppose Sunil is 5, so Anil is 8.
After 10 years Sunil is 15 and Anil is 18.
18 − 15 = 3. Both grow older by the same amount, so the gap stays the same.
So Anil will still be 3 years older.

misconceptions.A: Right! Both brothers grow 10 years older, so the gap stays 3.
misconceptions.B: 13 is 3 + 10. Sunil also grows 10 years older, so the gap does not grow.
misconceptions.C: 7 is 10 − 3. The gap between two people's ages never changes.
misconceptions.D: 30 is 3 × 10. The gap stays the same every year.

G4A_AGES_008.questionText: Ravi is 12 years old now. In how many years will he be 20 years old?
hints: You know the age now and the age later. The number of years in between is the gap.
Subtract Ravi's age now from 20.
Example: Simran is 9 now. She will be 15 in 15 − 9 = 6 years.

stepByStep.text: Ravi is 12 now and will be 20 later.
So Ravi will be 20 in 8 years.

misconceptions.A: 32 is 20 + 12. The question asks for the years in between, so subtract.
misconceptions.C: 7 is one short: 12 + 7 = 19. One more year is needed.
misconceptions.D: 9 is one too many: 12 + 9 = 21. Count on from 12 to 20.

G4A_AGES_009.questionText: Amit is 3 years older than Bina. Bina is 2 years older than Chirag. Chirag is 7 years old. How old is Amit?
hints: Start from the person whose age you know and work along the chain, one person at a time.
Chirag is 7 and Bina is 2 years older. Find Bina's age first.
Example: Pari is 4 years older than Qasim, Qasim is 1 year older than Ria, and Ria is 6. Then Qasim is 7 and Pari is 7 + 4 = 11.

stepByStep.text: Bina is 2 years older than Chirag: 7 + 2 = 9.
Amit is 3 years older than Bina: 9 + 3 = 12.
So Amit is 12 years old.

misconceptions.A: 9 is Bina's age. Amit is 3 years older than Bina.
misconceptions.B: 10 is 7 + 3, which skips Bina. Amit is 3 years older than Bina, and Bina is 9.
misconceptions.C: Right! Chirag is 7, Bina is 9 and Amit is 12.
misconceptions.D: 2 comes from subtracting both gaps. Amit is the oldest of the three, so add.

G4A_AGES_010.questionText: Farhan is 11 years old. His sister Rehana is 3 years younger than him. How old was Rehana 2 years ago?
hints: Find the sister's age now first. Then go back in time.
Rehana is 3 years younger than Farhan: 11 − 3.
Example: Mohan is 16 and his sister is 2 years younger, so she is 14. Five years ago she was 14 − 5 = 9.

stepByStep.text: Rehana's age now: 11 − 3 = 8.
Two years ago she was 2 years younger: 8 − 2 = 6.
So Rehana was 6 years old.

misconceptions.A: 8 is Rehana's age now. The question asks about 2 years ago.
misconceptions.B: 12 comes from adding the 3 years. Rehana is younger than Farhan, so subtract.
misconceptions.C: 10 is 8 + 2, her age two years from now. The word ago means going back.
misconceptions.D: Yes! She is 8 now, so two years ago she was 6.

G4A_AGES_011.questionText: Diya is 7 years old and her mother is 35 years old. After 7 years, how many times as old as Diya will her mother be?
hints: Both people grow older. Find both new ages first, then compare them by dividing.
After 7 years, Diya will be 7 + 7 and her mother will be 35 + 7.
Example: a boy is 4 and his father is 34. After 2 years they are 6 and 36, and 36 ÷ 6 = 6, so the father is 6 times as old.

stepByStep.text: After 7 years Diya will be 7 + 7 = 14.
Her mother will be 35 + 7 = 42.
So her mother will be 3 times as old as Diya.

misconceptions.A: Right! 42 is 3 times 14.
misconceptions.B: 5 times is true today, since 35 ÷ 7 = 5. After 7 years both ages change.
misconceptions.C: Check the dividing: 14 × 4 = 56, which is more than 42. Try 14 × 3.
misconceptions.D: 28 is the gap between their ages, which never changes. The words how many times ask you to divide.

G4A_AGES_012.questionText: The sum of the ages of Anu and her mother is 44 years. Anu is 8 years old. How old was her mother when Anu was born?
hints: Find the mother's age now. Then go back to the year Anu was born.
Mother's age now: 44 − 8.
Example: a boy of 5 and his father have ages adding up to 40. The father is 35 now, and when the boy was born, 5 years ago, he was 35 − 5 = 30.

stepByStep.text: Mother's age now: 44 − 8 = 36.
Anu was born 8 years ago.
Her mother was then 36 − 8 = 28.
So her mother was 28 years old when Anu was born.

misconceptions.A: 36 is her mother's age now. Anu was born 8 years ago, so go back 8 years.
misconceptions.B: Yes! She is 36 now, so she was 28 when Anu was born.
misconceptions.C: 44 is the two ages together. Take away Anu's 8 to get her mother's age, then go back 8 years.
misconceptions.D: 52 is 44 + 8. Take Anu's age away from the sum instead.

G4A_AGES_013.questionText: The ages of two sisters add up to 20 years. One sister is 4 years older than the other. How old is the older sister?
hints: You know the sum and the difference of two ages. Take away the extra years and the rest splits equally.
Take the extra 4 years away from 20. What is left is twice the younger sister's age.
Example: two ages add up to 34 and differ by 6. 34 − 6 = 28, and half of 28 is 14, so the younger is 14 and the older is 14 + 6 = 20.

stepByStep.text: Take away the extra years: 20 − 4 = 16.
Half of 16 is 8, so the younger sister is 8.
The older sister is 8 + 4 = 12.
So the older sister is 12 years old.

misconceptions.A: 8 is the younger sister's age. Add 4 for the older sister.
misconceptions.B: 16 is 20 − 4. It still has to be split between the two sisters.
misconceptions.C: Right! The sisters are 8 and 12: together 20, and 4 apart.
misconceptions.D: 10 is half of 20, which would make the sisters the same age. One is 4 years older.

G4A_AGES_014.questionText: A father is 3 times as old as his son. Their ages add up to 48 years. How old is the son?
hints: Think of the son's age as 1 part. Then the father's age is a number of the same parts, and you can count all the parts in the sum.
The son is 1 part and the father is 3 parts. That makes 4 parts adding up to 48.
Example: a mother is 4 times as old as her daughter and their ages add up to 40. That is 5 parts, so the daughter is 40 ÷ 5 = 8.

stepByStep.text: The son is 1 part and the father is 3 parts, so together they are 4 parts.
4 parts are 48, so one part is 48 ÷ 4 = 12.
So the son is 12 years old.

misconceptions.A: 16 is 48 ÷ 3. Count the son's own part too: there are 4 parts in all.
misconceptions.B: 36 is the father's age. The son is one part: 12.
misconceptions.C: 24 is half of 48, which would make them the same age. The father has 3 parts and the son has 1.
misconceptions.D: Yes! The son is 12 and the father is 36: together 48.

G4A_AGES_015.questionText: Three years ago, Kiran was 9 years old. How old will she be 4 years from now?
hints: Move along the timeline in two jumps: from the past to today, then from today to the future.
First find Kiran's age today: 9 + 3.
Example: four years ago Jai was 5, so he is 9 now. Two years from now he will be 9 + 2 = 11.

stepByStep.text: Kiran's age today: 9 + 3 = 12.
Four years from now: 12 + 4 = 16.
So Kiran will be 16 years old.

misconceptions.A: Right! She was 9 then, is 12 now, and will be 16 four years from now.
misconceptions.B: 13 is 9 + 4, which skips the 3 years that have already passed. Find her age today first.
misconceptions.C: 10 takes away 3 instead of adding. She was 9 in the past, so today she is 12.
misconceptions.D: 12 is Kiran's age today. Go 4 more years ahead.

G4A_AGES_016.questionText: The ages of Geeta and Hari add up to 25 years now. What did their ages add up to 3 years ago?
hints: Going back in time changes the age of each person, not just one. Count how many people are in the sum.
Three years ago Geeta was 3 years younger, and so was Hari. How much smaller was the sum?
Example: two friends' ages add up to 30. Five years ago each was 5 years younger, so the sum was 30 − 5 − 5 = 20.

stepByStep.text: Three years ago Geeta was 3 years younger and Hari was 3 years younger.
Together that is 3 + 3 = 6 years less.
25 − 6 = 19, so their ages added up to 19 years.

misconceptions.A: 22 takes away 3 only once. Both Geeta and Hari were 3 years younger.
misconceptions.B: Yes! Each was 3 years younger, so the sum was 6 less: 19.
misconceptions.C: 28 adds 3. The word ago goes back in time, so the ages were smaller.
misconceptions.D: 31 adds 6. The word ago goes back in time, so take 6 away instead.

G4A_AGES_017.questionText: Jay's grandfather is 72 years old. Jay's father is half as old as the grandfather. Jay is one-quarter as old as his father. How old is Jay?
hints: Work down the family one step at a time, using each age to find the next.
Find the father's age first: half of 72.
Example: a grandmother is 60, the mother is half as old, so 30, and the child is one-fifth as old as the mother: 30 ÷ 5 = 6.

stepByStep.text: Father's age: 72 ÷ 2 = 36.
Jay's age is one-quarter of 36: 36 ÷ 4 = 9.
So Jay is 9 years old.

misconceptions.A: 18 is one-quarter of the grandfather's age. Jay's age is one-quarter of his father's age, 36.
misconceptions.B: 36 is the father's age. Now take one-quarter of it.
misconceptions.C: Right! The father is 36, and 36 ÷ 4 = 9.
misconceptions.D: 12 is 36 ÷ 3. One-quarter means 4 equal parts: 36 ÷ 4.

G4A_AGES_018.questionText: Varun is 9 years old. His father is 27 years older than him. How old will his father be when Varun is 15?
hints: The gap between two people's ages stays the same for ever. Use it at the later time.
When Varun is 15, his father will still be 27 years older than him.
Example: Nita is 6 and her mother is 24 years older. When Nita is 10, her mother will be 10 + 24 = 34.

stepByStep.text: The father is always 27 years older than Varun.
When Varun is 15, his father will be 15 + 27 = 42.
So his father will be 42 years old.

misconceptions.A: 36 is the father's age now, 9 + 27. By the time Varun is 15, six more years have passed.
misconceptions.B: 33 is 27 + 6. The 27 is the gap, not the father's age: his age now is 36.
misconceptions.C: 51 is 36 + 15. Only 6 years pass between Varun being 9 and 15, so add 6 to 36.

G4A_AGES_019.questionText: Rahul is 10 years old and his father is 40 years old. After how many years will the father be 3 times as old as Rahul?
hints: Both ages go up together. Try a number of years, find both new ages, and check whether one is 3 times the other.
Try each choice. After 10 years they would be 20 and 50. Is 50 equal to 3 times 20?
Example: a girl is 6 and her mother is 30. After 2 years they are 8 and 32, and 32 is 4 times 8, so after 2 years the mother is 4 times as old.

stepByStep.text: After 5 years Rahul will be 10 + 5 = 15.
His father will be 40 + 5 = 45.
45 is 3 times 15, so the father is then 3 times as old.
So it happens after 5 years.

misconceptions.A: Right! After 5 years they are 15 and 45, and 45 is 3 times 15.
misconceptions.B: After 10 years they are 20 and 50, but 3 times 20 is 60. Try fewer years.
misconceptions.C: After 15 years they are 25 and 55, but 3 times 25 is 75. Try fewer years.
misconceptions.D: After 20 years they are 30 and 60, and 60 is only 2 times 30. Try fewer years.

G4A_AGES_020.questionText: Ali is 14 years old and his sister Sara is 8 years old. How old was Ali when Sara was exactly half his age?
hints: The gap between their ages never changes. When one person is half the other's age, the younger one's age equals the gap.
Find the gap: 14 − 8. When Sara's age was equal to this gap, Ali was twice as old as her.
Example: Ravi is 15 and Mala is 11, a gap of 4. When Mala was 4, Ravi was 4 + 4 = 8, exactly double.

stepByStep.text: Ali is always 14 − 8 = 6 years older than Sara.
Sara is half Ali's age when her age equals the gap, so Sara was 6.
Ali was then 6 + 6 = 12.
So Ali was 12 years old.

misconceptions.A: 7 is half of Ali's age today. When Ali was 7, Sara was only 1. Use the gap of 6 years.
misconceptions.B: Yes! When Ali was 12, Sara was 6, exactly half.
misconceptions.C: 6 was Sara's age at that time. The question asks for Ali's age.
misconceptions.D: When Ali was 10, Sara was 4, and half of 10 is 5. Go to the time when Sara was 6.

G4A_AGES_021.questionText: Five years ago, a mother was 7 times as old as her daughter. The mother is 33 years old now. How old is the daughter now?
hints: Go back to the time the clue talks about, work out the ages then, and return to today.
Find the mother's age five years ago: 33 − 5.
Example: four years ago a father was 6 times as old as his son. The father is 40 now, so he was 36 then and the son was 36 ÷ 6 = 6. Today the son is 6 + 4 = 10.

stepByStep.text: Five years ago the mother was 33 − 5 = 28.
The daughter was then 28 ÷ 7 = 4.
Today the daughter is 4 + 5 = 9.
So the daughter is 9 years old now.

misconceptions.A: 4 was the daughter's age five years ago. Add the 5 years to come back to today.
misconceptions.B: 14 adds the 5 years twice. From 4, add 5 just once.
misconceptions.C: Right! She was 4 then, so she is 9 now.
misconceptions.D: 28 was the mother's age five years ago. Divide by 7 for the daughter's age then, and come back to today.

G4A_AGES_022.questionText: Aman is twice as old as Bhavna. Four years ago, Aman was three times as old as Bhavna was then. How old is Bhavna now?
hints: Two clues must both be true. Try an age, use the first clue to get the other age, then test the second clue.
Try a choice: if Bhavna is 12, Aman is 24. Four years ago they were 8 and 20. Is 20 three times 8?
Example: Meena is twice as old as Nitu, and five years ago she was three times as old. Try Nitu 10 and Meena 20: five years ago they were 5 and 15, and 15 is 3 times 5. So Nitu is 10.

stepByStep.text: Try Bhavna as 8: then Aman is 2 × 8 = 16.
Four years ago Bhavna was 8 − 4 = 4 and Aman was 16 − 4 = 12.
12 is 3 times 4, so both clues fit.
So Bhavna is 8 years old now.

misconceptions.A: 16 is Aman's age. The question asks for Bhavna, who is half as old.
misconceptions.B: 4 was Bhavna's age four years ago. Add the 4 years to come back to today.
misconceptions.C: If Bhavna were 12, Aman would be 24, and four years ago they would be 8 and 20. But 3 times 8 is 24, not 20.
misconceptions.D: Yes! Bhavna is 8 and Aman is 16 now; four years ago they were 4 and 12, and 12 is 3 times 4.

G4A_AGES_023.questionText: A grandfather is 9 times as old as his grandson. Their ages add up to 70 years. How old will the grandfather be when the grandson is 10 years old?
hints: Use parts to find both ages now. Then move both people forward by the same number of years.
The grandson is 1 part and the grandfather is 9 parts, so 10 parts make 70. Find one part.
Example: a father is 5 times as old as his daughter and their ages add up to 36. Six parts make 36, so she is 6 and he is 30. When she is 8, two years later, he will be 30 + 2 = 32.

stepByStep.text: The grandson is 1 part and the grandfather is 9 parts. 10 parts are 70, so one part is 70 ÷ 10 = 7.
The grandson is 7 and the grandfather is 9 × 7 = 63.
The grandson will be 10 after 10 − 7 = 3 years.
63 + 3 = 66, so the grandfather will be 66 years old.

misconceptions.A: Right! He is 63 now, and 3 years later he is 66.
misconceptions.B: 63 is the grandfather's age now. The grandson is 7 now, so move 3 years ahead.
misconceptions.C: 73 adds 10 years. The grandson needs only 3 more years to reach 10.
misconceptions.D: 90 is 9 × 10. He is 9 times as old only now; later, both simply grow older by the same number of years.

G4A_AGES_024.questionText: Neel says that in 6 years he will be twice as old as he was 2 years ago. How old is Neel now?
hints: Compare two moments: one in the past and one in the future. Count the years between them.
From 2 years ago to 6 years from now is 2 + 6 = 8 years. In those 8 years his age doubles.
Example: in 5 years Tanu will be twice as old as she was 1 year ago. Those moments are 6 years apart, so she was 6 one year ago, and she is 6 + 1 = 7 now.

stepByStep.text: From 2 years ago to 6 years from now is 2 + 6 = 8 years.
His age doubles in those 8 years, so 2 years ago he was 8.
Now he is 8 + 2 = 10.
Check: in 6 years he will be 16, which is twice 8. So Neel is 10 years old now.

misconceptions.A: 8 was Neel's age 2 years ago. Add 2 to come to today.
misconceptions.B: Yes! Two years ago he was 8, and in 6 years he will be 16, which is twice 8. So he is 10 now.
misconceptions.C: 16 will be Neel's age in 6 years. Come back 6 years to today.
misconceptions.D: If Neel were 14, he would be 20 in 6 years, but twice his age 2 years ago would be 24. Try a smaller age.

G4A_AGES_025.questionText: Three sisters were born 2 years apart, one after another. Their ages add up to 27 years. How old is the youngest sister?
hints: When ages are equally spaced, the middle one is the equal share. Find the middle age first.
Share 27 equally among the three sisters to find the middle sister's age: 27 ÷ 3.
Example: three brothers born 3 years apart have ages adding up to 45. The middle one is 45 ÷ 3 = 15, so the youngest is 15 − 3 = 12.

stepByStep.text: The middle sister's age is 27 ÷ 3 = 9.
The youngest is 2 years younger: 9 − 2 = 7.
So the youngest sister is 7 years old.

misconceptions.A: 9 is the middle sister's age. The youngest is 2 years younger.
misconceptions.B: 11 is the oldest sister's age. The question asks for the youngest.
misconceptions.C: Right! The sisters are 7, 9 and 11, which add up to 27.
misconceptions.D: 5 takes away 2 twice from the middle age. The youngest is just 2 years younger than the middle sister.

G4A_DATA_001.questionText: Rohit's runs in five cricket matches were: Match 1 34, Match 2 52, Match 3 47, Match 4 25, Match 5 43. In which match did he score the most runs?
hints: This asks you to find the biggest number in a list and say which match it belongs to.
Compare the tens digits of the five scores first. Which scores have the biggest tens digit?
Example: Scores of Game 1 18, Game 2 31, Game 3 27. The biggest number is 31, so the most runs came in Game 2.

stepByStep.text: Look at the tens digits: 34, 52, 47, 25 and 43 have tens digits 3, 5, 4, 2 and 4.
The biggest tens digit is 5, so 52 is the biggest score.
52 runs were scored in Match 2, so the answer is Match 2.

misconceptions.A: Match 3 has 47 runs, which is the second biggest score. Check whether any score is in the fifties.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 52 is bigger than 34, 47, 25 and 43, and it belongs to Match 2.
misconceptions.C: Match 5 has 43 runs. Compare it with 52 and 47 to see which is biggest.
misconceptions.D: Match 4 has 25 runs, which is the smallest score. The question asks for the most runs, so look for the biggest number.

G4A_DATA_002.questionText: In a pictograph, each picture of a book stands for 5 books sold. Monday has 4 pictures, Tuesday has 6 pictures, Wednesday has 3 pictures and Thursday has 5 pictures. On which day were the fewest books sold?
hints: Every picture stands for the same number of books, so think about what the number of pictures tells you.
The day with the fewest pictures has the fewest books. Compare 4, 6, 3 and 5.
Example: Each picture stands for 2 kites. Ravi has 7 pictures, Sita has 2 pictures and Anu has 5 pictures. Sita has the fewest pictures, so Sita has the fewest kites.

stepByStep.text: Each picture stands for the same number of books, so fewer pictures means fewer books.
The numbers of pictures are 4, 6, 3 and 5. The smallest is 3.
Wednesday has 3 pictures, which is 15 books.
The fewest books were sold on Wednesday.

misconceptions.A: Monday has 4 pictures, which is 20 books. Is there a day with fewer pictures than 4?
misconceptions.B: Tuesday has 6 pictures, the most of all. The question asks for the fewest, so look for the smallest number of pictures.
misconceptions.C: Thursday has 5 pictures, which is 25 books. Look for a day with fewer pictures.
misconceptions.D: Well done! Wednesday has only 3 pictures, fewer than any other day, so it has the fewest books.

G4A_DATA_003.questionText: In a tally chart, each bundle stands for 5 and each single stroke stands for 1. The row for parrots has 3 bundles and 2 single strokes. How many parrots were counted?
hints: A tally chart counts in fives. Work out the bundles first, then add the single strokes.
Find how many the 3 bundles stand for by multiplying 3 by 5.
Example: 2 bundles and 4 single strokes. The bundles give 2 x 5 = 10, and 10 + 4 = 14.

stepByStep.text: Each bundle stands for 5, so 3 bundles stand for 15.
Add the 2 single strokes.
17 parrots were counted.

misconceptions.A: Great counting! 3 bundles make 15, and 2 more strokes make 17.
misconceptions.B: This adds 3 and 2 as if every mark stood for 1. Remember that each bundle stands for 5.
misconceptions.C: This counts the 3 bundles but leaves out the 2 single strokes. Add them on.
misconceptions.D: This writes the 3 and the 2 side by side. Each bundle is worth 5, so multiply 3 by 5 and then add 2.

G4A_DATA_004.questionText: The number of children present in Class 4 was: Mon 38, Tue 35, Wed 40, Thu 32. How many more children were present on Wednesday than on Tuesday?
hints: The words 'how many more' ask you to compare two numbers from the list.
Pick out the numbers for Wednesday and Tuesday only. They are 40 and 35.
Example: Mon 26, Tue 19. To find how many more on Monday, subtract: 26 - 19 = 7.

stepByStep.text: Wednesday has 40 children and Tuesday has 35 children.
Subtract to find how many more.
5 more children were present on Wednesday.

misconceptions.A: This adds 40 and 35. To find how many more, subtract the smaller number from the bigger one.
misconceptions.B: This compares Wednesday with Thursday. The question asks about Wednesday and Tuesday.
misconceptions.C: That is right! 40 - 35 = 5, so 5 more children came on Wednesday.
misconceptions.D: This compares Monday with Tuesday. Use Wednesday's number, 40, and Tuesday's number, 35.

G4A_DATA_005.questionText: A bar graph shows the samosas sold at a stall: Monday 12, Tuesday 15, Wednesday 9, Thursday 15, Friday 11. Which two days have bars of the same height?
hints: Bars of the same height show the same number. Look for a number that appears twice.
Read the five numbers one by one: 12, 15, 9, 15, 11. Which number do you see two times?
Example: Red 7, Blue 4, Green 7, Yellow 6. The number 7 appears twice, so the bars for Red and Green are equally tall.

stepByStep.text: Bars are equally tall when their numbers are equal.
In the list 12, 15, 9, 15, 11 only the number 15 appears twice.
15 belongs to Tuesday and Thursday, so the equal bars are Tuesday and Thursday.

misconceptions.A: Yes! Both Tuesday and Thursday show 15 samosas, so their bars are the same height.
misconceptions.B: Monday shows 12 and Friday shows 11. They are close, but not equal. Look for two numbers that match exactly.
misconceptions.C: Monday shows 12 and Thursday shows 15. Find the other day that also shows 15.
misconceptions.D: Wednesday shows 9 and Friday shows 11. Look for two days with exactly the same number.

G4A_DATA_006.questionText: The children of Class 4 each chose one favourite fruit: Mango 14, Banana 6, Apple 9, Guava 5. How many children chose banana or guava?
hints: You need to put two groups from the table together.
Pick out only the numbers for banana and guava. They are 6 and 5.
Example: Rose 8, Lily 7, Lotus 4. The children who chose rose or lotus are 8 + 4 = 12.

stepByStep.text: Banana was chosen by 6 children and guava by 5 children.
Add the two groups.
11 children chose banana or guava.

misconceptions.A: This subtracts 5 from 6. The question asks for both groups together, so add them.
misconceptions.B: This adds mango and banana. The question asks about banana and guava.
misconceptions.C: This adds all four fruits. Only banana and guava are needed.
misconceptions.D: Well done! 6 children and 5 children make 11 children.

G4A_DATA_007.questionText: Six children got these marks in a spelling test: 14, 18, 9, 20, 12, 17. How many children got more than 15 marks?
hints: Here you count how many numbers in a list are bigger than a given number.
Go through the marks one at a time and tick each one that is bigger than 15. Start with 14: is it bigger than 15?
Example: Marks 6, 11, 8, 13, 5. The marks more than 10 are 11 and 13, so 2 children got more than 10.

stepByStep.text: Check each mark against 15.
14, 9 and 12 are less than 15. The marks 18, 20 and 17 are more than 15.
That makes 3 children with more than 15 marks.

misconceptions.A: One of the marks above 15 has been missed. Check 18, 20 and 17 again.
misconceptions.B: Good checking! 18, 20 and 17 are the marks above 15, so the count is 3.
misconceptions.C: This also counts 14, but 14 is less than 15. Count only the marks bigger than 15.
misconceptions.D: This counts all six children. Count only the children whose marks are bigger than 15.

G4A_DATA_008.questionText: Each child in a class chose one favourite game: Cricket 13, Kho-kho 8, Football 7, Carrom 4. How many children are there in the class?
hints: Every child chose exactly one game, so the whole class is all the groups put together.
Add the four numbers. A good start is 13 + 7, which makes a round number.
Example: Tea 9, Milk 11, Juice 5. All together that is 9 + 11 + 5 = 25 people.

stepByStep.text: Add cricket and football first.
Add kho-kho and carrom.
Put the two sums together.
There are 32 children in the class.

misconceptions.A: This leaves out the 4 children who chose carrom. Add all four groups.
misconceptions.B: This counts the number of games. The question asks for the number of children, so add the four numbers.
misconceptions.C: That is right! 13 + 8 + 7 + 4 = 32.
misconceptions.D: The ones add up to more than 10 here, so a ten must be carried. Try adding 13 + 7 first, then 8 + 4.

G4A_DATA_009.questionText: In a tally chart, a bundle stands for 5 and a single stroke stands for 1. Which of these shows 23?
hints: Think about how many full fives fit into the number, and what is left over.
Count in fives: 5, 10, 15, 20. How many fives is that, and how many more do you need to reach 23?
Example: To show 12, count in fives: 5, 10. That is 2 bundles, and 12 - 10 = 2 single strokes.

stepByStep.text: Four fives make 20.
Find what is left after 20.
So 23 is shown by 4 bundles and 3 strokes.

misconceptions.A: This copies the digits 2 and 3 of the number 23. But 2 bundles are only 10, so this shows 13.
misconceptions.B: Lovely! 4 bundles make 20 and 3 strokes make 23.
misconceptions.C: 5 bundles are already 25, which is more than 23. Use fewer bundles.
misconceptions.D: 3 bundles make 15, and 4 more strokes make 19. Count in fives until you are close to 23.

G4A_DATA_010.questionText: In a pictograph, each picture of a sun stands for 2 sunny days. January has 5 pictures, February has 8 pictures, March has 6 pictures and April has 9 pictures. Which month had 16 sunny days?
hints: Each picture stands for more than one day, so the number of pictures is not the number of days.
Work out how many pictures are needed to show 16 days when each picture stands for 2 days.
Example: Each picture stands for 5 pens. To show 20 pens you need 20 divided by 5 = 4 pictures, so look for the row with 4 pictures.

stepByStep.text: Each picture stands for 2 days, so 16 days need 8 pictures.
The month with 8 pictures is February.
February had 16 sunny days.

misconceptions.A: January has 5 pictures, which stand for 10 sunny days. Find the month with 8 pictures.
misconceptions.B: March has 6 pictures, which stand for 12 sunny days. Find the month with 8 pictures.
misconceptions.C: April has 9 pictures, which stand for 18 sunny days. That is a little too many.
misconceptions.D: Yes! February has 8 pictures and 8 x 2 = 16 sunny days.

G4A_DATA_011.questionText: The heights of five plants in centimetres are: Rose 34, Tulsi 28, Neem 41, Mint 19, Lily 37. Which plant is the second tallest?
hints: Put the numbers in order from biggest to smallest, then pick the one in second place.
Find the tallest plant first. Which height is the biggest of 34, 28, 41, 19 and 37?
Example: Asha 22, Bina 30, Charu 26. From biggest to smallest: 30, 26, 22. The second biggest is 26, so Charu is second tallest.

stepByStep.text: From biggest to smallest the heights are 41, 37, 34, 28, 19.
The tallest is 41 (Neem). The next is 37.
37 cm is the height of Lily, so the second tallest plant is Lily.

misconceptions.A: Super! Neem is tallest at 41 cm, and Lily comes next at 37 cm.
misconceptions.B: Neem is the tallest plant. The question asks for the second tallest, the one just below it.
misconceptions.C: Rose is 34 cm, which is third. One plant is taller than Rose but shorter than Neem.
misconceptions.D: Tulsi is second in the list, but the list is not in order of height. Arrange the heights from biggest to smallest first.

G4A_DATA_012.questionText: The side of a bar graph is marked 0, 10, 20, 30, 40. The top of Tuesday's bar is exactly halfway between the marks 20 and 30. What number does Tuesday's bar show?
hints: When a bar ends between two marks, its value is between those two numbers.
Find the number that is exactly in the middle of 20 and 30. How far apart are 20 and 30?
Example: A bar ends halfway between 40 and 60. The marks are 20 apart, half of 20 is 10, and 40 + 10 = 50.

stepByStep.text: The marks 20 and 30 are 10 apart.
Half of 10 is 5.
Go 5 above 20.
Tuesday's bar shows 25.

misconceptions.A: 20 is the mark below the top of the bar. The bar goes up beyond 20, halfway to 30.
misconceptions.B: 30 is the mark above the top of the bar. The bar stops halfway before it reaches 30.
misconceptions.C: That is right! 25 is exactly in the middle of 20 and 30.
misconceptions.D: This adds 20 and 30. The bar ends between the two marks, so find the number in the middle of them.

G4A_DATA_013.questionText: In a pictograph, each picture stands for 3 kites. Ravi's row has 5 pictures and Meena's row has 8 pictures. How many more kites does Meena have than Ravi?
hints: This is a pictograph comparison. Remember that each picture stands for more than one kite.
Find how many more pictures Meena has than Ravi: 8 - 5.
Example: Each picture stands for 4 balls. Amit has 6 pictures and Sunil has 4 pictures. Amit has 2 more pictures, and 2 x 4 = 8 more balls.

stepByStep.text: Meena has 3 more pictures than Ravi.
Each picture stands for 3 kites.
Meena has 9 more kites than Ravi.

misconceptions.A: Well done! 3 extra pictures, each worth 3 kites, make 9 kites.
misconceptions.B: This is how many more pictures Meena has. Each picture stands for 3 kites, so multiply by 3.
misconceptions.C: This is the number of kites Meena has. The question asks how many more she has than Ravi.
misconceptions.D: This adds Ravi's 15 kites and Meena's 24 kites. To find how many more, subtract.

G4A_DATA_014.questionText: In a pictograph of library books, each picture stands for 5 books. Monday has 4 pictures, Tuesday has 6 pictures and Wednesday has 3 pictures. How many books were borrowed on the three days altogether?
hints: Find the total number of pictures, then change pictures into books.
Add the pictures for the three days: 4 + 6 + 3.
Example: Each picture stands for 2 pens. Three rows have 3, 5 and 4 pictures. That is 12 pictures, and 12 x 2 = 24 pens.

stepByStep.text: Add the pictures for the three days.
