Each picture stands for 5 books.
65 books were borrowed altogether.

misconceptions.A: This is the number of pictures. Each picture stands for 5 books, so multiply by 5.
misconceptions.B: That is right! 13 pictures stand for 13 x 5 = 65 books.
misconceptions.C: This adds 5 to the 13 pictures. Each of the 13 pictures stands for 5 books, so multiply.
misconceptions.D: One picture has been missed. There are 4 + 6 + 3 = 13 pictures in all, not 12.

G4A_DATA_015.questionText: In a pictograph, each picture stands for 6 eggs. A farmer's chart has 5 pictures for Monday and 3 pictures for Tuesday. He packs all these eggs in boxes of 12. How many boxes does he fill?
hints: There are two parts here: first find the number of eggs, then share them into boxes.
Find the total number of pictures for the two days, then multiply by 6 to get the eggs.
Example: Each picture stands for 4 buns. There are 6 pictures, so 24 buns. Packed in bags of 8, that is 24 divided by 8 = 3 bags.

stepByStep.text: Add the pictures.
Each picture stands for 6 eggs.
Put the eggs in boxes of 12.
He fills 4 boxes.

misconceptions.A: This is the number of pictures. Change the pictures into eggs, then into boxes of 12.
misconceptions.B: This is the number of eggs. The question asks how many boxes of 12 they fill.
misconceptions.C: Great work! 48 eggs fill 4 boxes of 12.
misconceptions.D: This subtracts the pictures. Both days' eggs are packed, so add the pictures first.

G4A_DATA_016.questionText: A sweet shop sold 60 laddoos in four days. The table shows: Mon 12, Tue 18, Thu 14, but the number for Wednesday is smudged. How many laddoos were sold on Wednesday?
hints: You know the whole and three of its four parts. Think about how to find the missing part.
Add the three numbers you can read: 12 + 18 + 14.
Example: Total 50, and three days show 10, 15 and 5. These add to 30, so the missing day is 50 - 30 = 20.

stepByStep.text: Add the three known days.
Take this away from the total.
16 laddoos were sold on Wednesday.

misconceptions.A: This is the total for the three known days. Take it away from 60 to find Wednesday.
misconceptions.B: This shares 60 equally among four days. The days are not equal, so subtract the known days from the total.
misconceptions.C: This adds the three days to 60. The 60 already includes them, so subtract.

G4A_DATA_017.questionText: Tickets sold at a mela: on Saturday, 20 adult tickets and 35 child tickets; on Sunday, 28 adult tickets and 30 child tickets. How many more tickets were sold on Sunday than on Saturday?
hints: Each day has two kinds of ticket. Find each day's total before you compare.
Add the adult and child tickets for Saturday: 20 + 35.
Example: Day 1 has 10 and 12 tickets, total 22. Day 2 has 15 and 14 tickets, total 29. Day 2 sold 29 - 22 = 7 more.

stepByStep.text: Saturday's total.
Sunday's total.
Compare the totals.
3 more tickets were sold on Sunday.

misconceptions.A: That is right! Sunday's 58 tickets are 3 more than Saturday's 55.
misconceptions.B: This compares only the adult tickets. Child tickets count too, so find each day's total.
misconceptions.C: This compares only the child tickets. Add adult and child tickets for each day first.
misconceptions.D: This adds all the tickets of both days. To find how many more, subtract Saturday's total from Sunday's.

G4A_DATA_018.questionText: In a pictograph, each picture stands for 4 children and Monday's row has 6 pictures. The chart is drawn again with each picture standing for 8 children. How many pictures will Monday's row have now?
hints: The number of children stays the same. Only the value of each picture changes.
Find how many children Monday's row shows: 6 pictures of 4 children each.
Example: 10 pictures of 2 pens each show 20 pens. If each picture stands for 5 pens, you need 20 divided by 5 = 4 pictures.

stepByStep.text: Find the number of children.
Each new picture stands for 8 children.
Monday's row will have 3 pictures.

misconceptions.A: This doubles the pictures. When each picture stands for more children, fewer pictures are needed.
misconceptions.B: Well done! 24 children need only 3 pictures of 8.
misconceptions.C: This is the number of children. The question asks how many pictures of 8 children are needed.
misconceptions.D: This multiplies 6 by 8. Find the number of children first, then divide by 8.

G4A_DATA_019.questionText: In a pictograph, a full picture stands for 10 coconuts and a half picture stands for 5 coconuts. Monday's row has 3 full pictures and 1 half picture. Tuesday's row has 2 full pictures. How many coconuts were sold on the two days together?
hints: Work out each day's coconuts, counting full pictures and half pictures separately.
For Monday, find 3 full pictures of 10 and then add 5 for the half picture.
Example: A full picture is 4 and a half picture is 2. A row with 2 full pictures and 1 half picture shows 8 + 2 = 10.

stepByStep.text: Monday: 3 full pictures and a half picture.
Tuesday: 2 full pictures.
Add the two days.
55 coconuts were sold on the two days.

misconceptions.A: This leaves out the half picture. A half picture stands for 5 coconuts, so add 5.
misconceptions.B: This counts the half picture as a full one. A half picture stands for only 5 coconuts.
misconceptions.C: Yes! Monday's 35 and Tuesday's 20 make 55.
misconceptions.D: This is how many more were sold on Monday. The question asks for both days together.

G4A_DATA_020.questionText: A tally chart of birds uses bundles of 5 and single strokes. Crows: 2 bundles and 3 strokes. Sparrows: 3 bundles and 1 stroke. Pigeons: 1 bundle and 4 strokes. How many birds were counted in all?
hints: Change each tally row into a number, then add the rows.
Start with crows: 2 bundles are 10, and 3 strokes more.
Example: Row one has 1 bundle and 2 strokes, which is 7. Row two has 2 bundles and 1 stroke, which is 11. Together 7 + 11 = 18.

stepByStep.text: Crows.
Sparrows.
Pigeons.
Add the three rows.
38 birds were counted in all.

misconceptions.A: This counts every bundle as 1. Each bundle stands for 5 birds.
misconceptions.B: This counts the bundles but leaves out the single strokes. Add the 3, 1 and 4 strokes too.
misconceptions.C: This adds only the single strokes. The 6 bundles stand for 30 more birds.

G4A_DATA_021.questionText: A bar graph shows kites sold: Mon 14, Tue 9, Wed 17, Thu 11. Friday's bar is twice as tall as Tuesday's bar. How many kites were sold on the five days altogether?
hints: One value is not given directly. Find it from the clue, then add all five days.
Find Friday's number first. It is twice Tuesday's number, which is 9.
Example: Mon 5, Tue 8, and Wednesday is twice Monday. Wednesday is 10, and the total is 5 + 8 + 10 = 23.

stepByStep.text: Friday is twice Tuesday.
Add Monday to Thursday.
Add Friday.
69 kites were sold altogether.

misconceptions.A: Yes! Four days give 51, Friday gives 18, and 51 + 18 = 69.
misconceptions.B: This is the total for Monday to Thursday. Friday's kites must be added too.
misconceptions.C: This adds 2 for Friday. Twice as tall means 2 times Tuesday's 9, which is 18.
misconceptions.D: This takes Friday the same as Tuesday. Friday's bar is twice as tall, so it shows 18.

G4A_DATA_022.questionText: 40 children each chose one favourite game. Cricket was chosen by 16, football by 10 and badminton by 8. All the others chose kabaddi. How many children chose kabaddi?
hints: The whole group is known. The children who are left over after three games chose the fourth game.
Add the children who chose cricket, football and badminton: 16 + 10 + 8.
Example: 30 children; 12 chose red and 9 chose blue, the rest chose green. 12 + 9 = 21, so green got 30 - 21 = 9.

stepByStep.text: Add the three known games.
Take this away from all the children.
6 children chose kabaddi.

misconceptions.A: This is the number who chose the other three games. Take it away from 40.
misconceptions.B: That is right! 40 - 34 = 6.
misconceptions.C: This takes away cricket and football only. Badminton's 8 children must be taken away too.
misconceptions.D: This takes away cricket and badminton only. Football's 10 children must be taken away too.

G4A_DATA_023.questionText: Meera read 12 pages on Monday, 0 pages on Tuesday, 9 pages on Wednesday and 15 pages on Thursday. What is the average number of pages she read per day over these four days?
hints: An average shares the total equally over all the days, even a day when nothing was read.
Add the pages for all four days: 12 + 0 + 9 + 15.
Example: Goals in three matches are 4, 0 and 2. The total is 6, and 6 divided by 3 matches = 2 goals per match.

stepByStep.text: Add the pages.
There are 4 days, and Tuesday counts as a day too.
Share the total equally.
The average is 9 pages per day.

misconceptions.A: This divides by 3 and leaves Tuesday out. Tuesday is still one of the four days, so divide by 4.
misconceptions.B: This is the total number of pages. For the average, share the total equally among the 4 days.
misconceptions.C: Well done! 36 pages shared over 4 days is 9 pages per day.
misconceptions.D: This is the biggest number in the list. The average is the total shared equally over the 4 days.

G4A_DATA_024.questionText: A bar graph shows cups of tea sold: Mon 22, Tue 17, Wed 25, Thu 19. Which list puts the days in order from the shortest bar to the tallest bar?
hints: The shortest bar shows the smallest number and the tallest bar shows the biggest number.
Find the smallest of 22, 17, 25 and 19. That day comes first.
Example: Sun 8, Mon 5, Tue 9. From smallest to biggest the numbers are 5, 8, 9, so the order is Mon, Sun, Tue.

stepByStep.text: From smallest to biggest the numbers are 17, 19, 22, 25.
17 is Tuesday, 19 is Thursday, 22 is Monday and 25 is Wednesday.
The order from shortest to tallest is Tue, Thu, Mon, Wed.

misconceptions.A: This list goes from the tallest bar to the shortest. The question asks for shortest first.
misconceptions.B: Tuesday and Wednesday are in the right places, but Thursday's 19 is smaller than Monday's 22.
misconceptions.C: This is the order of the days in the week. Put them in order of their numbers instead.
misconceptions.D: Lovely! 17, 19, 22, 25 gives Tue, Thu, Mon, Wed.

G4A_DATA_025.questionText: A school has three clubs. Art: 9 girls and 6 boys. Music: 7 girls and 11 boys. Chess: 5 girls and 12 boys. Which club has the most children?
hints: Each club has girls and boys. Find each club's total before comparing.
Add the girls and boys in the Art club: 9 + 6.
Example: Team P has 4 girls and 9 boys, 13 in all. Team Q has 8 girls and 6 boys, 14 in all. Team Q has more children.

stepByStep.text: Art club.
Music club.
Chess club.
18 is the biggest total, so the club with the most children is Music.

misconceptions.A: Yes! Music has 18 children, more than Art's 15 and Chess's 17.
misconceptions.B: Art has the most girls, but the question asks about all children. Add girls and boys for each club.
misconceptions.C: Chess has the most boys, but with its girls it has 17 children. One club has more.
misconceptions.D: The totals are 15, 18 and 17, so they are not equal. Find the biggest total.

G4A_DATA_026.questionText: Children chose their favourite fruit: Mango 18, Apple 9, Banana 12, Orange 6, Grapes 3. Which fruit was chosen by exactly twice as many children as orange?
hints: Twice as many means two times a number. Find that number, then look for it in the list.
Orange was chosen by 6 children. Work out 2 times 6.
Example: Tea 4, Milk 8, Juice 10. Twice as many as tea is 2 x 4 = 8, and that is milk.

stepByStep.text: Orange was chosen by 6 children.
Twice as many as 6.
12 children chose banana, so the answer is Banana.

misconceptions.A: Mango's 18 is three times orange's 6. Twice 6 is 12.
misconceptions.B: That is right! 2 x 6 = 12, and 12 children chose banana.
misconceptions.C: Apple's 9 is 3 more than orange's 6, not twice as many. Twice 6 is 12.
misconceptions.D: Grapes' 3 is half of orange's 6. Twice as many means 2 times 6.

G4A_DATA_027.questionText: Hardik played 5 cricket matches. His average score was 32 runs per match. How many runs did he score in the 5 matches altogether?
hints: An average tells you what each match would have if the total were shared equally. Here you go back from the average to the total.
Think of every one of the 5 matches as having 32 runs.
Example: The average of 4 matches is 20 runs. The total is 4 x 20 = 80 runs.

stepByStep.text: The average is the total shared equally among the matches.
So the total is the average multiplied by the number of matches.
He scored 160 runs altogether.

misconceptions.A: This adds 32 and 5. The total is 5 lots of 32, so multiply.
misconceptions.B: This subtracts 5 from 32. The total is 5 lots of 32, so multiply.
misconceptions.C: Well done! 5 matches of 32 runs make 160 runs.
misconceptions.D: This is 2 lots of 32. There are 5 matches, so find 5 lots of 32.

G4A_DATA_028.questionText: The rainfall in a town, in millimetres, was: Mon 6, Tue 10, Wed 4, Thu 12, Fri 8. On how many days was the rainfall more than the average for the five days?
hints: There are two jobs here: find the average first, then compare each day with it.
Add the five numbers and divide the total by 5 to get the average.
Example: Values 3, 9, 6. The average is 18 divided by 3 = 6. Only 9 is more than 6, so 1 value is above the average.

stepByStep.text: Add the rainfall.
Find the average.
Compare each day with 8: only 10 and 12 are more than 8. Friday's 8 is equal to the average, not more.
The rainfall was more than the average on 2 days.

misconceptions.A: This also counts Friday. Friday's rainfall is equal to the average, and the question asks for more than the average.
misconceptions.B: This is the average itself. Now count the days whose rainfall is more than 8.
misconceptions.C: This counts every day that is different from the average. Count only the days above 8.
misconceptions.D: Well done! The average is 8, and only Tuesday and Thursday are above it.

G4A_DATA_029.questionText: Ananya's average mark in 4 tests was 18. After the 5th test, her average for all 5 tests became 20. How many marks did she get in the 5th test?
hints: An average multiplied by the number of tests gives the total. Compare the total before and after.
Find Ananya's total marks in the first 4 tests: 4 times 18.
Example: The average of 2 tests is 10, so the total is 20. After a 3rd test the average is 12, so the total is 36. The 3rd test was 36 - 20 = 16 marks.

stepByStep.text: Total of the first 4 tests.
Total of all 5 tests.
The difference is the 5th test.
She got 28 marks in the 5th test.

misconceptions.A: That is right! The total rose from 72 to 100, so the 5th test was 28.
misconceptions.B: A 5th mark of 20 would not pull an average of 18 all the way up to 20. Compare the two totals.
misconceptions.C: This adds 2 to 20. The 5th test has to lift the average of all five tests by 2, so compare the totals 72 and 100.
misconceptions.D: This adds the two averages. Change each average into a total first, then subtract.

G4A_DATA_030.questionText: A pictograph shows old newspapers collected by two classes. Class 4A has 7 pictures and Class 4B has 4 pictures. Each picture stands for the same number of newspapers. Class 4A collected 21 more newspapers than Class 4B. How many newspapers did Class 4A collect?
hints: The value of one picture is not given. Use the extra pictures and the extra newspapers to find it.
Class 4A has 7 - 4 = 3 more pictures. These 3 pictures stand for the 21 extra newspapers.
Example: Row one has 6 pictures, row two has 4, and row one shows 10 more. The 2 extra pictures stand for 10, so each picture is 5 and row one shows 6 x 5 = 30.

stepByStep.text: Class 4A has 3 more pictures.
These 3 pictures stand for 21 newspapers.
Class 4A has 7 pictures of 7 newspapers each.
Class 4A collected 49 newspapers.

misconceptions.A: This is what Class 4B collected: 4 pictures of 7. The question asks about Class 4A.
misconceptions.B: Great thinking! Each picture stands for 7, so 7 pictures stand for 49.
misconceptions.C: This is how many more Class 4A collected. Use it to find the value of one picture, then find 7 pictures.
misconceptions.D: This multiplies 21 by 7. The 21 newspapers are shared by the 3 extra pictures, so each picture is 7.

G4A_DATA_031.questionText: Class 4 has 42 children, and 23 of them are girls. 15 children come to school by bus, and 9 of these are girls. How many boys do NOT come by bus?
hints: Sort the children two ways: girls or boys, and bus or no bus. Find the boys' numbers step by step.
Find how many boys are in the class: 42 - 23.
Example: 30 children, 18 girls, so 12 boys. 10 come by bus and 6 of them are girls, so 4 bus boys. Boys not by bus: 12 - 4 = 8.

stepByStep.text: Boys in the class.
Boys who come by bus.
Boys who do not come by bus.
13 boys do not come by bus.

misconceptions.A: This is the number of boys who do come by bus. Take them away from all the boys.
misconceptions.B: This is the number of girls who do not come by bus. The question asks about boys.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 19 boys in all, 6 by bus, so 13 not by bus.
misconceptions.D: This is the number of all the boys. Take away the 6 boys who come by bus.

G4A_DATA_032.questionText: Vikram found the average of five numbers to be 20. Then he saw that he had copied one number as 25 when it was really 15. What is the correct average?
hints: A slip in one number changes the total, and the change is shared among all five numbers.
Find the total Vikram used: 5 times 20.
Example: The average of 4 numbers is 10, so the total is 40. One number was written as 12 instead of 4, so the true total is 40 - 8 = 32 and the true average is 32 divided by 4 = 8.

stepByStep.text: The total Vikram used.
The number was 10 too big, so take 10 off.
Share the correct total among the five numbers.
The correct average is 18.

misconceptions.A: This makes the total bigger. The copied number was too big, so the correct total is smaller.
misconceptions.B: This takes the whole 10 away from the average. The 10 is shared among five numbers, so the average falls by only 2.
misconceptions.C: This is the number that was copied badly. The average comes from the corrected total, 90, divided by 5.
misconceptions.D: Well done! The total drops from 100 to 90, and 90 divided by 5 is 18.

G4A_DATA_033.questionText: A shop sold school bags: Mon 14, Tue 18, Wed 10. On Saturday it sold as many bags as on Monday and Tuesday together. On Sunday it sold half as many bags as on Saturday. How many bags did it sell on these five days altogether?
hints: Two of the five numbers are hidden in clues. Find them one at a time, then add everything.
Find Saturday's number first: add Monday's 14 and Tuesday's 18.
Example: Mon 4, Tue 6. Saturday equals both together, 10, and Sunday is half of that, 5. The total is 4 + 6 + 10 + 5 = 25.

stepByStep.text: Saturday.
Sunday is half of Saturday.
Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday together.
Add all five days.
The shop sold 90 bags altogether.

misconceptions.B: This leaves out Sunday's 16 bags. Sunday is half of Saturday.
misconceptions.C: This leaves out Saturday's 32 bags. Saturday equals Monday and Tuesday together.
misconceptions.D: This takes Sunday the same as Saturday. Sunday is half of Saturday, so it is 16.

G4A_DATA_034.questionText: Four friends have 8, 14, 11 and 7 marbles. They share the marbles so that all four have the same number. How many marbles must the friend who had 14 give away?
hints: Sharing equally gives everyone the average. Find what each friend ends up with.
Add all the marbles: 8 + 14 + 11 + 7.
Example: Three friends have 1, 9 and 2 sweets. The total is 12, so each gets 12 divided by 3. The friend with 9 keeps that equal share and gives away the other 5 sweets.

stepByStep.text: Add all the marbles.
Share equally among 4 friends.
The friend with 14 keeps 10.
That friend must give away 4 marbles.

misconceptions.A: This is how many marbles each friend ends up with. The question asks how many the friend with 14 gives away.
misconceptions.B: That is right! Each friend ends with 10, so the friend with 14 gives away 4.
misconceptions.C: This is the gap between 14 and 8. Find the equal share first, then see how far 14 is above it.
misconceptions.D: This is the gap between 14 and 7. Find the equal share first, then see how far 14 is above it.

G4A_DATA_035.questionText: Riya and Kabir each drew a pictograph of their stamps. In Riya's chart each picture stands for 5 stamps and there are 12 pictures. In Kabir's chart each picture stands for 8 stamps and there are 7 pictures. Who has more stamps, and by how many?
hints: The two charts use different values for a picture, so you cannot compare the pictures directly.
Change Riya's pictures into stamps: 12 pictures of 5 stamps each.
Example: Chart one has 6 pictures of 2, which is 12. Chart two has 3 pictures of 5, which is 15. Chart two shows 15 - 12 = 3 more.

stepByStep.text: Riya's stamps.
Kabir's stamps.
Compare.
Riya has more stamps, by 4.

misconceptions.A: The gap of 4 is right, but check who has more: Riya has 60 stamps and Kabir has 56.
misconceptions.B: This compares the numbers of pictures, 12 and 7. Change the pictures into stamps first.
misconceptions.C: Super! Riya's 60 stamps are 4 more than Kabir's 56.
misconceptions.D: This compares the values of one picture, 8 and 5. Find each child's total stamps first.

G4A_CIRCLE_001.questionText: The diameter of a circular plate is 18 cm. What is its radius?
hints: Think about how the radius and the diameter of a circle are related.
The radius is half of the diameter. Find half of 18.
Example: A circle has diameter 10 cm. Its radius is 10 divided by 2 = 5 cm.

stepByStep.text: The radius goes from the centre to the circle. The diameter goes right across through the centre, so it is two radii.
Halve the diameter.
The radius is 9 cm.

misconceptions.A: This doubles 18. Doubling turns a radius into a diameter; here you need to go from diameter to radius, so halve.
misconceptions.B: The radius is shorter than the diameter. It is exactly half of it.
misconceptions.C: This divides 18 by 3. A diameter is made of 2 radii, so divide by 2.
misconceptions.D: Well done! Half of 18 cm is 9 cm.

G4A_CIRCLE_002.questionText: Kiran wants to draw a circle of diameter 12 cm with a compass. How far apart should the needle point and the pencil tip be?
hints: The needle of a compass sits at the centre and the pencil draws the circle. Think about which length that is.
The opening of the compass is the radius. Find the radius of a circle whose diameter is 12 cm.
Example: For a circle of diameter 20 cm, the compass is opened to the radius, 20 divided by 2 = 10 cm.

stepByStep.text: The needle is at the centre and the pencil is on the circle, so the opening of the compass is the radius.
The radius is half the diameter.
The needle point and pencil tip should be 6 cm apart.

misconceptions.A: Yes! The compass is opened to the radius, and half of 12 cm is 6 cm.
misconceptions.B: An opening of 12 cm would give a circle 24 cm across. The compass is opened to the radius, not the diameter.
misconceptions.C: This doubles 12. The compass opening is the radius, which is half of the diameter.
misconceptions.D: This halves 12 twice. Halve only once to go from diameter to radius.

G4A_CIRCLE_003.questionText: A circle has a radius of 8 cm. How long is the longest chord that can be drawn in this circle?
hints: A chord joins two points on a circle. Think about which chord is the longest of all.
The longest chord passes through the centre, so it is the diameter. Find the diameter when the radius is 8 cm.
Example: In a circle of radius 5 cm, the longest chord is the diameter, 2 x 5 = 10 cm.

stepByStep.text: The longest chord of a circle is the one through the centre, which is the diameter.
The diameter is twice the radius.
The longest chord is 16 cm.

misconceptions.A: 8 cm is the radius. The longest chord goes right across the circle through the centre.
misconceptions.B: That is right! The longest chord is the diameter, 16 cm.
misconceptions.C: This halves the radius. The longest chord is the diameter, which is twice the radius.
misconceptions.D: This multiplies 8 by 8. The longest chord is the diameter, 2 times the radius.

G4A_CIRCLE_004.questionText: A circle has a radius of 6 cm. Point P is 4 cm away from the centre of the circle. Where is point P?

options.text: At the centre of the circle

hints: Every point on a circle is exactly one radius away from the centre. Compare the point's distance with the radius.
Is 4 cm less than, equal to, or more than the radius of 6 cm?
Example: A circle has radius 5 cm and a point is 9 cm from the centre. Since 9 is more than 5, that point is outside the circle.

stepByStep.text: Points on the circle are exactly 6 cm from the centre.
Point P is 4 cm from the centre, and 4 is less than 6.
A point closer to the centre than the radius lies inside the circle, so P is inside the circle.

misconceptions.A: A point on the circle would be exactly 6 cm from the centre. P is only 4 cm away.
misconceptions.B: A point outside the circle would be more than 6 cm from the centre. P is only 4 cm away.
misconceptions.C: Well done! 4 cm is less than the radius of 6 cm, so P is inside the circle.
misconceptions.D: The centre is 0 cm away from itself. P is 4 cm away from the centre, so it is not at the centre.

G4A_CIRCLE_005.questionText: O is the centre of a circle. A and B are two different points on the circle. If OA = 7 cm, how long is OB?
hints: Think about what kind of line joins the centre of a circle to a point on the circle.
OA and OB both go from the centre to the circle, so both are radii. What do you know about all the radii of one circle?
Example: In a circle with centre C, if CP = 4 cm and Q is also on the circle, then CQ is also a radius, so CQ = 4 cm.

stepByStep.text: OA joins the centre to a point on the circle, so OA is a radius.
OB also joins the centre to a point on the circle, so OB is a radius too.
All radii of a circle are equal, so OB = 7 cm.

misconceptions.A: 14 cm is the diameter. OB stops at the centre, so it is a radius.
misconceptions.B: This halves the radius. OB is a full radius, just like OA.
misconceptions.C: This is three radii. OB is one radius, just like OA.
misconceptions.D: Yes! Every radius of the same circle has the same length, 7 cm.

G4A_CIRCLE_006.questionText: Four equal circles, each of radius 3 cm, are drawn in a straight row so that each circle touches the next one. What is the distance from the centre of the first circle to the centre of the last circle?
hints: When two equal circles touch, think about how far apart their centres are.
The centres of two touching circles are one radius plus one radius apart. Find that distance for radius 3 cm.
Example: Three circles of radius 2 cm touch in a row. Neighbouring centres are 4 cm apart, and there are 2 gaps from first to last, so the distance is 2 x 4 = 8 cm.

stepByStep.text: Centres of neighbouring circles are two radii apart.
From the first centre to the fourth centre there are 3 gaps.
Multiply.
The distance between the first and last centres is 18 cm.

misconceptions.A: Great thinking! 3 gaps of 6 cm make 18 cm.
misconceptions.B: This is the full length of the row, 4 diameters. From centre to centre, half a circle is left out at each end.
misconceptions.C: This multiplies 4 circles by the radius. Count the gaps between centres: there are 3, each 6 cm.
misconceptions.D: This uses 3 gaps of 3 cm. Each gap between centres is two radii, 6 cm.

G4A_CIRCLE_007.questionText: Six round bangles, each of radius 4 cm, are placed in a straight row on a table so that each bangle touches the next. How long is the row from end to end?
hints: Each bangle takes up its full width in the row. Think about which length of a circle is its width.
The width of one bangle is its diameter. Find the diameter when the radius is 4 cm.
Example: Five coins of radius 1 cm in a row. Each coin is 2 cm wide, so the row is 5 x 2 = 10 cm long.

stepByStep.text: Each bangle is one diameter wide.
There are 6 bangles in the row.
The row is 48 cm long.

misconceptions.A: This uses the radius as the width. Each bangle is a full diameter, 8 cm, wide.
misconceptions.B: That is right! 6 bangles, each 8 cm wide, make 48 cm.
misconceptions.C: This counts 5 gaps between centres. From end to end, all 6 full bangles are counted.
misconceptions.D: This doubles the diameter again. Each bangle is 8 cm wide, and there are 6 of them.

G4A_CIRCLE_008.questionText: A circle is drawn inside a square of side 10 cm so that it just touches all four sides of the square. What is the radius of the circle?
hints: Picture the circle fitting snugly in the square. Think about which length of the circle stretches from one side of the square to the opposite side.
The circle reaches from one side to the opposite side, so its diameter equals the side of the square, 10 cm.
Example: A circle just fits in a square of side 8 cm. Its diameter is 8 cm, so its radius is 4 cm.

stepByStep.text: The circle touches opposite sides of the square, so its diameter equals the side of the square.
The diameter is 10 cm.
The radius is half the diameter.
The radius of the circle is 5 cm.

misconceptions.A: 10 cm is the diameter of the circle. The radius is half of that.
misconceptions.B: This doubles the side. The side of the square equals the diameter, and the radius is half of it.
misconceptions.C: Well done! The diameter is 10 cm, so the radius is 5 cm.
misconceptions.D: This is the perimeter of the square. The radius is half of one side.

G4A_CIRCLE_009.questionText: A circle of radius 6 cm fits exactly inside a square, touching all four sides. What is the perimeter of the square?
hints: First find the side of the square from the circle, then find the distance around the square.
The side of the square equals the diameter of the circle. Find the diameter when the radius is 6 cm.
Example: A circle of radius 2 cm fits exactly in a square. The side is 4 cm, so the perimeter is 4 x 4 = 16 cm.

stepByStep.text: The side of the square equals the diameter.
A square has 4 equal sides.
The perimeter of the square is 48 cm.

misconceptions.A: This uses the radius as the side. The side of the square is the diameter, 12 cm.
misconceptions.B: This is one side of the square. The perimeter is all 4 sides together.
misconceptions.C: This is the area of the square, 12 x 12. The perimeter is 4 times the side.
misconceptions.D: Yes! Each side is 12 cm, and 4 sides make 48 cm.

G4A_CIRCLE_010.questionText: Two coins lie flat on a table and touch each other. The radius of one coin is 5 cm and the radius of the other is 3 cm. How far apart are their centres?
hints: Imagine a straight line from one centre to the other. It passes through the point where the coins touch.
The line goes from the first centre to the touching point (one radius), then on to the second centre (the other radius).
Example: Circles of radius 4 cm and 2 cm touch side by side. Their centres are 4 + 2 = 6 cm apart.

stepByStep.text: The line joining the centres passes through the point where the coins touch.
It is made of the radius of one coin and the radius of the other.
Add the two radii.
The centres are 8 cm apart.

misconceptions.A: That is right! One radius of 5 cm and one of 3 cm make 8 cm.
misconceptions.B: This subtracts the radii. The coins lie side by side, so the two radii are added.
misconceptions.C: This adds the two diameters. From centre to centre you need only one radius of each coin.
misconceptions.D: This multiplies the radii. The distance is one radius plus the other radius.

G4A_CIRCLE_011.questionText: Two circles are drawn with the same centre. The radius of the big circle is 9 cm and the radius of the small circle is 5 cm. How wide is the ring between the two circles?
hints: Walk in a straight line from the centre outwards. You cross the small circle first and then the big circle.
The width of the ring is how much farther the big circle is from the centre than the small circle.
Example: Circles with the same centre have radii 10 cm and 7 cm. The ring between them is 10 - 7 = 3 cm wide.

stepByStep.text: Going out from the centre, the small circle is 5 cm away and the big circle is 9 cm away.
The ring is the gap between them.
The ring is 4 cm wide.

misconceptions.A: This adds the radii. The ring is the gap between the circles, so subtract.
misconceptions.B: Well done! The big circle is 4 cm farther from the centre than the small one.
misconceptions.C: This subtracts the diameters, 18 and 10. The ring's width on one side is the difference of the radii.
misconceptions.D: This halves the gap. The ring's width is the full difference of the radii, 9 - 5.

G4A_CIRCLE_012.questionText: The diameter of a circle is 12 cm longer than its radius. What is the radius of the circle?
hints: A diameter is made of two radii. Think about what is left when you take one radius away from the diameter.
Diameter = radius + radius. If the diameter is also radius + 12 cm, what must the second radius be?
Example: A diameter is 5 cm longer than its radius. Since the diameter is radius + radius, the extra part is one radius, so the radius is 5 cm.

stepByStep.text: The diameter is two radii: radius + radius.
We are told the diameter is radius + 12 cm.
Comparing the two, the second radius must be the extra 12 cm.
Check: the diameter is 24 cm, and it is 12 cm longer than the radius.
The radius is 12 cm.

misconceptions.A: This halves 12. Check it: a radius of 6 cm gives a diameter of 12 cm, which is only 6 cm longer.
misconceptions.B: 24 cm is the diameter of this circle. The question asks for the radius.
misconceptions.C: Great thinking! The diameter, 24 cm, is exactly 12 cm longer than the radius, 12 cm.
misconceptions.D: This divides 12 by 3. Check it: a radius of 4 cm gives a diameter of 8 cm, which is only 4 cm longer.

G4A_CIRCLE_013.questionText: A circle has a radius of 6 cm. Which of these lengths can NOT be the length of a chord of this circle?
hints: A chord joins two points on the circle. Think about how long the longest possible chord is.
The longest chord is the diameter. Find the diameter when the radius is 6 cm.
Example: In a circle of radius 5 cm the longest chord is 10 cm, so a chord of 11 cm is not possible, but chords of 3 cm or 10 cm are.

stepByStep.text: The longest chord is the diameter.
So a chord can be any length up to 12 cm, but never longer.
4 cm, 9 cm and 12 cm are all possible. The length that cannot be a chord is 13 cm.

misconceptions.A: A short chord of 4 cm fits easily near the edge of the circle. Look for a length longer than the diameter.
misconceptions.B: A chord of 9 cm is shorter than the diameter of 12 cm, so it fits. Look for a length longer than the diameter.
misconceptions.C: 12 cm is exactly the diameter, which is the longest chord, so it is possible.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 13 cm is longer than the diameter of 12 cm, so no chord can be that long.

G4A_CIRCLE_014.questionText: A rectangular tray is 20 cm long and 8 cm wide. Round biscuits of radius 2 cm are laid flat on it in straight rows, touching each other but not overlapping. What is the greatest number of biscuits that fit on the tray?
hints: Each round biscuit needs a square space as wide as the biscuit. Find how many fit along the length and along the width.
The width of one biscuit is its diameter. Find the diameter when the radius is 2 cm.
Example: A tray 12 cm by 6 cm holds circles of radius 3 cm. Each is 6 cm wide, so 2 fit along the length and 1 along the width: 2 x 1 = 2 circles.

stepByStep.text: Each biscuit is one diameter wide.
Biscuits along the length.
Rows along the width.
Multiply.
The tray holds 10 biscuits.

misconceptions.A: Well done! 2 rows of 5 biscuits make 10.
misconceptions.B: This is one row only. The tray is 8 cm wide, so a second row of 4 cm biscuits fits too.
misconceptions.C: This uses 2 cm as the width of a biscuit across the tray. Each biscuit is a full 4 cm wide in both directions.
misconceptions.D: This uses the radius, 2 cm, as the width of a biscuit. Each biscuit is one diameter, 4 cm, wide.

G4A_CIRCLE_015.questionText: A piece of wire is bent to make a circle of radius 7 cm. The same wire is straightened and bent again to make a square. What is the side of the square? (Use π = 22/7)
hints: The length of the wire does not change. It is the distance around the circle, and then the distance around the square.
Find the circumference of the circle: 2 times 22/7 times 7.
Example: A wire makes a circle of radius 14 cm. Its length is 2 x 22/7 x 14 = 88 cm. Bent into a square, each side is 88 divided by 4 = 22 cm.

stepByStep.text: The length of the wire is the circumference of the circle.
The same 44 cm of wire goes around the square.
A square has 4 equal sides.
The side of the square is 11 cm.

misconceptions.A: 44 cm is the whole length of the wire. Share it among the 4 sides of the square.
misconceptions.B: That is right! 44 cm of wire makes a square of side 11 cm.
misconceptions.C: 14 cm is the diameter of the circle. The side of the square comes from the wire's length, 44 cm, shared among 4 sides.
misconceptions.D: This divides the wire by 2. A square has 4 equal sides, so divide 44 by 4.

G4A_CIRCLE_016.questionText: The radius of a big circle is equal to the diameter of a small circle. The radius of the small circle is 3 cm. What is the diameter of the big circle?
hints: Go one step at a time: small radius, small diameter, big radius, big diameter.
Find the diameter of the small circle first: twice 3 cm.
Example: A small circle has radius 2 cm, so its diameter is 4 cm. A big circle with radius 4 cm has diameter 8 cm.

stepByStep.text: Diameter of the small circle.
This is the radius of the big circle, so the big radius is 6 cm.
Diameter of the big circle.
The diameter of the big circle is 12 cm.

misconceptions.A: 6 cm is the radius of the big circle. Double it to get the big circle's diameter.
misconceptions.B: 3 cm is the radius of the small circle. Double it to get the big radius, then double again.
misconceptions.C: Well done! Doubling twice takes 3 cm to 6 cm and then to 12 cm.
misconceptions.D: This multiplies 3 by 3. Each step from radius to diameter is a doubling.

G4A_CIRCLE_017.questionText: Three equal circles with centres A, B and C each have a radius of 4 cm. Each circle touches the other two. What is the perimeter of triangle ABC?
hints: Each side of the triangle joins the centres of two touching circles. Find the length of one side first.
When two circles touch, the distance between their centres is one radius plus the other radius: 4 + 4.
Example: Three circles of radius 5 cm touch each other. Each side of the triangle of centres is 10 cm, so its perimeter is 3 x 10 = 30 cm.

stepByStep.text: Each side joins two centres of touching circles.
The triangle has 3 such sides.
The perimeter of triangle ABC is 24 cm.

misconceptions.A: This uses 4 cm for each side. Each side is two radii, 8 cm.
misconceptions.B: 8 cm is one side of the triangle. The perimeter is all 3 sides together.
misconceptions.C: This doubles once too often. Each side is 8 cm, and 3 sides make the perimeter.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 3 sides of 8 cm make 24 cm.

G4A_CIRCLE_018.questionText: Ten equal circles are drawn inside a rectangle in 2 rows of 5. Each circle touches the circles next to it, and the outer circles touch the sides of the rectangle. The perimeter of the rectangle is 84 cm. What is the radius of each circle?
hints: Write the length and the width of the rectangle as a number of diameters, then use the perimeter.
The length is 5 diameters and the width is 2 diameters. How many diameters make up half of the perimeter?
Example: Six circles in 2 rows of 3 fill a rectangle of perimeter 40 cm. Length + width = 3 + 2 = 5 diameters = 20 cm, so a diameter is 4 cm and the radius is 2 cm.

stepByStep.text: The length is 5 diameters and the width is 2 diameters.
Length + width is half the perimeter.
Length + width is 7 diameters.
The radius is half the diameter.
The radius of each circle is 3 cm.

misconceptions.A: Great work! The diameter is 6 cm, so the radius is 3 cm.
misconceptions.B: 6 cm is the diameter of each circle. The radius is half of it.
misconceptions.C: This divides the whole perimeter by 7. Only half the perimeter, 42 cm, equals 7 diameters.
misconceptions.D: This divides 84 by 4 as if the rectangle were a square. The length is 5 diameters and the width is 2 diameters.

G4A_CIRCLE_019.questionText: A small circle of radius 3 cm lies inside a big circle of radius 10 cm and touches it at exactly one point. How far apart are the centres of the two circles?
hints: Draw a line from the big centre to the touching point. The small circle's centre lies on this line.
From the big centre to the touching point is 10 cm. From the small centre to the same point is 3 cm.
Example: A circle of radius 2 cm touches a circle of radius 8 cm from inside. The centres are 8 - 2 = 6 cm apart.

stepByStep.text: The big centre, the small centre and the touching point lie on one straight line.
The big centre is 10 cm from the touching point, and the small centre is 3 cm from it.
The distance between the centres is the difference.
The centres are 7 cm apart.

misconceptions.A: Adding the radii is for circles that touch side by side from outside. Here the small circle is inside the big one.
misconceptions.B: That is right! The small centre is 3 cm back from the touching point, so it is 7 cm from the big centre.
misconceptions.C: This takes away the small circle's diameter. Only its radius lies between its centre and the touching point.
misconceptions.D: This multiplies the radii. The centres are apart by the difference of the radii.

G4A_CIRCLE_020.questionText: Three circles of radii 2 cm, 3 cm and 4 cm are drawn in a row with their centres on one straight line. The middle circle, of radius 3 cm, touches the other two. What is the distance from the centre of the first circle to the centre of the last circle?
hints: Travel along the line from the first centre to the last centre and note which parts of each circle you cross.
You cross one radius of the first circle, then the whole middle circle, then one radius of the last circle.
Example: Circles of radii 1 cm, 2 cm and 5 cm in a row. From first centre to last centre: 1 + (2 + 2) + 5 = 10 cm.

stepByStep.text: From the first centre to its edge is one radius, 2 cm.
Crossing the whole middle circle is its diameter.
From the edge of the last circle to its centre is one radius, 4 cm.
Add the three parts.
The distance between the first and last centres is 12 cm.

misconceptions.A: This adds the three radii once each. The middle circle is crossed completely, so its radius is counted twice.
misconceptions.B: This is the full length of the row from end to end. From centre to centre, only one radius of each end circle is counted.
misconceptions.C: Well done! 2 + 6 + 4 = 12.
misconceptions.D: This counts the whole last circle. Stop at its centre, so count only one radius, 4 cm, for it.

G4A_CIRCLE_021.questionText: The circumference of a circle is 88 cm. The circle fits exactly inside a square, touching all four sides. What is the side of the square? (Use π = 22/7)
hints: Work backwards from the circumference to the radius, then think about how the circle sits in the square.
Circumference = 2 times 22/7 times radius. So 44/7 times the radius is 88.
Example: A circle has circumference 44 cm. Then 44/7 times the radius is 44, so the radius is 7 cm. The square around it has side equal to the diameter, 14 cm.

stepByStep.text: The circumference is 2 times 22/7 times the radius.
So the radius is 14 cm.
The side of the square equals the diameter.
The side of the square is 28 cm.

misconceptions.A: 14 cm is the radius of the circle. The side of the square is the diameter.
misconceptions.B: This shares 88 cm among 4 sides. The 88 cm goes around the circle, not around the square.
misconceptions.C: This doubles the diameter. The side of the square is equal to one diameter.
misconceptions.D: Yes! The radius is 14 cm, so the diameter and the side of the square are 28 cm.

G4A_CIRCLE_022.questionText: A circle of radius 7 cm is cut out of a square sheet of paper of side 14 cm. What is the area of the paper that is left? (Use π = 22/7)
hints: The paper left is the square with the circle taken away. Find two areas.
Find the area of the square first: 14 times 14.
Example: A circle of area 154 sq cm is cut from a square sheet of side 20 cm. The square is 400 sq cm, so 400 - 154 = 246 sq cm is left.

stepByStep.text: Area of the square.
Area of the circle.
Take the circle away from the square.
The area of paper left is 42 sq cm.

misconceptions.A: That is right! 196 - 154 = 42.
misconceptions.B: This takes away the circumference, 44, from the area of the square. Take away the area of the circle, 154.
misconceptions.C: This is the area of the circle that was cut out. The question asks for the paper left behind.
misconceptions.D: This adds the two areas. The circle is cut out, so subtract it from the square.

G4A_CIRCLE_023.questionText: Five points are marked on a circle. Every pair of points is joined by a straight line. How many chords are drawn?
hints: Each chord joins two of the points. Count the pairs in an orderly way so that none is counted twice.
Call the points P, Q, R, S, T. Start by counting the chords from P to each of the other four points.
Example: With 4 points on a circle, the first point joins 3 others, the next joins 2 new ones, and the next joins 1 new one: 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 chords.

stepByStep.text: From the first point, 4 chords go to the other points.
From the second point, 3 new chords can be drawn, then 2 from the third and 1 from the fourth.
Add them.
10 chords are drawn.

misconceptions.A: This counts only the chords joining neighbouring points. Points that are not neighbours are joined too.
misconceptions.B: Well done! 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10 chords.
misconceptions.C: This counts 4 chords from each of the 5 points, but then every chord is counted twice, once from each end.
misconceptions.D: This multiplies 5 by 5. A point is not joined to itself, and each chord should be counted only once.

G4A_CIRCLE_024.questionText: Two square trays each have a side of 24 cm. The first tray is exactly filled by 9 equal round plates in 3 rows of 3. The second tray is exactly filled by 16 equal round plates in 4 rows of 4. In each tray the plates touch each other and the sides. How much longer is the radius of a plate in the first tray than in the second tray?
hints: In each tray, the plates in one row share the 24 cm side equally. Find each plate's diameter, then its radius.
In the first tray, 3 plates fit across 24 cm. Find the diameter of one plate: 24 divided by 3.
Example: A 20 cm square tray holds 2 plates across, so each is 10 cm wide with radius 5 cm. If it holds 5 plates across, each is 4 cm wide with radius 2 cm. The radii differ by 5 - 2 = 3 cm.

stepByStep.text: First tray: 3 plates across.
So the radius of a plate in the first tray is 4 cm.
Second tray: 4 plates across.
So the radius of a plate in the second tray is 3 cm.
Compare the radii.
The radius in the first tray is longer by 1 cm.

misconceptions.A: This compares the diameters, 8 cm and 6 cm. The question asks about the radii, 4 cm and 3 cm.
misconceptions.B: 3 cm is the radius of a plate in the second tray. Compare it with the radius in the first tray, 4 cm.
misconceptions.C: Great work! The radii are 4 cm and 3 cm, so the difference is 1 cm.
misconceptions.D: This adds the two radii. To find how much longer, subtract.

G4A_CIRCLE_025.questionText: A wire 132 cm long is cut into 3 equal pieces. Each piece is bent to make a circle. What is the radius of each circle? (Use π = 22/7)
hints: Each piece of wire becomes the distance around one circle. Find the length of one piece first.
Divide 132 cm by 3 to find the length of one piece.
Example: A wire 176 cm long is cut into 2 equal pieces of 88 cm. For a circle, 44/7 times the radius is 88, so the radius is 14 cm.

stepByStep.text: Length of one piece.
This is the circumference of one circle: 2 times 22/7 times the radius is 44.
A radius of 7 cm fits.
The radius of each circle is 7 cm.

misconceptions.A: 14 cm is the diameter of each circle. The radius is half of it.
misconceptions.B: This is the radius if the whole 132 cm wire made one circle. The wire is first cut into 3 equal pieces.
misconceptions.C: 44 cm is the length of one piece, which is the circumference. Use it to find the radius.
misconceptions.D: Yes! Each piece is 44 cm, and a circle of radius 7 cm has circumference 44 cm.

G4A_TIME_001.questionText: A train leaves Pune station at 17:20 on the 24-hour clock. What is this time on the 12-hour clock?
hints: On the 24-hour clock, hours bigger than 12 are afternoon or evening times.
Take 12 away from the hours: 17 - 12. The minutes stay the same.
Example: 14:35 on the 24-hour clock. 14 - 12 = 2, so it is 2:35 pm.

stepByStep.text: 17 is more than 12, so the time is after noon and is a pm time.
Take 12 away from the hours.
The minutes stay as 20, so the time is 5:20 pm.

misconceptions.A: That is right! 17 - 12 = 5, so 17:20 is 5:20 pm.
misconceptions.B: This takes 10 away from 17. Noon is 12 o'clock, so take away 12.
misconceptions.C: The hour 5 is right, but 17:20 comes after noon, so it is pm.
misconceptions.D: This takes 13 away from 17. Noon is 12 o'clock, so take away 12.

G4A_TIME_002.questionText: How many days are there altogether in the months of June and July?
hints: You need to remember how many days each month has. The knuckle trick or the rhyme 'Thirty days has September' can help.
June has 30 days. How many days does July have?
Example: December has 31 days and January has 31 days. Together they have 31 + 31 = 62 days.

stepByStep.text: June has 30 days.
July has 31 days.
Add them.
June and July have 61 days altogether.

misconceptions.A: This takes both months as 30 days. July has 31 days.
misconceptions.B: Well done! 30 + 31 = 61.
misconceptions.C: This takes both months as 31 days. June has only 30 days.
misconceptions.D: This is too few. June has 30 days and July has 31 days.

G4A_TIME_003.questionText: How many days are there in February 2028?
hints: February is the only month whose length changes. It depends on whether the year is a leap year.
A year like this is a leap year if 4 divides it exactly. Try dividing 2028 by 4.
Example: For February 2023, divide 2023 by 4. It leaves a remainder of 3, so 2023 is not a leap year and its February has 28 days.

stepByStep.text: Check whether 4 divides 2028 exactly.
There is no remainder, so 2028 is a leap year.
In a leap year February has one extra day, so February 2028 has 29 days.

misconceptions.A: February has 28 days in an ordinary year. Check whether 2028 is a leap year by dividing it by 4.
misconceptions.B: February never has 30 days. It has 28 days, or one more in a leap year.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 2028 is a leap year, so February has 29 days.
misconceptions.D: February never has 31 days. It has 28 days, or one more in a leap year.

G4A_TIME_004.questionText: A film is 135 minutes long. How long is that in hours and minutes?
hints: One hour is 60 minutes. See how many full hours fit into the minutes, and what is left.
Two hours are 120 minutes. Is 135 more than 120? How much more?
Example: 80 minutes. One hour is 60 minutes, and 80 - 60 = 20, so 80 minutes is 1 hour 20 minutes.

stepByStep.text: Two full hours fit into 135 minutes.
Find the minutes left over.
135 minutes is 2 hours 15 minutes.

misconceptions.A: This reads 135 as 1 hour and 35 minutes. An hour has 60 minutes, not 100.
misconceptions.B: The 2 hours are right, but 2 hours use up 120 minutes, leaving 15 minutes.
misconceptions.C: 3 hours would be 180 minutes, which is more than 135. Only 2 full hours fit.
misconceptions.D: Well done! 120 minutes make 2 hours, and 15 minutes are left.

G4A_TIME_005.questionText: Today is Wednesday. What day of the week will it be 10 days from today?
hints: The days of the week repeat every 7 days. Take out the full weeks first.
7 days from Wednesday is Wednesday again. How many days are left out of 10 after taking away 7?
Example: Today is Monday. 9 days later: 7 days bring Monday again, and 2 more days give Wednesday.

stepByStep.text: After 7 days it is Wednesday again.
Days still to count.
Three days after Wednesday: Thursday, Friday, Saturday.
It will be Saturday.

misconceptions.A: That is right! 7 days bring Wednesday again, and 3 more days bring Saturday.
misconceptions.B: This counts Wednesday itself as the first day. Start counting from tomorrow, Thursday.
misconceptions.C: This counts one day too many. After the full week, only 3 more days are needed.
misconceptions.D: Wednesday comes again after 7 days. There are 3 more days to count after that.

G4A_TIME_006.questionText: Arjun's school starts at 8:00 am and ends at 1:30 pm. How long is his school day?
hints: The time passes 12 noon, so count in two parts: up to noon, and after noon.
Find how long it is from 8:00 am to 12 noon.
Example: From 9:00 am to 2:15 pm. From 9:00 am to noon is 3 hours, and from noon to 2:15 pm is 2 hours 15 minutes, so 5 hours 15 minutes in all.

stepByStep.text: From 8:00 am to 12 noon.
From 12 noon to 1:30 pm is 1 hour 30 minutes.
4 hours and 1 hour 30 minutes make 5 hours 30 minutes.

misconceptions.A: This subtracts 1 from 8. The clock passes 12 noon, so count up to noon and then on to 1:30 pm.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 4 hours before noon and 1 hour 30 minutes after noon make 5 hours 30 minutes.
misconceptions.C: This counts one hour too many. From 8:00 am to noon is 4 hours, then add 1 hour 30 minutes.
misconceptions.D: This leaves out an hour. From 8:00 am to noon is 4 hours, then add 1 hour 30 minutes.

G4A_TIME_007.questionText: Dadi's favourite TV serial starts at a quarter to 7 in the evening. What is this time on the 24-hour clock?
hints: First write the time with hours and minutes, then change it to the 24-hour clock.
A quarter to 7 means 15 minutes before 7 o'clock. Which hour is it still in, and how many minutes past?
Example: A quarter to 4 in the afternoon is 3:45 pm. Adding 12 to the hours gives 15:45.

stepByStep.text: A quarter to 7 is 15 minutes before 7 o'clock, which is 6:45.
It is evening, so the time is 6:45 pm.
For a pm time, add 12 to the hours.
On the 24-hour clock the time is 18:45.

misconceptions.A: This is a quarter past 7 in the evening. A quarter to 7 is 15 minutes before 7 o'clock.
misconceptions.B: 6:45 is right, but this is the morning time. For the evening, add 12 to the hours.
misconceptions.C: Well done! A quarter to 7 in the evening is 6:45 pm, which is 18:45.
misconceptions.D: This puts 45 minutes after 7 o'clock. A quarter to 7 is before 7, in the hour of 6.

G4A_TIME_008.questionText: A train journey from Kanyakumari to Jammu takes exactly 3 days. How many hours is that?
hints: Think about how many hours make one full day, counting day and night together.
One day has 24 hours. Find 3 lots of 24.
Example: 2 days are 2 x 24 = 48 hours.

stepByStep.text: One full day has 24 hours.
Multiply by 3 days.
The journey takes 72 hours.

misconceptions.A: This uses 12 hours for a day. A full day, with its night, has 24 hours.
misconceptions.B: This multiplies by 60. There are 60 minutes in an hour, but 24 hours in a day.
misconceptions.C: This adds 3 and 24. Three days are 3 lots of 24 hours, so multiply.
misconceptions.D: That is right! 3 x 24 = 72 hours.

G4A_TIME_009.questionText: A night bus leaves Bengaluru at 9:30 pm. The journey to Chennai takes 6 hours 45 minutes. At what time does the bus reach Chennai?
hints: The journey crosses midnight, so the answer will be an am time on the next day. Add the hours and the minutes in parts.
Add the 6 hours first. Going 6 hours on from 9:30 pm passes midnight: where do you land?
Example: Leave at 10:40 pm and travel 3 hours 30 minutes. Three hours later it is 1:40 am, and 30 more minutes make 2:10 am.

stepByStep.text: Add 6 hours to 9:30 pm: it becomes 3:30 am the next day.
Now add 45 minutes. 30 minutes take the time to 4:00 am.
The remaining minutes.
The bus reaches Chennai at 4:15 am.

misconceptions.A: The 75 minutes from 30 + 45 make 1 hour and 15 minutes. Carry that extra hour to the hours.
misconceptions.B: Well done! 6 hours later is 3:30 am, and 45 minutes more is 4:15 am.
misconceptions.C: The numbers are right, but the bus travels through the night, so it arrives in the early morning, am.
misconceptions.D: This goes back 6 hours 45 minutes. The journey time must be added to the starting time.

G4A_TIME_010.questionText: A train leaves Mumbai at 22:40 and reaches Goa at 05:10 the next morning. How long is the journey?
hints: The journey crosses midnight. Split it into the part before midnight and the part after midnight.
Find how long it is from 22:40 to midnight, which is 24:00.
Example: From 23:15 to 02:30 the next day. Up to midnight is 45 minutes, and after midnight is 2 hours 30 minutes, so 3 hours 15 minutes in all.

stepByStep.text: From 22:40 to midnight is 1 hour 20 minutes.
From midnight to 05:10 is 5 hours 10 minutes.
Add: 1 hour 20 minutes and 5 hours 10 minutes make 6 hours 30 minutes.
The journey takes 6 hours 30 minutes.

misconceptions.A: This subtracts 05:10 from 22:40. The train arrives the next day, so count on through midnight.
misconceptions.B: This is one hour too long. From 22:40 to midnight is only 1 hour 20 minutes.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 1 hour 20 minutes before midnight and 5 hours 10 minutes after make 6 hours 30 minutes.
misconceptions.D: This adds 40 minutes and 10 minutes. Before midnight there are only 20 minutes left in the hour after 22:40.

G4A_TIME_011.questionText: In a certain month, the 5th is a Tuesday. What day of the week is the 23rd of the same month?
hints: The same day of the week comes again every 7 days. Jump forward in sevens from the date you know.
Add 7 to the 5th again and again to find other Tuesdays: 5, 12, and so on.
Example: The 3rd is a Monday. The 10th and 17th are also Mondays, so the 20th, three days later, is a Thursday.

stepByStep.text: The Tuesdays are 7 days apart.
So the 19th is a Tuesday.
Days from the 19th to the 23rd.
Four days after Tuesday: Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday.
The 23rd is a Saturday.

misconceptions.A: This stops one day early. From Tuesday the 19th, count 4 days on to reach the 23rd.
misconceptions.B: This goes one day too far. From Tuesday the 19th, count 4 days on to reach the 23rd.
misconceptions.C: This counts only 2 days on from the 19th. The 23rd is 4 days after the 19th.
misconceptions.D: That is right! The 19th is a Tuesday, and 4 days later is Saturday.

G4A_TIME_012.questionText: How many days after 20 February 2024 is 5 March 2024?
hints: Count the days left in February, then the days in March. Check how long February is in that year.
2024 can be divided exactly by 4, so it is a leap year. How many days does its February have?
Example: From 25 February 2023 to 4 March 2023. February 2023 has 28 days, so 3 days are left in February, and 4 more in March make 7 days.

stepByStep.text: 2024 is a leap year, so February has 29 days.
Days left in February after the 20th.
Add the 5 days of March.
5 March 2024 is 14 days after 20 February 2024.

misconceptions.A: Well done! 9 days are left in February 2024, and 5 days of March make 14.
misconceptions.B: This takes February as 28 days. 2024 is a leap year, so its February has 29 days.
misconceptions.C: This takes February as 30 days. In the leap year 2024, February has 29 days.
misconceptions.D: This takes February as 31 days. In the leap year 2024, February has 29 days.

G4A_TIME_013.questionText: Anil practises the tabla for 40 minutes every day. For how long does he practise in one week?
hints: Find the total minutes for the week, then change the minutes into hours and minutes.
A week has 7 days. Find 7 lots of 40 minutes.
Example: 50 minutes a day for 3 days is 150 minutes. Two hours are 120 minutes, so that is 2 hours 30 minutes.

stepByStep.text: Minutes in one week.
Four hours are 240 minutes.
Minutes left over.
He practises for 4 hours 40 minutes in one week.

misconceptions.A: This counts only 5 days. Anil practises every day, and a week has 7 days.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 280 minutes is 4 hours 40 minutes.
misconceptions.C: This reads 280 as 2 hours and 80 minutes. An hour has 60 minutes, so 280 minutes hold 4 full hours.
misconceptions.D: The 4 hours are right. Check the minutes left: 280 - 240.

G4A_TIME_014.questionText: A month has 30 days, and its 1st day is a Saturday. How many Sundays are there in this month?
hints: Find the date of the first Sunday, then keep jumping forward 7 days until the month ends.
If the 1st is a Saturday, the first Sunday is the very next day, the 2nd.
Example: A month of 30 days begins on a Monday. Its first Sunday is the 7th, and the others are the 14th, 21st and 28th, so that month has 4 Sundays.

stepByStep.text: The 1st is a Saturday, so the 2nd is the first Sunday.
Add 7 each time: the Sundays are the 2nd, 9th, 16th, 23rd and 30th.
The 30th is still inside the month.
There are 5 Sundays in this month.

misconceptions.A: 30 days hold 4 full weeks and 2 extra days. The extra days here are a Saturday and a Sunday, so there is one more Sunday.
misconceptions.B: A sixth Sunday would be on the 37th, and the month has only 30 days.
misconceptions.C: Great counting! The Sundays are the 2nd, 9th, 16th, 23rd and 30th.
misconceptions.D: Keep adding 7 until the month ends: 2, 9, 16, 23 and 30 are all Sundays.

G4A_TIME_015.questionText: Kavya's train leaves at 14:10. She wants to reach the station 25 minutes before the train leaves, and it takes her 35 minutes to travel from home to the station. What is the latest time she can leave home?
hints: Work backwards from the train time. Both the early arrival and the travel time come before the train leaves.
Add the two amounts of time she needs before 14:10: 25 minutes and 35 minutes.
Example: A bus leaves at 16:30. Rahul wants to be 10 minutes early and needs 20 minutes to get there. He needs 30 minutes in all, so he leaves at 16:00, which is 4:00 pm.

stepByStep.text: Total time needed before the train leaves.
60 minutes is 1 hour.
One hour before 14:10 is 13:10.
Change to the 12-hour clock.
The latest she can leave home is 1:10 pm.

misconceptions.A: This is the time she wants to reach the station. She must leave home 35 minutes before that.
misconceptions.B: This takes away only the 35 minutes of travel. She also wants to be 25 minutes early.
misconceptions.C: This goes forward from the train time. She has to leave home before the train, so count backwards.
misconceptions.D: Well done! She needs 60 minutes in all, and one hour before 14:10 is 1:10 pm.

G4A_FRACTIONS_001.questionText: A jug holds 7/8 litre of lassi. Meena pours out 5/12 litre for her brother. How much lassi is left in the jug?
hints: This is a taking-away problem with fractions whose bottom numbers are different. The pieces must be the same size before you can subtract.
Find a number that both 8 and 12 divide into exactly, and change both fractions so that they have that bottom number.
A similar one: 3/4 − 1/6. Both 4 and 6 divide into 12, so 3/4 = 9/12 and 1/6 = 2/12. Then 9/12 − 2/12 = 7/12.

stepByStep.text: The smallest number that both 8 and 12 divide into is 24.
Change both fractions to twenty-fourths.
Subtract the top numbers and keep the bottom number.
11/24 litre of lassi is left in the jug.

misconceptions.A: Yes! In twenty-fourths, 21/24 − 10/24 leaves 11/24 litre.
misconceptions.B: This comes from subtracting the tops and the bottoms separately (7 − 5 and 12 − 8). Make the bottom numbers the same first, then subtract only the tops.
misconceptions.C: This is what you get by adding the two amounts. Lassi was poured out, so take 10/24 away from 21/24.
misconceptions.D: Here the bottom number became 24 but the tops stayed 7 and 5. When 8 becomes 24 the 7 must become 21, and the 5 becomes 10.

G4A_FRACTIONS_002.questionText: A ribbon is 5 1/4 m long. Kavya cuts off 2 2/3 m to wrap a gift. How long is the ribbon now?
hints: This is subtraction of mixed numbers. Make the fraction parts the same kind, then check whether the first fraction part is big enough to subtract from.
Write 1/4 and 2/3 in twelfths. Is 3/12 big enough to take 8/12 away from? If not, break one whole from the 5 into 12/12.
A similar one: 4 1/6 − 1 1/2. In sixths, 1/2 = 3/6. 1/6 is too small, so 4 1/6 becomes 3 7/6. Then 3 7/6 − 1 3/6 = 2 4/6 = 2 2/3.

stepByStep.text: Write the fraction parts in twelfths.
3/12 is smaller than 8/12, so take one whole from the 5 and turn it into 12/12.
Subtract the wholes and the fraction parts.
The ribbon is now 2 7/12 m long.

misconceptions.A: This takes 5 − 2 = 3 and then the smaller fraction from the bigger one (2/3 − 1/4). The 2/3 has to be taken from the 5 1/4, so one whole must be broken up first.
misconceptions.B: The fraction part 7/12 is right, but one whole was broken into twelfths to get it. That leaves 4 wholes, and 4 − 2 = 2.
misconceptions.C: The whole number 2 is right. For the fraction part, 15/12 − 8/12 is 7/12, not 8/12 − 3/12.
misconceptions.D: Well done! After breaking one whole into twelfths, 4 15/12 − 2 8/12 = 2 7/12 m.

G4A_FRACTIONS_003.questionText: A baker cuts every cake into 6 equal slices. By evening she has sold 47 slices. How many cakes is that, written as a mixed number?
hints: Each cake is 6 sixths. You are turning a number of sixths into whole cakes and left-over slices.
Work out how many full groups of 6 slices fit into 47 slices, and how many slices are left over.
A similar one: 29 slices when each cake has 4 slices. 29 ÷ 4 = 7 remainder 1, so that is 7 whole cakes and 1/4 of a cake: 7 1/4.

stepByStep.text: 47 slices, each one-sixth of a cake, is the fraction 47/6.
Divide 47 by 6.
7 whole cakes and 5 slices out of 6 make 7 5/6 cakes.

misconceptions.A: Right! 7 full cakes use 42 slices, and the 5 slices left are 5/6 of a cake: 7 5/6.
misconceptions.B: The 7 and the 5 are right, but the left-over slices are sixths of a cake. The bottom number stays 6, not 47.
misconceptions.C: This rounds up to 48 slices. 47 slices is a little less than 8 cakes: 7 full cakes and 5 slices more.
misconceptions.D: The 7 and the 5 have changed places. The number of full cakes (7) is the whole number and the left-over slices (5) go on top of the 6.

G4A_FRACTIONS_004.questionText: Which of these numbers is the greatest? 3 2/5, 17/4, 4 1/8, 25/6
hints: Some of these are mixed numbers and some are improper fractions. Put them all in the same form before you compare.
Change 17/4 and 25/6 into mixed numbers. Then compare the whole-number parts first.
A similar one: which is greater, 13/5 or 2 1/2? 13/5 = 2 3/5. Both have 2 wholes, and 3/5 is more than 1/2, so 13/5 is greater.

stepByStep.text: Change the improper fractions to mixed numbers.
3 2/5 has only 3 wholes, so it is the smallest. The other three all have 4 wholes.
Compare the fraction parts 1/4, 1/8 and 1/6. With the same top number, the smaller bottom number gives the bigger piece, so 1/4 is the biggest.
The greatest number is 17/4.

misconceptions.A: 3 2/5 has only 3 wholes, while the others have 4 wholes each. Look at the whole-number part first.
misconceptions.B: Well done! 17/4 is 4 1/4, and a quarter is bigger than a sixth or an eighth.
misconceptions.C: 4 1/8 can look big because of the 8, but an eighth is a small piece. Compare 1/8 with 1/4 and 1/6.
misconceptions.D: 25/6 has the biggest top number, but it is only 4 1/6. Change each one to a mixed number before comparing.

hints: To put several fractions in order, give them all the same bottom number. Then the top numbers tell you the order.
4, 8, 12 and 3 all divide into 24. Change each fraction into twenty-fourths.
A similar one: order 1/2, 7/10 and 3/5. In tenths they are 5/10, 7/10 and 6/10, so from smallest to greatest: 1/2, 3/5, 7/10.

stepByStep.text: Change every fraction to twenty-fourths.
Do the same for the other two.
Order the top numbers: 14, 15, 16, 18.
From smallest to greatest: 7/12, 5/8, 2/3, 3/4.

misconceptions.A: These are in order, but from greatest to smallest. The question asks for smallest first.
misconceptions.B: This puts the top numbers 2, 3, 5, 7 in order. A bigger top number does not always mean a bigger fraction; change them all to twenty-fourths first.
misconceptions.C: Nearly there. Check the first two: 5/8 is 15/24 and 7/12 is 14/24, so 7/12 is the smaller one.
misconceptions.D: Yes! In twenty-fourths they are 14, 15, 16 and 18, which gives 7/12, 5/8, 2/3, 3/4.

G4A_FRACTIONS_006.questionText: Four friends ran before school. Asha ran 3/5 km, Bala ran 3/4 km, Chitra ran 3/10 km and Dev ran 3/7 km. Who ran the second longest distance?
hints: All four fractions have the same top number. Think about what the bottom number tells you about the size of each piece.
When the top numbers are the same, the fraction with the smallest bottom number is the biggest. Put 4, 5, 7 and 10 in order.
A similar one: 2/9, 2/3 and 2/5. Thirds are the biggest pieces, then fifths, then ninths. So the longest is 2/3 and the second longest is 2/5.

stepByStep.text: Every distance is 3 pieces of a kilometre, so only the size of the pieces matters.
Quarters are bigger than fifths, fifths are bigger than sevenths, and sevenths are bigger than tenths.
From longest to shortest: 3/4 (Bala), 3/5 (Asha), 3/7 (Dev), 3/10 (Chitra).
The second longest distance was run by Asha.

misconceptions.A: Right! Bala's 3/4 km is the longest and Asha's 3/5 km comes next.
misconceptions.B: Bala's 3/4 km is the longest of all. The question asks who came second.
misconceptions.C: Chitra's fraction has the biggest bottom number, but tenths are the smallest pieces, so 3/10 km is the shortest run.
misconceptions.D: Dev's 3/7 km is the third longest. Fifths are bigger pieces than sevenths, so 3/5 is more than 3/7.

G4A_FRACTIONS_007.questionText: Ravi has Rs. 240. He spends 3/8 of it on a cricket ball and 1/3 of it on a book. How much money does he have left?
hints: This is a fraction-of-an-amount story with two parts. Find each amount spent, then see what is left.
To find 3/8 of Rs. 240, first find 1/8 of 240 by dividing by 8.
A similar one: Rs. 120, with 1/4 and 1/3 of it spent. 1/4 of 120 is 30 and 1/3 of 120 is 40. 120 − 30 − 40 = Rs. 50 left.

stepByStep.text: Find 3/8 of 240. One eighth is 30, so three eighths is 90.
Find 1/3 of 240.
Add the money spent.
Subtract from Rs. 240. Ravi has Rs. 70 left.

misconceptions.A: Rs. 170 is the money Ravi spent. The question asks how much is left, so take it away from Rs. 240.
misconceptions.B: This takes away only the cricket ball (Rs. 90). The book costs 1/3 of Rs. 240 as well.
misconceptions.C: Well done! He spends Rs. 90 and Rs. 80, and 240 − 170 leaves Rs. 70.
misconceptions.D: This takes 1/3 of the money left after the ball. The story says 1/3 of it, meaning 1/3 of the whole Rs. 240.

G4A_FRACTIONS_008.questionText: In a class, 3/5 of the children are girls. There are 18 girls. How many children are there in the class?
hints: Here you know a part and must find the whole. Think of the class as 5 equal groups, with 3 of the groups being girls.
3 equal groups make 18 girls. Find how many children are in one group.
A similar one: 2/7 of a class is 8 children. One seventh is 8 ÷ 2 = 4, so the whole class is 4 × 7 = 28 children.

stepByStep.text: 3/5 of the class is 18 children, so 3 equal parts make 18.
Find one part (one fifth).
The whole class is 5 parts.
There are 30 children in the class.

misconceptions.A: This multiplies 18 by 3. But 18 is already three of the five parts; divide by 3 to find one part.
misconceptions.B: Yes! One fifth of the class is 6 children, so five fifths is 30 children.
misconceptions.C: This multiplies 18 by 5, as if 18 were one fifth. 18 is three fifths, so one fifth is 6.
misconceptions.D: 12 is the number of boys. The question asks for all the children, girls and boys together.

G4A_FRACTIONS_009.questionText: Kiran has read 2/7 of his storybook. He still has 150 pages to read. How many pages does the book have?
hints: The 150 pages are the part not yet read. First work out what fraction of the book that part is.
If 2/7 has been read, then 5/7 is left. So 5 equal parts of the book make 150 pages.
A similar one: after reading 1/4 of a book, 90 pages are left. 90 pages is 3/4, so 1/4 is 30 pages and the book has 4 × 30 = 120 pages.

stepByStep.text: Find the fraction still to be read.
5/7 of the book is 150 pages, so one seventh is 30 pages.
The whole book is seven sevenths.
The book has 210 pages.

misconceptions.A: Right! 150 pages is 5/7 of the book, so 1/7 is 30 pages and the book has 210 pages.
misconceptions.B: This treats the 150 pages as 2/7 of the book. They are the pages left, which is 5/7 of the book.
misconceptions.C: 60 is the number of pages Kiran has read. The question asks for all the pages in the book.
misconceptions.D: This adds one seventh (30 pages) to 150. Kiran has read two sevenths, so add 60 pages.

G4A_FRACTIONS_010.questionText: What must be subtracted from 3 1/2 to get 1 5/6?
hints: The number you take away is the gap between the two numbers. So this is a subtraction of mixed numbers.
Work out 3 1/2 − 1 5/6. Start by writing 1/2 in sixths.
A similar one: what must be subtracted from 2 1/4 to get 1 1/2? 2 1/4 − 1 1/2 = 9/4 − 6/4 = 3/4.

stepByStep.text: The number to subtract is 3 1/2 − 1 5/6.
Write both as improper fractions in sixths.
Subtract.
10/6 = 5/3 = 1 2/3, so 1 2/3 must be subtracted.

misconceptions.A: This takes 3 − 1 = 2 and then 5/6 − 1/2. The 5/6 has to be taken from the 1/2, so a whole must be broken into sixths first.
misconceptions.B: Well done! 21/6 − 11/6 = 10/6, which is 1 2/3.
misconceptions.C: This adds the two numbers. The number to subtract is the gap between them: 3 1/2 − 1 5/6.
misconceptions.D: The whole number 1 is right. The fraction part is 4/6, and dividing top and bottom by 2 gives 2/3.

G4A_FRACTIONS_011.questionText: Twelve beads are threaded on a string in this order: R R B G R B B R G R B R, where R is a red bead, B is a blue bead and G is a green bead. What fraction of the beads are blue, in lowest terms?
hints: A fraction of a group is the number you are counting over the number in the whole group. Then make the fraction as simple as you can.
Count the blue beads carefully along the row. That count goes on top, and 12 goes on the bottom.
A similar one: in a row of 10 beads, 4 are yellow. The fraction is 4/10, and dividing the top and bottom by 2 gives 2/5.

stepByStep.text: Count the blue beads in the row: there are 4.
There are 12 beads in all, so the fraction that is blue is 4/12.
Divide the top and bottom by 4.
1/3 of the beads are blue.

misconceptions.A: 1/2 is the fraction of red beads (6 out of 12). The question asks about the blue beads.
misconceptions.B: 1/6 is the fraction of green beads (2 out of 12). Count the blue beads instead.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 4 of the 12 beads are blue, and 4/12 in lowest terms is 1/3.
misconceptions.D: There are 4 blue beads, but the fraction is 4 out of 12, not 1 out of 4. Put the count over 12 and then simplify.

G4A_FRACTIONS_012.questionText: A fraction is equal to 3/5. Its numerator and denominator add up to 40. What is its denominator?
hints: Fractions equal to 3/5 are made by multiplying its top and bottom by the same number. Look for the one whose two numbers have the right total.
In 3/5 itself the top and bottom add up to 8. How many times does 8 go into 40?
A similar one: a fraction equal to 2/3 whose top and bottom add up to 20. 2 + 3 = 5 and 20 ÷ 5 = 4, so multiply both by 4 to get 8/12. Its denominator is 12.

stepByStep.text: Fractions equal to 3/5 come from multiplying the top and bottom by the same number: 6/10, 9/15, 12/20 and so on.
In 3/5 the top and bottom add up to 8. We need a total of 40, which is 5 times as much.
Multiply the top and bottom by 5.
15 + 25 = 40, so the denominator is 25.

misconceptions.A: 15 is the numerator of the fraction 15/25. The question asks for the denominator, the bottom number.
misconceptions.B: 24 is 3/5 of 40. But 40 is the total of the top and bottom together, so share it into 3 parts and 5 parts.
misconceptions.C: 8 is 3 + 5, a useful first step. Next see how many times 8 goes into 40 and multiply the top and bottom by that number.
misconceptions.D: Right! 15/25 equals 3/5 and 15 + 25 = 40, so the denominator is 25.

G4A_FRACTIONS_013.questionText: Anu drank 1/2 litre of water in the morning, 3/4 litre in the afternoon and 5/8 litre in the evening. How much water did she drink in all?
hints: You are adding three fractions with different bottom numbers. Change them into the same kind of piece first.
2 and 4 both divide into 8, so write 1/2 and 3/4 as eighths.
A similar one: 1/2 + 1/4 + 3/8. In eighths that is 4/8 + 2/8 + 3/8 = 9/8, which is 1 1/8.

stepByStep.text: Change the first two fractions to eighths.
Add the three fractions.
15/8 is 8/8 and 7/8 more, so Anu drank 1 7/8 litres.

misconceptions.A: This adds the tops (1 + 3 + 5) and the bottoms (2 + 4 + 8). Only the tops are added, and only after the bottoms are made the same.
misconceptions.B: Here 1/2 was written as 2/8. Half of 8 eighths is 4 eighths, so 1/2 = 4/8.
misconceptions.C: Well done! 4/8 + 6/8 + 5/8 = 15/8, which is 1 7/8 litres.
misconceptions.D: The top 15 is right, but the bottom numbers were added as well. When eighths are added, the answer is still in eighths: 15/8.

G4A_FRACTIONS_014.questionText: Rahul's school day is 6 hours long. He spends 1 hour 30 minutes of it in maths lessons. What fraction of the school day is spent on maths?
hints: To write one time as a fraction of another, both must be in the same unit.
Change 6 hours into minutes and 1 hour 30 minutes into minutes. Then put the maths time over the whole school day.
A similar one: what fraction of 3 hours is 36 minutes? 3 hours = 180 minutes, so the fraction is 36/180, and that simplifies to 1/5.

stepByStep.text: Change both times into minutes.
Write the maths time over the school day.
Divide the top and bottom by 90.
1/4 of the school day is spent on maths.

misconceptions.A: This uses only the 1 hour and leaves out the 30 minutes. The maths time is 90 minutes in all.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 90 minutes out of 360 minutes is 1/4 of the school day.
misconceptions.C: This reads 1 hour 30 minutes as 1.30 hours. Thirty minutes is half an hour, so work in minutes: 90 out of 360.
misconceptions.D: 1/3 of 6 hours would be 2 hours. Maths takes 1 hour 30 minutes, which is 90 minutes out of 360.

G4A_FRACTIONS_015.questionText: Which of these fractions lies between 1/3 and 1/2?
hints: To see whether a fraction lies between two others, write them all with the same bottom number.
In twelfths, 1/3 = 4/12 and 1/2 = 6/12. Look for a fraction that is more than 4/12 but less than 6/12.
A similar one: which lies between 1/4 and 1/2, 3/8 or 5/8? In eighths, 1/4 = 2/8 and 1/2 = 4/8. 3/8 sits between 2/8 and 4/8, so there it is 3/8.

stepByStep.text: Write 1/3 and 1/2 in twelfths.
5/12 is more than 4/12 and less than 6/12.
The fraction that lies between 1/3 and 1/2 is 5/12.

misconceptions.A: Right! 1/3 is 4/12 and 1/2 is 6/12, and 5/12 sits exactly between them.
misconceptions.B: 1/4 is 3/12, which is less than 1/3 (4/12). A bigger bottom number means smaller pieces.
misconceptions.C: 7/12 is more than 6/12, so it is bigger than 1/2. Look for a fraction just under one half.
misconceptions.D: 3/10 is very close, but 3/10 = 9/30 and 1/3 = 10/30, so 3/10 is just below 1/3.

G4A_FRACTIONS_016.questionText: A tailor uses 2 3/4 m of cloth for a kurta and 1 5/6 m of cloth for a shirt. How much cloth does he use altogether?
