hints: This is addition of mixed numbers. Add the whole numbers, add the fraction parts, and watch for fraction parts that make more than one whole.
Write 3/4 and 5/6 in twelfths and add them. Is the total more than 12/12?
A similar one: 1 2/3 + 2 1/2. In sixths, 4/6 + 3/6 = 7/6 = 1 1/6. The wholes are 1 + 2 = 3. So the total is 3 + 1 1/6 = 4 1/6.

stepByStep.text: Add the whole numbers.
Add the fraction parts in twelfths.
19/12 is one whole and 7/12.
3 + 1 7/12 = 4 7/12, so he uses 4 7/12 m of cloth.

misconceptions.A: The fraction parts add up to 19/12, which is 1 7/12. That extra whole must be added to the 3 wholes.
misconceptions.B: This adds the tops (3 + 5) and the bottoms (4 + 6). Change 3/4 and 5/6 to twelfths before adding.
misconceptions.C: Here 3/4 was written as 3/12. When 4 becomes 12 the top must be multiplied by 3 too, so 3/4 = 9/12.
misconceptions.D: Well done! The fraction parts make 19/12 = 1 7/12, and with the 3 wholes that is 4 7/12 m.

G4A_FRACTIONS_017.questionText: 3 pizzas are shared equally among 4 children. Each child eats only half of his or her share. What fraction of a pizza does each child eat?
hints: There are two steps: first find each child's share, then find half of that share.
3 pizzas shared equally among 4 children gives each child 3/4 of a pizza. Now think about half of 3/4.
A similar one: 2 cakes shared equally among 5 children gives each child 2/5 of a cake. Half of 2 fifths is 1 fifth, so each child would eat 1/5.

stepByStep.text: 3 pizzas shared among 4 children gives each child 3/4 of a pizza.
Cut each quarter into two eighths, so 3/4 is the same as 6/8.
Half of 6 eighths is 3 eighths, so each child eats 3/8 of a pizza.

misconceptions.A: 3/4 is each child's full share. Each child eats only half of that share.
misconceptions.B: This takes 1/2 away from 3/4. Half of a share means splitting the share into two equal parts, not subtracting one half.
misconceptions.C: Yes! Each share is 3/4, and half of 3/4 is 3/8 of a pizza.
misconceptions.D: This doubles the share. Eating half of the share gives a smaller amount than 3/4, not a bigger one.

G4A_FRACTIONS_018.questionText: Which of these fractions is closest to 1/2? 3/8, 5/9, 2/3, 4/11
hints: Closest to 1/2 means the smallest gap from 1/2. Half of the bottom number tells you what the top would be for exactly one half.
For 3/8, exactly half would be 4/8, so 3/8 is 1/8 away. Find the gap for each of the other three in the same way.
A similar one: is 4/7 or 3/5 closer to 1/2? 4/7 − 1/2 = 1/14 and 3/5 − 1/2 = 1/10. 1/14 is the smaller gap, so 4/7 is closer.

stepByStep.text: Find how far 3/8 is from 1/2.
Find how far 5/9 is from 1/2.
In the same way, 2/3 is 1/6 away and 4/11 is 3/22 away.
Compare the gaps 1/8, 1/18, 1/6 and 3/22. The smallest is 1/18, because 3/22 is even more than 3/24, which is 1/8.
The fraction closest to 1/2 is 5/9.

misconceptions.A: 3/8 is 1/8 away from 1/2. That is close, but 5/9 is only 1/18 away.
misconceptions.B: Well done! 5/9 is just 1/18 more than 1/2, the smallest gap of the four.
misconceptions.C: 2/3 is 1/6 away from 1/2, the biggest gap of the four. Work out each gap by subtracting.
misconceptions.D: 4/11 is 3/22 below 1/2, which is a little more than 1/8. Look for a fraction with a smaller gap.

G4A_FRACTIONS_019.questionText: A cricket match has 50 overs. 35 overs have been bowled. What fraction of the overs is still to be bowled, in lowest terms?
hints: Read carefully which part the question asks about: the overs already bowled, or the overs still to come.
First subtract to find how many overs are still to be bowled. Put that number over 50.
A similar one: 40 overs with 24 bowled. 16 are left, so the fraction is 16/40. Dividing the top and bottom by 8 gives 2/5.

stepByStep.text: Find the overs still to be bowled.
Write this as a fraction of all 50 overs.
Divide the top and bottom by 5.
3/10 of the overs is still to be bowled.

misconceptions.A: 7/10 is the fraction already bowled (35 out of 50). The question asks for the part still to come.
misconceptions.B: This compares the 15 overs left with the 35 overs bowled. The fraction must be out of all 50 overs.
misconceptions.C: Here the top was divided by 5 but the bottom by 10. Divide both 15 and 50 by the same number, 5.
misconceptions.D: Right! 15 of the 50 overs are left, and 15/50 in lowest terms is 3/10.

G4A_FRACTIONS_020.questionText: □ − 2/3 = 3/4. Which number goes in the box?
hints: Something had 2/3 taken away and 3/4 was left. To get back to the start, undo the taking away.
Add 2/3 back on to 3/4. Use twelfths, because both 3 and 4 divide into 12.
A similar one: □ − 1/2 = 2/5. Add back: 2/5 + 1/2 = 4/10 + 5/10 = 9/10, so that box holds 9/10.

stepByStep.text: Undo the subtraction by adding: the box is 3/4 + 2/3.
Change both fractions to twelfths.
Add.
17/12 is one whole and 5/12, so the box holds 1 5/12.

misconceptions.A: This subtracts 2/3 from 3/4. The box is the number before 2/3 was taken away, so it must be bigger than 3/4: add instead.
misconceptions.C: This adds the tops (3 + 2) and the bottoms (4 + 3). Change both fractions to twelfths first, then add only the tops.
misconceptions.D: Here 2/3 was written as 4/12. Multiplying the bottom by 4 means multiplying the top by 4 too, so 2/3 = 8/12.

G4A_FRACTIONS_021.questionText: Meera spent 1/3 of her money on books. Then she spent 1/4 of the remaining money on a pen. She now has Rs. 90 left. How much money did she have at first?
hints: Work backwards from the money left. Notice that the second fraction is a fraction of what remained, not of all the money.
After spending 1/4 of the remaining money, 3/4 of it is left, and that is Rs. 90. Find the remaining money first.
A similar one: Raj spends 1/2 of his money, then 1/3 of the rest, and has Rs. 40 left. Rs. 40 is 2/3 of the rest, so the rest was Rs. 60. Rs. 60 is half of his money, so he began with Rs. 120.

stepByStep.text: After the pen, 3/4 of the remaining money is left, and this is Rs. 90. So 1/4 of it is Rs. 30.
The money left after buying the books was 4 quarters.
The books took 1/3 of all the money, so Rs. 120 is 2/3 of it. One third is Rs. 60.
Meera had 3 × 60 = Rs. 180 at first.

misconceptions.A: Well done! From Rs. 180, the books take Rs. 60, the pen takes 1/4 of Rs. 120 = Rs. 30, and Rs. 90 is left.
misconceptions.B: This adds 1/3 and 1/4 as if both were fractions of all the money. The 1/4 is taken from the money that remained after the books.
misconceptions.C: This undoes only one step. Rs. 90 is 3/4 of the money left after the books; find that amount first, then go back one more step.
misconceptions.D: This treats Rs. 90 as one quarter of all the money. Rs. 90 is three quarters of what remained after the books.

G4A_FRACTIONS_022.questionText: In a basket of mangoes, 2/5 are ripe, 1/3 are raw and the remaining 16 are half-ripe. How many mangoes are in the basket?
hints: The 16 half-ripe mangoes are whatever fraction is left after the ripe and raw ones. Find that fraction first.
Add 2/5 and 1/3 using fifteenths, then see how many fifteenths are left for the half-ripe mangoes.
A similar one: 1/2 of a box of balls are red, 1/3 are blue and the remaining 5 are green. 1/2 + 1/3 = 5/6, so the green balls are 1/6 of the box. The box has 5 × 6 = 30 balls.

stepByStep.text: Add the ripe and raw fractions.
The half-ripe mangoes are the rest of the basket.
4/15 of the basket is 16 mangoes, so 1/15 is 4 mangoes.
The whole basket is 15 × 4 = 60 mangoes.

misconceptions.A: This multiplies 16 by 4. The 16 mangoes are 4 of the 15 equal parts, so divide by 4 to find one part and then multiply by 15.
misconceptions.B: Yes! The half-ripe mangoes are 4/15 of the basket, so 1/15 is 4 mangoes and the basket holds 60.
misconceptions.C: This treats 16 as just one fifteenth. The half-ripe mangoes are four fifteenths of the basket.
misconceptions.D: 44 is the number of ripe and raw mangoes together. The question asks for all the mangoes in the basket.

G4A_FRACTIONS_023.questionText: The fractions 4/7, 5/9, 7/12 and 3/5 are arranged from smallest to greatest. Which fraction comes third?
hints: All four fractions are a little more than one half, so you need an exact way to compare them, such as cross-multiplying two at a time.
Start with 4/7 and 5/9: compare 4 × 9 with 5 × 7. The fraction whose top number gives the bigger product is the bigger fraction.
A similar one: order 2/3, 3/5 and 5/8. For 3/5 and 5/8: 3 × 8 = 24 and 5 × 5 = 25, so 3/5 is smaller. For 5/8 and 2/3: 5 × 3 = 15 and 2 × 8 = 16, so 5/8 is smaller. The order is 3/5, 5/8, 2/3.

stepByStep.text: Compare 5/9 and 4/7 by cross-multiplying: 5 × 7 = 35 and 4 × 9 = 36, so 5/9 is smaller than 4/7.
Compare 4/7 and 7/12: 4 × 12 = 48 and 7 × 7 = 49, so 4/7 is smaller than 7/12.
Compare 7/12 and 3/5: 7 × 5 = 35 and 3 × 12 = 36, so 7/12 is smaller than 3/5.
The order is 5/9, 4/7, 7/12, 3/5, so the third fraction is 7/12.

misconceptions.A: 4/7 comes second. It is bigger than 5/9 but smaller than 7/12, because 4 × 12 = 48 is less than 7 × 7 = 49.
misconceptions.B: 5/9 is the smallest of the four, so it comes first. Compare the fractions two at a time.
misconceptions.C: Right! The order is 5/9, 4/7, 7/12, 3/5, and 7/12 is third.
misconceptions.D: 3/5 is the greatest, so it comes last. The question asks for the third fraction.

G4A_FRACTIONS_024.questionText: 1/4 + 1/6 − 1/□ = 1/3. Which number goes in the box?
hints: Work out the part you can, 1/4 + 1/6. Then ask how much must be taken away from it to leave 1/3.
Write 1/4, 1/6 and 1/3 with the same bottom number. The gap between the first sum and 1/3 is the fraction with the box.
A similar one: 1/2 + 1/5 − 1/□ = 3/5. In tenths, 5/10 + 2/10 = 7/10 and 3/5 = 6/10. The part taken away is 1/10, so that box holds 10.

stepByStep.text: Add the first two fractions in twelfths.
Write 1/3 in twelfths too.
The amount taken away is the gap between them.
So 1/□ is 1/12, and the number in the box is 12.

misconceptions.A: Using twenty-fourths gives 10/24 − 8/24 = 2/24. That fraction must be simplified to 1/12 before reading off the box.
misconceptions.B: This adds and subtracts the bottom numbers (4 + 6 − 3). Change the fractions to the same bottom number instead.
misconceptions.C: Check 1/3 in twelfths: it is 4/12, not 2/12. Then 5/12 − 4/12 leaves 1/12.
misconceptions.D: Well done! 5/12 − 1/12 = 4/12, which is 1/3, so the box holds 12.

G4A_FRACTIONS_025.questionText: A tank has 10 litres of water. In the morning 3 3/4 litres are used and in the afternoon 2 5/8 litres are used. In the evening 1 1/2 litres are poured in. How much water is in the tank now?
hints: Follow the story in order: water used is taken away and water poured in is added. Write all the fractions as eighths.
First add the two amounts used: 3 3/4 + 2 5/8. Remember that 3/4 = 6/8.
A similar one: a 6 litre can loses 1 1/2 litres and then 2 1/4 litres, and then gains 1/2 litre. Used: 1 1/2 + 2 1/4 = 3 3/4. Left: 6 − 3 3/4 = 2 1/4. After adding 1/2: 2 3/4 litres.

stepByStep.text: Add the water used, in eighths.
Take this away from 10 litres.
Add the water poured in.
There are 5 1/8 litres of water in the tank now.

misconceptions.A: Yes! 6 3/8 litres are used, leaving 3 5/8 litres, and adding 1 1/2 litres gives 5 1/8 litres.
misconceptions.B: This is the water left after the afternoon. In the evening 1 1/2 litres more are poured in.
misconceptions.C: Here the evening water was taken away too. Water poured in makes the amount bigger, so add 1 1/2 litres.
misconceptions.D: Check 10 − 6 3/8. One whole must be broken into eighths, so it is 3 5/8, not 4 5/8.

G4A_FRACTIONS_026.questionText: Sita cuts off 1/3 of a rope. Then she cuts off 10 m more. Now exactly 1/4 of the rope is left. How long was the rope at first?
hints: The rope is made of three parts: the first piece cut off, the 10 m piece and the piece left. Find what fraction of the rope the 10 m piece is.
Add 1/3 and 1/4 in twelfths. Whatever is missing from the whole rope is the 10 m piece.
A similar one: half of a rope is cut off, then 3 m more, and 1/5 of the rope is left. 1 − 1/2 − 1/5 = 3/10, so 3/10 of the rope is 3 m. Then 1/10 is 1 m and the rope was 10 m long.

stepByStep.text: The first piece and the piece left are 1/3 and 1/4 of the rope.
So the 10 m piece is the other part of the rope.
5/12 of the rope is 10 m, so 1/12 of the rope is 2 m.
The whole rope was 12 × 2 = 24 m long.

misconceptions.A: This treats the 10 m piece as the quarter that is left. The 10 m piece is a different part: the 5/12 between the first cut and the piece left.
misconceptions.B: This treats the 10 m piece as the 1/3 that was cut first. The 10 m was cut off after that.
misconceptions.C: Right! Cutting 8 m and then 10 m from 24 m leaves 6 m, which is exactly 1/4 of the rope.
misconceptions.D: This treats 10 m as only one twelfth of the rope. The 10 m piece is five twelfths, so one twelfth is 2 m.

G4A_FRACTIONS_027.questionText: The denominator of a fraction is 4 more than its numerator. When 1 is added to both the numerator and the denominator, the fraction becomes equal to 1/2. What is the original fraction?
hints: Adding 1 to both the top and the bottom does not change the gap between them. Think about what the new fraction must look like.
The new fraction equals 1/2, so its bottom is double its top, and the bottom is still 4 more than the top. Which fraction is that?
A similar one: the bottom is 3 more than the top, and adding 1 to both gives 1/2. The new fraction must be 3/6, because 6 is double 3 and 3 more than 3. Taking 1 off each gives 2/5.

stepByStep.text: After adding 1 to both, the bottom is still 4 more than the top, and the fraction equals 1/2.
A fraction equal to 1/2 has a bottom that is double its top. If the bottom is also 4 more than the top, the top is 4 and the bottom is 8.
Take away the 1 that was added to each.
The original fraction is 3/7.

misconceptions.A: 4/8 is the fraction after 1 has been added to both parts. Take 1 off the top and the bottom to get back to the original.
misconceptions.B: 1/5 fits the first clue, but adding 1 to both gives 2/6, which is 1/3 and not 1/2.
misconceptions.C: 5/9 fits the first clue, but adding 1 to both gives 6/10, which is 3/5 and not 1/2.
misconceptions.D: Well done! 7 is 4 more than 3, and adding 1 to both gives 4/8, which equals 1/2.

G4A_FRACTIONS_028.questionText: Arun, Bina and Chetan share 72 marbles. Arun takes 1/4 of them. Bina takes 2/3 of what is left. Chetan gets the rest. How many more marbles does Bina get than Chetan?
hints: Take the story one person at a time. Bina's fraction is a fraction of what is left after Arun, not of all 72 marbles.
Find 1/4 of 72 for Arun and subtract it. Bina's 2/3 is taken from that smaller number.
A similar one: 60 sweets. Asha takes 1/3, which is 20, leaving 40. Ravi takes 3/4 of the 40, which is 30, and Sara gets the other 10. Ravi gets 30 − 10 = 20 more than Sara.

stepByStep.text: Arun takes 1/4 of 72.
Marbles left after Arun.
Bina takes 2/3 of 54.
Chetan gets the rest.
Bina gets 36 − 18 = 18 more marbles than Chetan.

misconceptions.A: 36 is the number of marbles Bina gets. The question asks how many more she gets than Chetan.
misconceptions.B: Yes! Bina gets 36 marbles and Chetan gets 18, so Bina has 18 more.
misconceptions.C: This takes 2/3 of all 72 marbles for Bina. Her share is 2/3 of the 54 marbles left after Arun.
misconceptions.D: 54 is the number of marbles left after Arun takes his share. Go on to find Bina's and Chetan's shares.

G4A_FRACTIONS_029.questionText: How many of these fractions are greater than 1/2? 5/11, 7/13, 9/20, 13/25, 8/15, 49/100
hints: There is a quick test for one half: compare double the top number with the bottom number.
For 5/11, double 5 is 10, which is less than 11, so 5/11 is less than 1/2. Test each of the others in the same way.
A similar one: which of 4/9, 6/11 and 7/15 are greater than 1/2? Double the tops: 8 is less than 9, 12 is more than 11, 14 is less than 15. Only 6/11 is greater than 1/2, so the count there is 1.

stepByStep.text: A fraction is greater than 1/2 when double its top number is more than its bottom number.
5/11: 10 is less than 11. 9/20: 18 is less than 20. 49/100: 98 is less than 100. These three are less than 1/2.
7/13: 14 is more than 13. 13/25: 26 is more than 25. 8/15: 16 is more than 15. These three are greater than 1/2.
So 3 of the fractions are greater than 1/2.

misconceptions.A: One fraction too many has been counted. 49/100 looks large, but double 49 is 98, which is less than 100.
misconceptions.B: One has been missed. Check 13/25 again: double 13 is 26, which is more than 25.
misconceptions.C: Right! Only 7/13, 13/25 and 8/15 pass the doubling test, so 3 fractions are greater than 1/2.
misconceptions.D: All six are close to one half, but only some are above it. Test each one by doubling its top number.

G4A_FRACTIONS_030.questionText: Rita needs 3/4 m of ribbon to wrap one gift. She has 6 1/2 m of ribbon and wraps as many gifts as she can. How much ribbon is left over?
hints: Find how many whole gifts can be wrapped, then how much ribbon those gifts use. The left-over piece must be too short for one more gift.
4 gifts use 4 × 3/4 = 3 m of ribbon. Use this to see how many gifts fit into 6 1/2 m.
A similar one: each gift needs 2/3 m and there are 3 m of ribbon. 4 gifts use 8/3 = 2 2/3 m, and a fifth gift would need 3 1/3 m. So 3 − 2 2/3 = 1/3 m is left over.

stepByStep.text: 4 gifts use 3 m of ribbon.
So 8 gifts use 6 m. A ninth gift would need 6 3/4 m, which is more than 6 1/2 m.
Subtract the ribbon used from the ribbon she has.
1/2 m of ribbon is left over.

misconceptions.A: Well done! 8 gifts use 6 m, and the 1/2 m left is too short for another gift.
misconceptions.B: 6 1/2 ÷ 3/4 is 8 2/3, but that 2/3 means two thirds of one gift's ribbon, not 2/3 m. Subtract the ribbon used by 8 gifts.
misconceptions.C: Check how much ribbon 8 gifts use: 8 × 3/4 = 6 m. Then 6 1/2 − 6 leaves 1/2 m.
misconceptions.D: If 3/4 m were left, Rita could wrap one more gift. The left-over piece has to be shorter than 3/4 m.

G4A_FRACTIONS_031.questionText: What must be added to 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + 1/16 to make exactly 1?
hints: First find the sum of the four fractions. Then see how far the sum is from 1.
Write every fraction in sixteenths: 1/2 = 8/16, 1/4 = 4/16 and 1/8 = 2/16.
A similar one: 1/3 + 1/6 + 1/12. In twelfths that is 4/12 + 2/12 + 1/12 = 7/12, so 5/12 more is needed to make 1.

stepByStep.text: Write each fraction in sixteenths and add.
One whole is 16/16.
1/16 must be added to make exactly 1.

misconceptions.A: The sum so far is 15/16, not 7/8. Remember to include the last fraction, 1/16, in the sum.
misconceptions.B: Yes! The four fractions add up to 15/16, so just 1/16 more makes 1.
misconceptions.C: 15/16 is the sum of the four fractions. The question asks how much more is needed to reach 1.
misconceptions.D: 1/32 would be the next fraction in the halving pattern, but the gap up to 1 is the same size as the last fraction added, 1/16.

G4A_FRACTIONS_032.questionText: In a school, 5/9 of the pupils are boys and the rest are girls. There are 40 more boys than girls. How many pupils are there in the school?
hints: Find the fraction of pupils who are girls. The 40 extra boys are the gap between the two fractions.
Boys are 5/9 and girls are 4/9 of the school. What fraction of the school is the gap between them?
A similar one: 3/5 of a club are boys and there are 6 more boys than girls. Girls are 2/5, so the gap is 1/5 of the club. 1/5 is 6, so the club has 30 members.

stepByStep.text: Find the fraction who are girls.
The gap between boys and girls, as a fraction of the school.
So 1/9 of the school is 40 pupils.
The whole school has 9 × 40 = 360 pupils.

misconceptions.A: This treats 40 as 5/9 of the school. 40 is not the number of boys; it is how many more boys there are than girls.
misconceptions.B: 200 is the number of boys. The question asks for all the pupils, boys and girls together.
misconceptions.C: Right! The 40 extra boys are 1/9 of the school, so the school has 360 pupils (200 boys and 160 girls).
misconceptions.D: This treats 40 as the number of girls (4/9). 40 is the gap between boys and girls, which is 1/9 of the school.

G4A_FRACTIONS_033.questionText: Which fraction is exactly halfway between 1/4 and 2/3?
hints: The number halfway between two numbers is half of their sum.
Add 1/4 and 2/3 using twelfths. Then find half of the total.
A similar one: halfway between 1/2 and 3/4. Add: 2/4 + 3/4 = 5/4. Half of 5/4 is 5/8, so 5/8 is halfway.

stepByStep.text: Write both fractions in twelfths.
Add them.
The halfway number is half of this sum. Half of 11 twelfths is 11 twenty-fourths.
Check: 1/4 = 6/24 and 2/3 = 16/24, and 11/24 is 5/24 away from each. The answer is 11/24.

misconceptions.A: This adds the tops (1 + 2) and the bottoms (4 + 3). That gives a fraction between the two, but not the exact middle.
misconceptions.B: 11/12 is the sum of the two fractions. The halfway number is half of the sum.
misconceptions.C: 5/12 is the gap between the two fractions. To find the middle, add half of that gap to 1/4.
misconceptions.D: Well done! 11/24 is 5/24 above 1/4 and 5/24 below 2/3.

G4A_FRACTIONS_034.questionText: A recipe for 4 people needs 1 1/2 cups of rice. How many cups of rice are needed for 10 people?
hints: The rice grows in step with the number of people. Break 10 people into groups you already know about.
10 people is 4 people and 4 people and 2 people. Two people need half as much rice as four people.
A similar one: a recipe for 3 people needs 1 1/2 cups of flour. One person needs 1/2 cup, so 7 people need 7 × 1/2 = 3 1/2 cups.

stepByStep.text: 10 people is 4 people + 4 people + 2 people.
4 people need 1 1/2 cups, so 8 people need 3 cups.
2 people need half of 1 1/2 cups, which is 3/4 cup.
Altogether 3 + 3/4 = 3 3/4 cups of rice are needed.

misconceptions.A: Yes! 8 people need 3 cups and the other 2 people need 3/4 cup, making 3 3/4 cups.
misconceptions.B: This multiplies 1 1/2 cups by 10, as if 1 1/2 cups were for one person. That amount feeds 4 people.
misconceptions.C: 3 cups is enough for 8 people. Two more people still need rice: half of 1 1/2 cups.
misconceptions.D: This multiplies 1 1/2 cups by 5. Ten people is 2 1/2 times as many as four people, not 5 times.

G4A_FRACTIONS_035.questionText: Asha, Bela and Charu have the same homework. Asha has finished 5/6 of it, Bela 7/9 of it and Charu 3/4 of it. How much more of the homework has the girl who has done the most finished than the girl who has done the least?
hints: First decide who has done the most and who has done the least. Then subtract those two fractions.
6, 9 and 4 all divide into 36. Write the three fractions in thirty-sixths and compare the tops.
A similar one: 2/3, 3/5 and 7/10. In thirtieths they are 20/30, 18/30 and 21/30. Most minus least is 21/30 − 18/30 = 3/30 = 1/10.

stepByStep.text: Write all three in thirty-sixths: 5/6 = 30/36, 7/9 = 28/36 and 3/4 = 27/36.
Asha has done the most and Charu has done the least.
Subtract.
3/36 = 1/12, so the difference is 1/12 of the homework.

misconceptions.A: 1/18 is the gap between Asha and Bela. Bela is in the middle; the least has been done by Charu.
misconceptions.B: Right! Asha's 30/36 minus Charu's 27/36 is 3/36, which is 1/12.
misconceptions.C: 1/36 is the gap between Bela and Charu. The most has been done by Asha, with 30/36.
misconceptions.D: This subtracts the tops (5 − 3) and the bottoms (6 − 4). Change the fractions to thirty-sixths before subtracting.

G4A_DECIMALS_001.questionText: In the number 536.429, which digit is in the hundredths place?
hints: Places after the decimal point have their own names. Say them in order as you move to the right of the point.
The first digit after the point is in the tenths place. Which place comes next?
A similar one: in 0.917, the digits after the point are 9 (tenths), 1 (hundredths) and 7 (thousandths). So the thousandths digit there is 7.

stepByStep.text: After the decimal point the places are tenths, hundredths and thousandths. In 536.429 that is 4 tenths, 2 hundredths and 9 thousandths.
The digit in the hundredths place is 2.

misconceptions.A: 4 is in the tenths place, the first place after the point. Hundredths come one place further to the right.
misconceptions.B: 9 is in the thousandths place, the third place after the point. Hundredths are the second place.
misconceptions.C: 5 is in the hundreds place, to the left of the point. Hundredths, with a th, are to the right of the point.
misconceptions.D: Yes! The second digit after the decimal point is the hundredths digit, and here it is 2.

G4A_DECIMALS_002.questionText: Which decimal means seven and nine hundredths?
hints: The word and stands for the decimal point. The last word tells you the place where the number must end.
Hundredths are the second place after the point. If there are no tenths, that place still needs a digit.
A similar one: four and three hundredths. That is 4 wholes, 0 tenths and 3 hundredths, written 4.03.

stepByStep.text: Seven is the whole-number part, so the number starts with 7 and a decimal point.
Nine hundredths means 9 in the second place after the point, with 0 in the tenths place.
Seven and nine hundredths is 7.09.

misconceptions.A: 7.9 is seven and nine tenths. For nine hundredths, the 9 must be in the second place after the point.
misconceptions.B: 7.009 is seven and nine thousandths. Hundredths need only two places after the point.
misconceptions.C: Right! 7 wholes, 0 tenths and 9 hundredths is written 7.09.
misconceptions.D: 0.79 is seventy-nine hundredths, with no wholes. The seven here is 7 wholes.

hints: Each fraction tells you which decimal place its digit goes in. A place that is not mentioned gets a zero.
3/10 puts a 3 in the tenths place. Which place does 7/1000 use, and what goes in the place between?
A similar one: 2 + 5/100 + 9/1000. There are no tenths, so a 0 goes there: 2.059.

stepByStep.text: 4 is the whole-number part, and 3/10 puts 3 in the tenths place.
There are no hundredths, so that place gets 0. 7/1000 puts 7 in the thousandths place.
The number is 4.307.

misconceptions.A: Well done! 3 tenths, 0 hundredths and 7 thousandths after the 4 gives 4.307.
misconceptions.B: Here the 7 has slipped into the hundredths place. 7/1000 is thousandths, so a 0 is needed in the hundredths place first.
misconceptions.C: Here the 3 has slipped into the hundredths place. 3/10 is tenths, the first place after the point, and the 0 belongs in the hundredths place.
misconceptions.D: The 3 tenths and 7 thousandths belong after the decimal point. Only the 4 is a whole number.

G4A_DECIMALS_004.questionText: Which of these numbers is greater than 4.3 but less than 4.4?
hints: Give all the numbers the same number of decimal places so that they are easy to compare.
Think of 4.3 as 4.30 and 4.4 as 4.40. Which number sits between 4.30 and 4.40?
A similar one: a number between 2.6 and 2.7. Write them as 2.60 and 2.70; then 2.64 lies between them.

stepByStep.text: Write the two ends with two decimal places: 4.30 and 4.40.
4.35 is more than 4.30 and less than 4.40.
The number between 4.3 and 4.4 is 4.35.

misconceptions.A: 4.03 has 0 tenths, so it is less than 4.3. Compare the tenths digits first.
misconceptions.B: 4.43 has 4 tenths and 3 hundredths, so it is just past 4.4.
misconceptions.C: 4.5 has 5 tenths, which is more than 4.4.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 4.35 comes after 4.30 and before 4.40.

G4A_DECIMALS_005.questionText: Riya walks 1.6 km to school and then 0.85 km from school to the library. How far does she walk in all?
hints: When you add decimals, line up the decimal points so that tenths are added to tenths.
Write 1.6 as 1.60 so that both numbers have two decimal places. Then add.
A similar one: 2.7 + 0.45. Write 2.7 as 2.70. Then 2.70 + 0.45 = 3.15.

stepByStep.text: Write both distances with two decimal places: 1.60 and 0.85.
Add, keeping the decimal points in line.
Riya walks 2.45 km in all.

misconceptions.B: Here the last digits were lined up, so 1.6 was added as 0.16. Line up the decimal points instead.
misconceptions.C: 6 tenths and 8 tenths make 14 tenths, so 1 whole must be carried. Check the tenths column again.
misconceptions.D: This adds 16 and 85 without the decimal points. Keep the points in line: 1.60 + 0.85.

G4A_DECIMALS_006.questionText: A rope is 5 m long. A piece 1.35 m long is cut off. How long is the rope that is left?
hints: A whole number can be written with a decimal point and zeros after it. That makes the subtraction easy to line up.
Write 5 as 5.00 and put 1.35 under it with the points in line.
A similar one: 8 − 2.45. Write 8 as 8.00. Then 8.00 − 2.45 = 5.55.

stepByStep.text: Write 5 m as 5.00 m.
Subtract, keeping the decimal points in line.
The rope that is left is 3.65 m long.

misconceptions.A: This takes away only the 1 whole and keeps the .35. The 0.35 must be taken away as well.
misconceptions.B: Well done! 5.00 − 1.35 = 3.65 m, and 3.65 + 1.35 makes 5 again.
misconceptions.C: The .65 is right, but taking 0.35 away uses up part of one whole. 5 − 1.35 is less than 4.
misconceptions.D: Check the hundredths and tenths again: 1.35 + 3.75 would make 5.10, a little too much.

G4A_DECIMALS_007.questionText: One pencil costs Rs. 4.50. What is the cost of 10 such pencils?
hints: Multiplying by 10 makes every digit worth ten times as much.
When a decimal is multiplied by 10, each digit moves one place to the left. Move the digits of 4.50.
A similar one: one eraser costs Rs. 2.75. For 10 erasers each digit moves one place to the left, giving Rs. 27.50.

stepByStep.text: Multiply Rs. 4.50 by 10. Each digit moves one place to the left.
10 pencils cost Rs. 45.00.

misconceptions.A: Here the digits moved two places, which is multiplying by 100. For 10, move them one place.
misconceptions.B: This multiplies only the 4 rupees by 10 and leaves the 50 paise alone. Ten lots of 50 paise make Rs. 5 more.
misconceptions.C: Yes! Ten lots of Rs. 4.50 make Rs. 45.00.
misconceptions.D: This adds 10 to the price. Ten pencils means 10 times the price, not Rs. 10 more.

hints: A fraction is easy to write as a decimal when its bottom number is 10 or 100.
What can you multiply 20 by to make 100? Multiply the top by the same number.
A similar one: 9/25. Multiply the top and bottom by 4 to get 36/100, which is 0.36.

stepByStep.text: Multiply the top and bottom by 5 to make hundredths.
35 hundredths is written 0.35.

misconceptions.A: This just puts a decimal point between the digits of 7 and 20. Change 7/20 into hundredths instead.
misconceptions.B: Right! 7/20 = 35/100, and 35 hundredths is 0.35.
misconceptions.C: 0.7 is 7/10. The bottom number here is 20, so each piece is only half as big.
misconceptions.D: The digits 3 and 5 are right, but 35/100 is 35 hundredths, which is less than 1: 0.35.

G4A_DECIMALS_009.questionText: A ribbon 7.2 m long is cut into 6 equal pieces. How long is each piece?
hints: This is equal sharing, so divide. Divide as you would with whole numbers and keep the decimal point in its place.
7.2 is 72 tenths. Share 72 tenths into 6 equal groups.
A similar one: 8.4 m cut into 4 equal pieces. 84 tenths ÷ 4 = 21 tenths, so each piece is 2.1 m.

stepByStep.text: 7.2 m is 72 tenths of a metre.
Divide by 6.
12 tenths is 1.2, so each piece is 1.2 m long.

misconceptions.A: The decimal point has been left out. Each piece must be shorter than the whole 7.2 m ribbon.
misconceptions.B: The point has moved one place too far. 6 pieces of 0.12 m would make only 0.72 m.
misconceptions.C: Well done! 6 pieces of 1.2 m make 7.2 m.
misconceptions.D: An extra zero has slipped in. 72 tenths ÷ 6 is 12 tenths, which is 1.2.

G4A_DECIMALS_010.questionText: Aman has 8 rupees and 5 paise. How is this amount written in rupees?
hints: 100 paise make 1 rupee, so paise are hundredths of a rupee and always take two decimal places.
5 paise is 5 hundredths of a rupee. Which digit goes in the tenths place?
A similar one: 3 rupees and 7 paise. 7 paise is 7 hundredths of a rupee, so it is written Rs. 3.07.

stepByStep.text: 1 paisa is one hundredth of a rupee, so 5 paise is Rs. 0.05.
Add the 8 rupees. The amount is Rs. 8.05.

misconceptions.A: Yes! 5 paise is 5 hundredths of a rupee, so the amount is Rs. 8.05.
misconceptions.B: Rs. 8.50 is 8 rupees and 50 paise. For 5 paise a zero is needed in the tenths place.
misconceptions.C: This puts the 8 and the 5 together as rupees. The 5 paise are only a small part of one rupee.
misconceptions.D: Here the 8 rupees have gone after the decimal point. The rupees are whole numbers and stay before the point.

G4A_DECIMALS_011.questionText: In a long-jump contest, Anil jumped 3.38 m, Bharat jumped 3.045 m, Chirag jumped 3.4 m and Dinesh jumped 3.405 m. Who came second?
hints: To compare decimals, give them all the same number of decimal places. More digits does not mean a bigger number.
Write every jump with three decimal places, for example 3.4 as 3.400. Then compare from the left.
A similar one: 2.5, 2.48 and 2.507. With three decimal places they are 2.500, 2.480 and 2.507. The greatest is 2.507, then 2.500, then 2.480.

stepByStep.text: Write every jump with three decimal places: 3.380, 3.045, 3.400 and 3.405.
All have 3 wholes, so compare the parts after the point: 405 is the most, then 400, then 380, then 045.
The longest jump is 3.405 m by Dinesh, and the next longest is 3.4 m, so Chirag came second.

misconceptions.A: Anil's 3.38 is 3.380, which is less than 3.400. He came third.
misconceptions.B: Bharat's 3.045 has 0 tenths, so it is the shortest jump even though it has many digits.
misconceptions.C: Right! 3.405 is the longest and 3.4, which is 3.400, comes next, so Chirag came second.
misconceptions.D: Dinesh's 3.405 m is the longest jump of all. The question asks who came second.

G4A_DECIMALS_012.questionText: In the number 5.252, how many times as large is the value of the first 2 as the value of the second 2?
hints: The same digit has different values in different places. Each place is 10 times as large as the place to its right.
Name the place of each 2. Then count how many places apart they are.
A similar one: in 4.66, the first 6 is 0.6 and the second 6 is 0.06. They are one place apart, so 0.6 is 10 times as large as 0.06.

stepByStep.text: The first 2 is in the tenths place, so its value is 0.2.
The second 2 is in the thousandths place, so its value is 0.002.
From thousandths to tenths is two places to the left, and each place is 10 times as large.
The first 2 is 100 times as large as the second 2.

misconceptions.A: 10 times would be right if the two 2s were in neighbouring places. Here a 5 sits between them, so they are two places apart.
misconceptions.B: 1000 times would need the places to be three steps apart. Tenths to thousandths is two steps.
misconceptions.C: Both digits are 2, but the question is about their values, 0.2 and 0.002. Compare the places they are in.
misconceptions.D: Well done! 0.2 is 100 times 0.002, because the two places are two steps apart.

G4A_DECIMALS_013.questionText: Three parcels weigh 2.5 kg, 0.375 kg and 14 kg. What is their total weight?
hints: The numbers have different numbers of decimal places. Line up the decimal points before adding.
Write them as 2.500, 0.375 and 14.000. A whole number has its decimal point at the end.
A similar one: 1.2 + 0.45 + 6. Write 1.20 + 0.45 + 6.00, which gives 7.65.

stepByStep.text: Give every weight three decimal places: 2.500, 0.375 and 14.000.
Add the first two.
Add the 14 wholes.
The total weight is 16.875 kg.

misconceptions.B: Here 14 kg was added as 0.14. A whole number has its decimal point after its last digit: 14.000.
misconceptions.C: Here the last digits were lined up instead of the decimal points. The 14 wholes alone are more than this total.
misconceptions.D: Here 2.5 was written as 2.05. Extra zeros go at the end, 2.500, not in the middle.

G4A_DECIMALS_014.questionText: By how much is 10 greater than 3.607?
hints: By how much greater asks for the difference, so subtract. Give the whole number the same decimal places as the other number.
Write 10 as 10.000 and put 3.607 under it with the decimal points in line.
A similar one: 5 − 1.208. Write 5.000 − 1.208, which gives 3.792.

stepByStep.text: Write 10 as 10.000.
Subtract with the decimal points in line.
Check by adding back: 6.393 + 3.607 = 10. So 10 is greater than 3.607 by 6.393.

misconceptions.A: This takes away only the 3 wholes and then keeps the .607. The 0.607 must be taken away too.
misconceptions.B: Check the tenths and hundredths again: 3.607 + 6.403 would make 10.010, a little too much.
misconceptions.C: Right! 10.000 − 3.607 = 6.393, and adding 3.607 back gives 10.
misconceptions.D: The .393 is right, but taking away 0.607 uses part of a whole, so 10 − 3.607 is less than 7.

G4A_DECIMALS_015.questionText: One cricket ball weighs 0.16 kg. What is the weight of 25 such balls?
hints: Equal weights repeated many times means multiplication. Multiply as whole numbers, then put the decimal point back.
Work out 16 × 25 first. Since 0.16 has two decimal places, the answer needs two decimal places.
A similar one: balls of 0.12 kg each, 50 balls. 12 × 50 = 600, and with two decimal places that is 6.00, so 6 kg.

stepByStep.text: Multiply without the decimal point.
0.16 has two decimal places, so the answer has two decimal places.
25 balls weigh 4 kg.

misconceptions.A: Here the answer has only one decimal place. 0.16 has two decimal places, so 400 becomes 4.00.
misconceptions.B: Here the decimal point has moved one place too far. 400 hundredths is 4 wholes.
misconceptions.C: This adds 25 and 0.16. For 25 equal balls, multiply the weight of one ball by 25.
misconceptions.D: Well done! 16 × 25 = 400 hundredths of a kilogram, which is 4 kg.

hints: Multiplying by 10, 100 or 1000 moves the digits to the left. Dividing moves them to the right.
First multiply 0.045 by 1000 by moving every digit three places to the left. Then divide that answer by 10.
A similar one: 0.032 × 100 ÷ 10. Times 100 moves the digits two places left, giving 3.2. Dividing by 10 moves them one place right, giving 0.32.

stepByStep.text: Multiply by 1000: every digit moves three places to the left.
Divide by 10: every digit moves one place to the right.
The answer is 4.5.

misconceptions.A: 45 is the answer after multiplying by 1000. There is still a division by 10 to do.
misconceptions.C: Here the digits moved only one place to the left in all. Three places left and one place right is two places left.
misconceptions.D: Here the last step multiplied by 10 instead of dividing. Dividing by 10 makes 45 smaller.

G4A_DECIMALS_017.questionText: □ × 100 = 3.7. Which number goes in the box?
hints: The box was multiplied by 100 to give 3.7. To find the box, undo the multiplying.
Divide 3.7 by 100. Dividing by 100 moves every digit two places to the right.
A similar one: □ × 10 = 5.2. Undo it by dividing by 10: 5.2 ÷ 10 = 0.52.

stepByStep.text: Undo the multiplication by dividing: the box is 3.7 ÷ 100.
Move every digit two places to the right, filling the empty place with 0.
Check: 0.037 × 100 = 3.7. The number in the box is 0.037.

misconceptions.A: This multiplies 3.7 by 100. The box is the number before multiplying, so it must be smaller than 3.7.
misconceptions.B: Here the digits moved only one place. 0.37 × 100 would be 37, not 3.7.
misconceptions.C: Right! 0.037 × 100 moves the digits two places left and gives 3.7.
misconceptions.D: Here the digits moved three places. 0.0037 × 100 would be only 0.37.

G4A_DECIMALS_018.questionText: Which of these is the greatest? 0.58, 3/5, 5/8, 0.65
hints: Fractions and decimals are hard to compare when mixed. Put them all in the same form first.
Change 3/5 and 5/8 into decimals. For 3/5, think of tenths.
A similar one: which is greater, 1/4 or 0.3? 1/4 = 0.25, and 0.25 is less than 0.30, so 0.3 is greater.

stepByStep.text: Change 3/5 to a decimal.
Change 5/8 to a decimal. One eighth is 0.125, so five eighths is 0.625.
The greatest is 0.65.

misconceptions.A: 0.58 is the smallest of the four. It has 5 tenths, while the others are worth 6 tenths or more.
misconceptions.B: 3/5 is 0.6, which is more than 0.58 but less than 0.625 and 0.65.
misconceptions.C: 5/8 is 0.625. That is close, but 0.65 is 0.650, which is a little more.
misconceptions.D: Well done! As decimals the four are 0.58, 0.6, 0.625 and 0.65, and 0.65 is the greatest.

G4A_DECIMALS_019.questionText: Write 1.75 as a mixed number in lowest terms.
hints: The whole-number part stays as it is. The part after the decimal point becomes a fraction with 10 or 100 on the bottom.
0.75 is 75 hundredths, so write 75/100. Then divide the top and bottom by the same number until you cannot go further.
A similar one: 2.4. The 0.4 is 4/10, which simplifies to 2/5, so 2.4 = 2 2/5.

stepByStep.text: Keep the 1 whole. Write 0.75 as a fraction.
Divide the top and bottom by 25.

misconceptions.A: This uses the digits 7 and 5 as the top and bottom. Two decimal places mean hundredths: 75/100.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 0.75 is 75/100, which simplifies to 3/4, so 1.75 = 1 3/4.
misconceptions.C: Here 75 was divided by 25 but 100 was divided by 20. Divide the top and bottom by the same number, 25.
misconceptions.D: 1 1/4 is 1.25. The decimal 0.75 is three quarters, not one quarter.

G4A_DECIMALS_020.questionText: Tara buys a notebook for Rs. 37.50, a pen for Rs. 12.75 and an eraser for Rs. 4.25. She pays with a Rs. 100 note. How much change does she get?
hints: There are two steps: find the total bill, then find how much of the Rs. 100 is not needed.
Add the three prices with the decimal points in line. It helps to add Rs. 12.75 and Rs. 4.25 first.
A similar one: items of Rs. 15.50 and Rs. 8.25, paid with a Rs. 50 note. The total is Rs. 23.75, and 50.00 − 23.75 = Rs. 26.25 change.

stepByStep.text: Add the pen and the eraser.
Add the notebook to get the total bill.
Subtract the bill from Rs. 100.
Tara gets Rs. 45.50 as change.

misconceptions.A: Rs. 54.50 is the total bill. The change is what is left of the Rs. 100 after paying it.
misconceptions.B: Check the subtraction: 54.50 + 46.50 would make Rs. 101. Taking away 50 paise uses part of a rupee.
misconceptions.C: Check the bill again: 12.75 + 4.25 is exactly 17.00, so the total is Rs. 54.50, not Rs. 44.50.
misconceptions.D: Well done! The bill is Rs. 54.50, and 100.00 − 54.50 leaves Rs. 45.50.

G4A_DECIMALS_021.questionText: A bus ticket from Asha's home to her school costs Rs. 12.50. She goes to school and comes back by bus on 6 days. How much does she spend on tickets?
hints: Count the tickets carefully before multiplying. Going and coming back are two journeys.
Asha needs 2 tickets each day. Work out how many tickets she needs for 6 days.
A similar one: Rs. 7.50 each way for 4 days. That is 8 tickets, and 8 × 7.50 = Rs. 60.00.

stepByStep.text: She needs 2 tickets a day for 6 days.
Two tickets cost Rs. 25, so each day costs Rs. 25.
Multiply by the 6 days.
Asha spends Rs. 150.00 on tickets.

misconceptions.A: Right! 12 tickets at Rs. 12.50 each cost Rs. 150.00.
misconceptions.B: This counts only one ticket a day. Asha also comes back by bus, so she needs 2 tickets each day.
misconceptions.C: Rs. 25.00 is the cost for one day. She travels on 6 days.
misconceptions.D: Here 12 was multiplied by 12 rupees and the 50 paise were added once. Each of the 12 tickets has its own 50 paise.

G4A_DECIMALS_022.questionText: Four friends share a bill of Rs. 342 equally. How much does each friend pay?
hints: Equal sharing means division. If some rupees are left over, change them into paise and keep sharing.
Divide 342 by 4. You will have a remainder; change that remainder into paise and divide it by 4 as well.
A similar one: Rs. 126 shared by 4. Each gets Rs. 31 and Rs. 2 are left. Rs. 2 is 200 paise, which gives 50 paise each, so each pays Rs. 31.50.

stepByStep.text: Divide the rupees.
Change the Rs. 2 left over into 200 paise and share them.
Each friend pays 85 rupees and 50 paise, which is Rs. 85.50.

misconceptions.A: Here the remainder 2 was written straight after the point. The Rs. 2 left over must be shared among the 4 friends: 50 paise each.
misconceptions.B: Each friend's extra share is 50 paise, which is written .50. Rs. 85.05 would mean only 5 paise.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 4 × 85.50 = 342, so each friend pays Rs. 85.50.
misconceptions.D: This shares the bill between 2 people. There are 4 friends, so halve it once more.

G4A_DECIMALS_023.questionText: Which number is exactly halfway between 2.4 and 2.5?
hints: Between two tenths there are ten hundredths. Writing both numbers with two decimal places lets you see the middle.
Write the numbers as 2.40 and 2.50. Which number is the same distance from both?
A similar one: halfway between 1.2 and 1.3. Write 1.20 and 1.30; the middle is 1.25.

stepByStep.text: Write the numbers with two decimal places: 2.40 and 2.50.
The gap between them is 0.10, and half of the gap is 0.05.
Add half the gap to the smaller number.
The number exactly halfway is 2.45.

misconceptions.A: Well done! 2.45 is 0.05 more than 2.4 and 0.05 less than 2.5.
misconceptions.B: 2.405 is between the two numbers but very close to 2.4. The middle is 5 hundredths above 2.4, not 5 thousandths.
misconceptions.C: 4.9 is the sum of the two numbers. The halfway number is half of that sum.
misconceptions.D: 2.55 is more than 2.5, so it is not between the two numbers at all.

G4A_DECIMALS_024.questionText: A tailor has 20 m of cloth. He stitches 6 shirts and uses 2.25 m of cloth for each shirt. How much cloth is left?
hints: There are two steps: find the cloth used for all the shirts, then take it away from the cloth he had.
Multiply 2.25 by 6. You can do 6 × 2 and 6 × 0.25 separately and add them.
A similar one: 15 m of cloth and 4 curtains of 2.75 m each. 4 × 2.75 = 11, and 15 − 11 = 4 m left.

stepByStep.text: Find the cloth used for 6 shirts.
Subtract from 20 m.
6.5 m of cloth is left.

misconceptions.A: 13.5 m is the cloth used for the shirts. The question asks how much is left from 20 m.
misconceptions.B: Right! Six shirts use 13.5 m, and 20 − 13.5 leaves 6.5 m.
misconceptions.C: This takes away the cloth for only one shirt. He stitches 6 shirts.
misconceptions.D: Check 6 × 0.25: six quarters make 1.5, not 0.5. So the shirts use 13.5 m.

G4A_DECIMALS_025.questionText: A pattern goes 0.4, 0.7, 1.0, 1.3, ... and keeps growing in the same way. What is the 8th number in the pattern?
hints: Find how much is added each time. Then count how many jumps it takes to get from the 1st number to the 8th.
Each number is 0.3 more than the one before. From the 1st number to the 8th number there are 7 jumps.
A similar one: 0.2, 0.7, 1.2, ... The jump is 0.5. The 6th number is 5 jumps after the first: 0.2 + 5 × 0.5 = 2.7.

stepByStep.text: Find the jump between numbers.
From the 1st number to the 8th there are 7 jumps.
Add the jumps to the first number.
The 8th number is 2.5.

misconceptions.A: This makes 8 jumps from the first number. Getting to the 8th number takes only 7 jumps.
misconceptions.B: 2.2 is the 7th number. Count once more: one more jump of 0.3 is needed.
misconceptions.C: This is 8 × 0.3, as if the pattern started at 0.3. The first number is 0.4, so add 7 jumps to 0.4.

G4A_DECIMALS_027.questionText: 3 litres of juice are poured equally into 8 glasses. How much juice is in each glass?
hints: Sharing equally means dividing. Here the answer is less than 1 litre, so it will be a decimal.
Work out 3 ÷ 8 by writing 3 as 3.000 and dividing place by place.
A similar one: 1 litre poured equally into 4 glasses. 1.00 ÷ 4 = 0.25, so each glass has 0.25 litre.

stepByStep.text: Each glass gets 3 ÷ 8 litres. Write 3 as 3.000.
30 tenths ÷ 8 is 3 tenths with 6 tenths left. 60 hundredths ÷ 8 is 7 hundredths with 4 hundredths left. 40 thousandths ÷ 8 is 5 thousandths.
Each glass has 0.375 litre of juice.

misconceptions.A: Right! 8 glasses of 0.375 litre make exactly 3 litres.
misconceptions.B: The digits are right, but each glass must hold less than 1 litre, because 8 glasses share only 3 litres.
misconceptions.C: This multiplies 3 by 8 and adds a decimal point. Sharing means dividing: 3 ÷ 8.
misconceptions.D: The decimal point is one place too far to the left. 8 glasses of 0.0375 litre would make only 0.3 litre.

G4A_DECIMALS_028.questionText: The water in a tank was 36.8 cm deep. After rain it rose by 1.5 cm. Then some water was used and the level fell by 0.75 cm. How deep is the water now?
hints: Follow the story step by step: a rise is added and a fall is taken away.
First add 1.5 to 36.8. Then write that answer with two decimal places before taking away 0.75.
A similar one: 12.4 rises by 2.5 and then falls by 0.35. 12.4 + 2.5 = 14.9, and 14.90 − 0.35 = 14.55.

stepByStep.text: Add the rise.
Write 38.3 as 38.30 and take away the fall.
The water is now 37.55 cm deep.

misconceptions.A: Here the 0.75 cm was added. The level fell, so that amount must be taken away.
misconceptions.B: 38.3 cm is the depth just after the rain. After that the level fell by 0.75 cm.
misconceptions.D: Check the subtraction: 37.65 + 0.75 would make 38.40, a little more than 38.30.

G4A_DECIMALS_029.questionText: Each of the digits 0, 3, 5 and 8 is used once to fill the boxes in □.□□□. What is the difference between the greatest and the smallest numbers that can be made?
hints: The place furthest to the left is worth the most. Decide which digits should go there for the greatest and for the smallest number.
For the greatest number put the digits from biggest to smallest. For the smallest, put them from smallest to biggest; a 0 before the decimal point is allowed.
A similar one: the digits 0, 2 and 7 in □.□□. The greatest is 7.20 and the smallest is 0.27. The difference is 7.20 − 0.27 = 6.93.

stepByStep.text: The greatest number has the digits from biggest to smallest: 8.530.
The smallest number has the digits from smallest to biggest: 0.358.
Subtract.
The difference is 8.172.

misconceptions.A: This uses 3.058 as the smallest number. A 0 can stand before the decimal point, so 0.358 is smaller still.
misconceptions.B: 8.888 is the sum of 8.530 and 0.358. The question asks for the difference, so subtract.
misconceptions.C: The two numbers are right. Check the subtraction in the hundredths place: 8.530 − 0.358 = 8.172.
misconceptions.D: Well done! The greatest is 8.530, the smallest is 0.358, and their difference is 8.172.

G4A_DECIMALS_031.questionText: A plant is 1.5 cm tall. It grows 0.25 cm every day. After how many days will it be exactly 4 cm tall?
hints: The plant does not start from zero. Find how much more it has to grow, then see how many daily steps fit into that.
Subtract 1.5 from 4 to find the growth still needed. Then ask how many lots of 0.25 make that amount.
A similar one: a plant 2 cm tall grows 0.5 cm a day and must reach 5 cm. It needs 3 cm more, and 3 ÷ 0.5 = 6, so it takes 6 days.

stepByStep.text: Find how much the plant still has to grow.
0.25 cm is a quarter of a centimetre, so the plant grows 1 cm in 4 days.
2 cm takes 8 days, and the last 0.5 cm takes 2 more days.
The plant will be 4 cm tall after 10 days.

misconceptions.A: 16 days would be right for a plant starting from 0 cm. This plant is already 1.5 cm tall.
misconceptions.B: 6 is the number of 0.25 cm steps in the 1.5 cm it has already grown. Count the steps in the 2.5 cm still to grow.
misconceptions.C: This takes the growth needed as 2 cm. 4 − 1.5 is 2.5 cm, so two more days are needed.
misconceptions.D: Right! The plant must grow 2.5 cm, and ten daily steps of 0.25 cm make 2.5 cm.

G4A_DECIMALS_032.questionText: A dozen bananas cost Rs. 54. Guavas cost Rs. 7.50 each. Imran buys 8 bananas and 5 guavas. How much does he pay?
hints: The banana price is given for a dozen, but Imran does not buy a dozen. Find the price of one banana first.
A dozen is 12. Divide Rs. 54 by 12 to get the cost of one banana, then find the cost of 8.
A similar one: a dozen eggs cost Rs. 72, so one egg costs Rs. 6 and 5 eggs cost Rs. 30. Two buns at Rs. 4.50 each cost Rs. 9. The total is Rs. 39.00.

stepByStep.text: Find the cost of one banana.
Find the cost of 8 bananas.
Find the cost of 5 guavas.
Add the two amounts. Imran pays Rs. 73.50.

misconceptions.A: This charges for a whole dozen bananas. Imran buys only 8, so find the price of one banana first.
misconceptions.B: This adds the price of only one guava. He buys 5 guavas, which cost Rs. 37.50.
misconceptions.C: Well done! The bananas cost Rs. 36.00 and the guavas Rs. 37.50, making Rs. 73.50.
misconceptions.D: Here a dozen was taken as 10 bananas. A dozen is 12, so one banana costs Rs. 4.50.

G4A_DECIMALS_033.questionText: Rahul had to divide a number by 10. By mistake he multiplied it by 10 and got 62.5. What should his answer have been?
hints: First find the number Rahul started with by undoing what he did. Then do what he was meant to do.
He multiplied by 10 to get 62.5, so divide 62.5 by 10 to find his starting number.
A similar one: a number is multiplied by 10 instead of divided by 10, giving 48. The number was 4.8, and 4.8 ÷ 10 = 0.48.

stepByStep.text: Undo the multiplying to find the starting number.
Now divide the starting number by 10, as Rahul was asked to.
His answer should have been 0.625.

misconceptions.A: Yes! The number was 6.25, and 6.25 ÷ 10 = 0.625.
misconceptions.B: 6.25 is the number Rahul started with. He still has to divide it by 10.
misconceptions.C: This multiplies 62.5 by 10 again. Go back to the starting number by dividing, then divide once more.
misconceptions.D: Here the digits moved three places to the right. Only two divisions by 10 are needed: one to undo, one to do the sum.

hints: Put all four numbers in the same form before comparing. Decimals with three places work well here.
Change 3/8 and 7/20 into decimals. For 7/20, make the bottom number 100.
A similar one: order 0.3, 1/4 and 0.28. Since 1/4 = 0.25, the order from smallest is 1/4, 0.28, 0.3.

stepByStep.text: Change 7/20 to a decimal.
Change 3/8 to a decimal. One eighth is 0.125, so three eighths is 0.375.
Write all four with three decimal places: 0.400, 0.375, 0.380 and 0.350.
From smallest to greatest: 7/20, 3/8, 0.38, 0.4.

misconceptions.A: These are in order from greatest to smallest. The question asks for the smallest first.
misconceptions.B: 3/8 is 0.375 and 7/20 is 0.35, so 7/20 is the smaller of the two fractions.
misconceptions.C: 3/8 is 0.375, which is just under 0.38 (0.380). So 3/8 comes before 0.38.
misconceptions.D: Right! As decimals they are 0.350, 0.375, 0.380 and 0.400.

G4A_DECIMALS_035.questionText: Three numbers add up to 10. Two of them are 3.45 and 2.8. How much greater is the third number than the smallest of the three numbers?
hints: First find the missing third number. Then decide which of the three numbers is the smallest and subtract.
Add 3.45 and 2.8, and take the total away from 10 to find the third number.
A similar one: three numbers add up to 6 and two of them are 1.2 and 2.35. The third is 6 − 3.55 = 2.45. The smallest is 1.2, and 2.45 − 1.2 = 1.25.

stepByStep.text: Add the two numbers you know.
Find the third number.
The three numbers are 3.45, 2.8 and 3.75. The smallest is 2.8.
Subtract. The third number is 0.95 greater than the smallest.

misconceptions.A: 3.75 is the third number itself. The question asks how much greater it is than the smallest number.
misconceptions.B: Well done! The third number is 3.75, the smallest is 2.8, and 3.75 − 2.80 = 0.95.
misconceptions.C: This compares the third number with 3.45. The smallest of the three numbers is 2.8.
misconceptions.D: This is the gap between the two numbers given. Find the third number first, then compare it with 2.8.

G4A_DECIMALS_036.questionText: A bottle full of oil weighs 2.35 kg. When exactly half of the oil has been used, the bottle and the oil left in it weigh 1.3 kg. What is the weight of the empty bottle?
hints: Between the two weighings, only oil has gone. The drop in weight tells you the weight of half the oil.
Subtract 1.3 from 2.35 to get the weight of half the oil. Then find the weight of all the oil.
A similar one: a full jar weighs 1.8 kg and weighs 1.1 kg when half its honey is used. Half the honey is 0.7 kg, so all the honey is 1.4 kg and the jar is 1.8 − 1.4 = 0.4 kg.

stepByStep.text: The weight that went missing is half of the oil.
So all the oil weighs twice as much.
Take the oil away from the full bottle.
The empty bottle weighs 0.25 kg.

misconceptions.A: Yes! The oil weighs 2.1 kg, so the bottle alone weighs 0.25 kg.
misconceptions.B: 1.05 kg is the weight of half the oil. Use it to find all the oil, then take that from 2.35 kg.
misconceptions.C: This halves the full weight, bottle and all. Only the oil was halved; the bottle stays the same.
misconceptions.D: This halves 1.3 kg. That weight is the bottle and half the oil together, so it cannot simply be halved.

hints: Add the three decimals first, lining up the decimal points. Then compare the total with 1.
Write the three numbers as 0.900, 0.090 and 0.009 and add them. Then write 1 with three decimal places too.
A similar one: how much less than 1 is 0.5 + 0.25 + 0.125? The sum is 0.875, and 1.000 − 0.875 = 0.125.

stepByStep.text: Add the three numbers.
Subtract the sum from 1.
The sum is 0.001 less than 1.

misconceptions.A: 0.01 is how far 0.99 is from 1. With the 0.009 added, the sum is 0.999, which is closer still.
misconceptions.B: 0.1 is how far 0.9 alone is from 1. The other two numbers bring the sum closer to 1.
misconceptions.C: Right! The sum is 0.999, which is just one thousandth, 0.001, short of 1.
misconceptions.D: 0.999 is the sum of the three numbers. The question asks how far that sum is from 1.

G4A_DECIMALS_038.questionText: Mira thinks of a number. She multiplies it by 100, then subtracts 4.5, then divides by 10. Her answer is 2.05. What number did she think of?
hints: Work backwards from the answer. Undo each step in the opposite order, using the opposite operation.
The last thing Mira did was divide by 10. Undo that first by multiplying 2.05 by 10.
A similar one: a number is multiplied by 10 and then 1.5 is added, giving 4.7. Undo: 4.7 − 1.5 = 3.2, and 3.2 ÷ 10 = 0.32.

stepByStep.text: Undo the division by 10.
Undo the subtraction of 4.5.
Undo the multiplication by 100.
Mira thought of 0.25.

misconceptions.B: This does Mira's three steps to 2.05 itself. Her answer was 2.05, so go backwards from it.
misconceptions.C: The first two backward steps are right, giving 25. To undo multiplying by 100, divide by 100, not by 10.
misconceptions.D: Here 4.5 was subtracted again on the way back. To undo a subtraction, add: 20.5 + 4.5 = 25.

G4A_DECIMALS_039.questionText: Asha saves Rs. 2.50 on Monday. Each day after that she saves 50 paise more than she saved the day before. How much has she saved altogether after 6 days?
hints: The amount saved changes every day. Write out what she saves on each of the 6 days before adding.
50 paise is Rs. 0.50. The second day is Rs. 3.00 and the third is Rs. 3.50. Carry on to the sixth day.
A similar one: Rs. 1.50 on the first day and 50 paise more each day, for 4 days. 1.50 + 2.00 + 2.50 + 3.00 = Rs. 9.00.

stepByStep.text: List the six days: Rs. 2.50, Rs. 3.00, Rs. 3.50, Rs. 4.00, Rs. 4.50 and Rs. 5.00.
Three pairs of Rs. 7.50 make Rs. 22.50.

misconceptions.A: This is 6 lots of Rs. 2.50. But the amount goes up by 50 paise every day.
misconceptions.B: Rs. 5.00 is what Asha saves on the sixth day alone. The question asks for all six days together.
misconceptions.C: Yes! The six amounts from Rs. 2.50 up to Rs. 5.00 add up to Rs. 22.50.
misconceptions.D: This is the total for 5 days. Add the sixth day's Rs. 5.00 as well.

G4A_DECIMALS_040.questionText: How many pieces, each 0.125 m long, can be cut from a wire 2 1/2 m long?
hints: 0.125 is a decimal you may know as a simple fraction. Think about how many such pieces make 1 metre.
0.125 is 1/8, so 8 pieces fit into each metre. Now count the pieces in 2 1/2 metres.
A similar one: pieces of 0.25 m from a wire 1 1/2 m long. 0.25 is 1/4, so there are 4 pieces in a metre and 2 in half a metre: 6 pieces.

stepByStep.text: 0.125 m is one eighth of a metre, so 8 pieces can be cut from 1 m.
2 m gives 16 pieces.
The extra half metre gives 4 more pieces.
Altogether 16 + 4 = 20 pieces can be cut.

misconceptions.A: This divides 2.5 by 1.25. Each piece is 0.125 m, which is ten times shorter, so there are many more pieces.
misconceptions.B: Right! Eight pieces come from each metre, so 2 1/2 m gives 20 pieces.
misconceptions.C: This treats each piece as 0.0125 m. With 0.125 m pieces, 8 fit into a metre.
misconceptions.D: 16 pieces come from the 2 whole metres. The extra half metre gives 4 more.

G4A_UNITS_001.questionText: A cycle track is 4 km 75 m long. What is its length in kilometres?
hints: Kilometres are bigger than metres, so the metres become a decimal part of a kilometre. Remember how many metres make 1 km.
1 km = 1000 m, so divide the 75 m by 1000 to turn it into kilometres. Then join it to the 4 km.
A similar one: 2 km 40 m. 40 ÷ 1000 = 0.04, so 2 km 40 m = 2.04 km.

stepByStep.text: 1 km = 1000 m, so to change metres into kilometres we divide by 1000.
Change the 75 m into kilometres.
Add the 4 whole kilometres. The track is 4.075 km long.

misconceptions.A: Yes! 75 m is 75 thousandths of a kilometre, which is 0.075 km, so the track is 4.075 km long.
misconceptions.B: This treats 75 m as 0.75 km, but 0.75 km is 750 m. Since 1 km has 1000 m, 75 m needs three decimal places: 0.075.
misconceptions.C: This puts one zero too many after the point. 75 m out of 1000 m is 0.075 km, not 0.0075 km.
misconceptions.D: The whole kilometres must stay as 4. Only the 75 m changes into a decimal part of a kilometre: 75 ÷ 1000.

G4A_UNITS_002.questionText: Meera's water bottle holds 1.2 litres. She drinks 350 ml. How many millilitres of water are left in the bottle?
hints: The two amounts are in different units. Make the units the same before you subtract.
Change 1.2 litres into millilitres: multiply by 1000. Then take away what Meera drank.
A similar one: a jug holds 1.5 litres and 400 ml is poured out. 1.5 litres = 1500 ml, and 1500 − 400 = 1100 ml are left.

stepByStep.text: Change litres into millilitres: 1 litre = 1000 ml.
Take away the 350 ml that Meera drank.
850 ml of water are left in the bottle.

misconceptions.A: This adds the 350 ml. Meera drank that water, so take it away from 1200 ml.
misconceptions.B: This reads 1.2 litres as 1020 ml. But 0.2 litre is 200 ml, so 1.2 litres is 1200 ml.
misconceptions.C: Well done! 1.2 litres is 1200 ml, and 1200 − 350 = 850 ml.
misconceptions.D: Changing 1.2 litres to 1200 ml is the right start. Check the subtraction once more: 1200 − 350 leaves 850.

G4A_UNITS_003.questionText: A new pencil is 14 cm 6 mm long. After a month of sharpening it is 12 cm 9 mm long. How many millimetres shorter has it become?
hints: Both lengths mix centimetres and millimetres. It is easiest to write each one in millimetres only.
1 cm = 10 mm, so 14 cm 6 mm = 140 mm + 6 mm. Do the same for the other length, then subtract.
A similar one: 9 cm 2 mm − 7 cm 8 mm. That is 92 mm − 78 mm = 14 mm.

stepByStep.text: Change the first length into millimetres.
Change the second length into millimetres.
Subtract. The pencil has become 17 mm shorter.

misconceptions.A: This takes 12 cm from 14 cm and 6 mm from 9 mm. The 9 mm belongs to the shorter pencil, so change both lengths fully into millimetres first: 146 and 129.
misconceptions.B: Close! When 9 mm cannot be taken from 6 mm, one centimetre is borrowed, so only 1 cm is left over, not 2 cm. 146 − 129 = 17.
misconceptions.C: This looks only at the millimetre parts. The centimetres matter too: 14 cm 6 mm is 146 mm and 12 cm 9 mm is 129 mm.
misconceptions.D: Lovely! 146 mm − 129 mm = 17 mm.

G4A_UNITS_004.questionText: Amma buys 1 kg 750 g of potatoes and 2 kg 400 g of onions. What is the total weight of the vegetables in kilograms?
hints: Add kilograms to kilograms and grams to grams. Watch out if the grams come to more than 1000.
750 g + 400 g = 1150 g. Think about how many kilograms and grams that is.
A similar one: 2 kg 600 g + 1 kg 900 g. The grams make 1500 g = 1 kg 500 g, so the total is 4 kg 500 g = 4.5 kg.

stepByStep.text: Add the grams.
1150 g is 1 kg 150 g. Add the kilograms, with the 1 kg carried over.
The total is 4 kg 150 g. Since 150 g = 0.15 kg, the vegetables weigh 4.15 kg.

misconceptions.A: The grams add up to 1150 g, which is more than 1 kg. That extra kilogram must be carried over to the kilograms.
misconceptions.C: The total is 4 kg 150 g. 150 g is 0.150 kg, so it is written 4.15 kg, not 4.015 kg.
misconceptions.D: This writes 3 kg and 1150 g side by side. 1150 g is 1 kg 150 g, so the total is 4 kg 150 g.

G4A_UNITS_005.questionText: A fruit seller has 7 dozen bananas. He sells 3 score bananas. How many bananas are left?
hints: Dozen and score are names for fixed numbers. Change both into plain numbers of bananas first.
1 dozen = 12, so find 7 × 12. 1 score = 20, so find 3 × 20.
A similar one: 5 dozen eggs, and 2 score are sold. 5 × 12 = 60 and 2 × 20 = 40, so 60 − 40 = 20 eggs are left.

stepByStep.text: 1 dozen = 12.
1 score = 20.
Subtract the bananas sold. 24 bananas are left.

misconceptions.A: This counts a score as 12. A dozen is 12, but a score is 20, so 3 score is 60 bananas.
misconceptions.B: Well done! 7 dozen is 84 and 3 score is 60, and 84 − 60 = 24.
misconceptions.C: This counts a score as 10. A score is 20, so 3 score is 60 bananas.
misconceptions.D: This adds the bananas sold. They have gone, so take 60 away from 84.

G4A_UNITS_006.questionText: A box holds 1 gross of pencils. A teacher takes pencils from it and gives 2 pencils to each of 54 children. How many pencils remain in the box?
hints: A gross is a fixed number, like a dozen. Find how many pencils are in the box and how many are given out.
1 gross = 12 dozen = 144. Now work out 54 × 2.
A similar one: from 1 gross of erasers, 3 are given to each of 40 children. 40 × 3 = 120, and 144 − 120 = 24 remain.

stepByStep.text: 1 gross = 12 dozen.
Pencils given to the children.
Subtract. 36 pencils remain in the box.

misconceptions.A: This gives only 1 pencil to each child. Each child gets 2, so 54 × 2 = 108 pencils are given away.
misconceptions.B: This counts a gross as 120. A gross is 12 dozen, which is 144.
misconceptions.C: The plan is right: 144 − 108. Check the subtraction once more and you will get 36.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 1 gross is 144, the children get 108, and 144 − 108 = 36.

G4A_UNITS_007.questionText: A milkman pours 750 ml of milk into each of 6 packets. How many litres of milk does he use?
hints: First find the total in millilitres, then change it into litres.
Work out 6 × 750. Then remember that 1000 ml make 1 litre.
A similar one: 8 cups of 250 ml each. 8 × 250 = 2000 ml, and 2000 ÷ 1000 = 2 litres.

stepByStep.text: Find the total milk in millilitres.
Change into litres: 1000 ml = 1 litre.
The milkman uses 4.5 litres of milk.

misconceptions.A: Great! 6 × 750 ml = 4500 ml, and 4500 ÷ 1000 = 4.5 litres.
misconceptions.B: 6 × 750 = 4500 ml. To change millilitres into litres divide by 1000, not by 100.
misconceptions.C: 6 × 750 = 4500 ml. Dividing by 1000 gives 4.5, so check where the decimal point goes.
misconceptions.D: 4500 is the number of millilitres. The question asks for litres, so divide by 1000.

G4A_UNITS_008.questionText: Ravi's school is 850 m from his home. He walks to school and back on each of the 5 school days. How many kilometres does he walk in the week?
hints: Find how far Ravi walks in one day, then in five days. Change to kilometres at the end.
To school and back is 850 m two times. Work out 850 × 2 first.
A similar one: a park is 600 m away and Tara goes there and back on 4 days. 600 × 2 = 1200 m a day, and 1200 × 4 = 4800 m = 4.8 km.

stepByStep.text: Distance in one day, there and back.
Distance in 5 days.
Change metres into kilometres. Ravi walks 8.5 km in the week.

misconceptions.A: This counts only the walk to school. Ravi also walks back, so each day he walks 850 m twice.
misconceptions.B: The total is 8500 m. Dividing by 1000 gives 8.5 km, so check the decimal point.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 850 × 2 = 1700 m a day, 1700 × 5 = 8500 m in the week, and that is 8.5 km.
misconceptions.D: This is the distance for one day. There are 5 school days, so multiply by 5.

G4A_UNITS_009.questionText: A carpenter cuts a plank 3 m long into 8 equal pieces. How long is each piece in centimetres?
hints: The answer is wanted in centimetres, so change the plank's length into centimetres before sharing it.
3 m = 300 cm. Now divide 300 by 8.
A similar one: a 2 m ribbon cut into 8 equal pieces. 2 m = 200 cm, and 200 ÷ 8 = 25 cm each.

stepByStep.text: Change metres into centimetres: 1 m = 100 cm.
Share equally among 8 pieces.
Each piece is 37.5 cm long.

misconceptions.B: One piece cannot be longer than the whole plank of 300 cm. 300 ÷ 8 = 37.5.
misconceptions.C: Well done! 3 m = 300 cm, and 300 ÷ 8 = 37.5 cm.
misconceptions.D: This multiplies 3 by 8. The plank is being cut into pieces, so change 3 m into 300 cm and divide by 8.

G4A_UNITS_010.questionText: A stack of 40 equal coins is 6 cm tall. How thick is one coin, in millimetres?
hints: All 40 coins together make the height of the stack. Change the height into millimetres, then share it.
6 cm = 60 mm. Now divide 60 by 40.
A similar one: 20 coins make a stack 5 cm tall. 5 cm = 50 mm, and 50 ÷ 20 = 2.5 mm for each coin.

stepByStep.text: Change centimetres into millimetres: 1 cm = 10 mm.
Share the height among 40 coins.
One coin is 1.5 mm thick.

misconceptions.A: Yes! 6 cm = 60 mm, and 60 ÷ 40 = 1.5 mm for each coin.
misconceptions.B: Forty coins that are each 15 mm thick would make a stack 600 mm tall. 6 cm is only 60 mm, and 60 ÷ 40 = 1.5.
misconceptions.C: This divides 6 by 40 without changing centimetres into millimetres. 6 cm = 60 mm, and 60 ÷ 40 = 1.5.
misconceptions.D: This comes from multiplying 6 and 40. The stack's height is shared among the coins, so divide 60 mm by 40.

G4A_UNITS_011.questionText: Which of these lengths is the greatest?
hints: Lengths can be compared only when they are in the same unit. Metres is a good choice here.
Change each length into metres. For example, 1.08 km = 1.08 × 1000 m.
A similar one: which is greater, 2.5 km or 2 km 60 m? 2.5 km = 2500 m and 2 km 60 m = 2060 m, so 2.5 km is greater.

stepByStep.text: Change each length into metres: 1.08 km = 1080 m and 1 km 800 m = 1800 m.
1008 m is already in metres, and 10800 cm = 108 m.
Compare 1080, 1800, 1008 and 108. The greatest is 1800 m, which is 1 km 800 m.

misconceptions.A: 1.08 km is 1080 m. That is less than 1 km 800 m, which is 1800 m.
misconceptions.B: Yes! In metres the four lengths are 1800 m, 1080 m, 1008 m and 108 m, so 1 km 800 m is the greatest.
misconceptions.C: 1008 m is only a little more than 1 km. 1 km 800 m is 1800 m, which is greater.
misconceptions.D: The number looks big, but centimetres are small. 10800 cm is only 108 m.

G4A_UNITS_012.questionText: One tablet contains 250 mg of medicine. How many grams of medicine are there in a strip of 10 tablets?
hints: Find the total in milligrams first, then change it into grams.
10 × 250 = 2500 mg. Remember that 1000 mg make 1 g.
A similar one: 4 tablets of 500 mg each. 4 × 500 = 2000 mg, and 2000 ÷ 1000 = 2 g.

stepByStep.text: Medicine in 10 tablets, in milligrams.
Change milligrams into grams: 1000 mg = 1 g.
The strip contains 2.5 g of medicine.

misconceptions.A: 10 × 250 = 2500 mg. To change milligrams into grams divide by 1000, not by 100.
misconceptions.B: This is the medicine in one tablet: 250 mg = 0.25 g. The strip has 10 tablets.
misconceptions.C: 2500 is the number of milligrams. Divide by 1000 to change it into grams.

G4A_UNITS_013.questionText: A tailor has 5 m of cloth. He uses 2 m 35 cm to stitch a kurta. How much cloth is left?
hints: This is a subtraction of lengths. It helps to write both lengths in centimetres.
5 m = 500 cm and 2 m 35 cm = 235 cm. Now subtract.
A similar one: 4 m − 1 m 20 cm. That is 400 cm − 120 cm = 280 cm, which is 2 m 80 cm.

stepByStep.text: Write both lengths in centimetres: 5 m = 500 cm and 2 m 35 cm = 235 cm.
Subtract.
265 cm is 2 m 65 cm. So 2 m 65 cm of cloth is left.

misconceptions.A: This takes away only the 2 m and keeps the 35 cm. The 35 cm must be taken away as well.
misconceptions.B: 100 − 35 = 65 is right, but one of the 5 metres was changed into 100 cm, so only 4 − 2 = 2 whole metres are left.
misconceptions.C: This adds the two lengths. The cloth was used up, so subtract.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 500 cm − 235 cm = 265 cm, which is 2 m 65 cm.

G4A_UNITS_014.questionText: A running track is 4 hectometres long. Sunil runs 5 rounds of the track. How many kilometres does he run?
hints: Change hectometres into metres first. 'Hecto' means one hundred.
1 hectometre = 100 m, so one round is 4 × 100 m. Then find 5 rounds.
A similar one: a path is 3 hectometres long and Riya walks it 10 times. 3 × 100 = 300 m, and 300 × 10 = 3000 m = 3 km.

stepByStep.text: 1 hectometre = 100 m. Find the length of one round in metres.
Distance for 5 rounds.
Change metres into kilometres. Sunil runs 2 km.

misconceptions.A: This takes a hectometre as 1000 m. A hectometre is 100 m, so one round is 400 m.
misconceptions.B: Great! One round is 400 m, 5 rounds are 2000 m, and 2000 m is 2 km.
misconceptions.C: This takes a hectometre as 10 m. A hectometre is 100 m, so one round is 400 m.
misconceptions.D: 5 rounds make 2000 m. To change metres into kilometres divide by 1000.

G4A_UNITS_015.questionText: Rina needs 150 laddoos for a function. The shop sells laddoos only in boxes of one dozen. What is the least number of boxes she must buy?
hints: A dozen is 12. Find how many 12s are needed to reach at least 150.
Divide 150 by 12 and look at the remainder. Think about what the remainder means for Rina.
A similar one: 100 cups are needed and they come in packs of a dozen. 100 ÷ 12 = 8 remainder 4, so 8 packs are not enough and 9 packs are needed.

stepByStep.text: 1 dozen = 12. Divide 150 by 12.
12 boxes hold 144 laddoos, so 6 more laddoos are still needed.
One more box is needed. Rina must buy 13 boxes.

misconceptions.A: 12 boxes hold only 144 laddoos, which is 6 short. Rina needs one more box.
misconceptions.B: This counts a dozen as 10. A dozen is 12, so divide 150 by 12.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 12 boxes give 144 laddoos, which is not enough, so she needs 13 boxes, which give 156.
misconceptions.D: 13 boxes already hold 156 laddoos, which is enough. A 14th box is not needed.

G4A_UNITS_016.questionText: On a trek, Arjun walks 2 km 75 m before breakfast, 850 m before lunch and 1.5 km in the evening. How many kilometres does he walk in all?
hints: The three distances are written in three different ways. Change them all into metres, add, then change back.
2 km 75 m = 2075 m and 1.5 km = 1500 m. Now add these to 850 m.
A similar one: 1 km 40 m + 700 m + 2.5 km. In metres that is 1040 + 700 + 2500 = 4240 m, which is 4.24 km.

stepByStep.text: Write each distance in metres: 2 km 75 m = 2075 m, and 1.5 km = 1500 m.
Add the three distances.
Change metres into kilometres. Arjun walks 4.425 km in all.

misconceptions.A: Well done! 2075 m + 850 m + 1500 m = 4425 m, which is 4.425 km.
misconceptions.B: This takes 75 m as 750 m. 2 km 75 m is 2075 m, because 75 m is 0.075 km.
misconceptions.C: This takes 850 m as 8.5 km. 850 m is less than 1 km: it is 0.85 km.
misconceptions.D: This leaves out the 1.5 km walked in the evening. Add all three distances.

G4A_UNITS_017.questionText: An empty basket weighs 600 g. When 12 mangoes of equal weight are put in it, the basket weighs 4 kg 200 g. What is the weight of one mango?
hints: The weight given includes the basket. Find the weight of the mangoes alone first.
4 kg 200 g = 4200 g. Take away the 600 g basket to get the weight of the 12 mangoes.
A similar one: a 500 g box with 10 equal apples weighs 2 kg 500 g. The apples weigh 2500 − 500 = 2000 g, so each apple weighs 2000 ÷ 10 = 200 g.

stepByStep.text: Change to grams: 4 kg 200 g = 4200 g.
Take away the weight of the basket.
Share among 12 mangoes. One mango weighs 300 g.

misconceptions.A: Yes! The mangoes alone weigh 4200 − 600 = 3600 g, and 3600 ÷ 12 = 300 g each.
misconceptions.B: This shares the full 4200 g among the mangoes. The basket's own 600 g must be taken away first.
misconceptions.C: This adds the basket's weight. The basket is part of the 4 kg 200 g, so subtract 600 g.

G4A_UNITS_018.questionText: A leaking tap drips 5 ml of water every minute. How many litres of water does it waste in one full day?
hints: Go step by step: one minute, then one hour, then one day. Change to litres at the end.
An hour has 60 minutes, so the tap loses 5 × 60 ml in an hour. Then use 24 hours in a day.
A similar one: a tap drips 10 ml a minute. In an hour that is 10 × 60 = 600 ml, and in 5 hours it is 600 × 5 = 3000 ml = 3 litres.

stepByStep.text: Water lost in one hour.
Water lost in 24 hours.
Change millilitres into litres. The tap wastes 7.2 litres in a day.

misconceptions.A: This is the water lost in one hour: 5 × 60 = 300 ml. A day has 24 hours.
misconceptions.B: The tap loses 7200 ml in a day. Dividing by 1000 gives 7.2 litres.
misconceptions.C: Great! 5 × 60 = 300 ml in an hour, 300 × 24 = 7200 ml in a day, and that is 7.2 litres.
misconceptions.D: This multiplies 5 ml by 24, as if the tap dripped once an hour. It drips every minute, and an hour has 60 minutes.

G4A_UNITS_019.questionText: A snail crawls 3 cm 5 mm every minute. How many minutes does it take to crawl 2.1 m?
hints: Write both lengths in the same small unit, then see how many times one fits into the other.
3 cm 5 mm = 35 mm. Now change 2.1 m into millimetres.
A similar one: an ant moves 2 cm 5 mm a minute and must go 1 m. That is 25 mm a minute and 1000 mm in all, so it takes 1000 ÷ 25 = 40 minutes.

stepByStep.text: Change the snail's distance each minute into millimetres.
Change 2.1 m into millimetres: 1 m = 1000 mm.
Divide. The snail takes 60 minutes.

misconceptions.A: This takes 2.1 m as 210 mm. 2.1 m is 210 cm, which is 2100 mm.
misconceptions.B: This takes 2.1 m as 21000 mm. 1 m is 1000 mm, so 2.1 m is 2100 mm.
misconceptions.C: This leaves out the 5 mm. Each minute the snail moves 35 mm, not 30 mm.
misconceptions.D: Yes! The snail moves 35 mm a minute and has 2100 mm to go, and 2100 ÷ 35 = 60 minutes.

G4A_UNITS_020.questionText: Pencils are sold only in packets of a dozen, and erasers only in packets of a score. Asha wants to buy exactly as many pencils as erasers. What is the smallest number of pencils she can buy?
hints: The number of pencils is a multiple of 12 and the number of erasers is a multiple of 20. You need a number that is both.
List the multiples of 20: 20, 40, and so on. Check which is the first one that 12 also divides exactly.
A similar one: plates in packs of 6 and cups in packs of 8. Multiples of 8 are 8, 16, 24, and 24 is the first that 6 divides, so the smallest equal number is 24.

stepByStep.text: A dozen is 12 and a score is 20, so we need the smallest number that is a multiple of both.
Multiples of 20 are 20, 40, 60. Of these, 12 does not divide 20 or 40.
12 divides 60 exactly, so 60 is the smallest common multiple.
The smallest number of pencils Asha can buy is 60.

misconceptions.A: 12 × 20 = 240 would give equal numbers, but it is not the smallest. Look for the first number that is in both the 12 times and the 20 times tables.
misconceptions.B: Well done! 60 is the first number that is both 5 packets of 12 and 3 packets of 20.
misconceptions.C: 120 is a multiple of both 12 and 20, but there is a smaller one. Try listing the multiples of 20 and checking each.
