A similar one: for 20 − 2 × (1 + 6), the bracket is 7, then 2 × 7 = 14, then 20 − 14 = 6. A large first number can still give a small value.

stepByStep.text: First expression.
Second expression.
Third expression.
Fourth expression.
The smallest value is 8, which comes from 40 − 4 × (3 + 5).

misconceptions.A: This one is 24 ÷ 3 + 2 = 10. Another expression gives a smaller value.
misconceptions.B: This one is 6 + 3 = 9, because the division is done before the addition. It is close, but one expression is smaller.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 40 − 4 × 8 = 40 − 32 = 8, the smallest of the four.
misconceptions.D: This one is 50 ÷ 5 + 1 = 11, which is the greatest of the four.

G4A_OPERATIONS_004.questionText: A train has 12 coaches with 72 seats in each coach. It leaves the first station with 598 passengers. At the next station 135 passengers get off and 210 get on. Everyone has a seat. How many seats are empty now?
hints: Find two numbers: how many seats the train has, and how many passengers are on it now. The empty seats are the difference.
Seats: 12 times 72. Passengers now: start with 598, take away those who got off, and add those who got on.
A similar one: a bus has 50 seats and 38 riders. Ten get off and 6 get on, so there are 34 riders. Empty seats: 50 − 34 = 16.

stepByStep.text: Seats on the train.
Passengers after the next station.
Empty seats.
There are 191 empty seats.

misconceptions.A: 266 uses the 598 passengers from the first station. Some got off and more got on at the next station.
misconceptions.B: 341 adds the 135 and takes away the 210. It is the other way round: 135 got off and 210 got on.
misconceptions.C: 56 adds the 210 new passengers but leaves the 135 who got off still on the train. Take them away first.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 864 seats and 673 passengers leave 191 empty seats.

G4A_OPERATIONS_005.questionText: A shopkeeper buys 9 dozen bananas at ₹4 each. 12 bananas go bad and are thrown away. He sells all the rest at ₹6 each. How much more money does he get than he paid?
hints: Find the money he paid and the money he got from selling. The question asks for the difference between them.
One dozen is 12, so 9 dozen is 9 times 12 bananas. He pays ₹4 for every one of them, even the ones that go bad.
A similar one: a man buys 2 dozen eggs at ₹5 each and pays ₹120. Four break, and he sells the other 20 at ₹8 each for ₹160. He gets ₹40 more than he paid.

stepByStep.text: Number of bananas bought.
Money paid.
Bananas sold and money received.
Difference.
He gets ₹144 more than he paid.

misconceptions.A: Yes! He paid ₹432 and received ₹576, which is ₹144 more.
misconceptions.B: ₹216 sells all 108 bananas. Twelve went bad, so only 96 were sold.
misconceptions.C: ₹576 is the money he received. Take away the ₹432 he paid to find how much more it is.
misconceptions.D: ₹192 is ₹2 extra on each of the 96 bananas sold. He also paid for the 12 bananas that went bad.

hints: Look for numbers that multiply to make a round number. Then look for a number that both parts share.
25 times 4 is 100, so the first part is 37 times 100. Both parts are now a number of 37s.
A similar one: 5 × 13 × 2 − 13 × 9. Since 5 × 2 = 10, this is ten 13s minus nine 13s, which leaves one 13. The value is 13.

stepByStep.text: Multiply 25 and 4 first, because they make 100.
The sum is now a hundred 37s minus ninety-nine 37s.
That leaves just one 37.
The value is 37.

misconceptions.A: 3700 is only the first part, 25 × 37 × 4. The second part, 37 × 99, still has to be taken away.
misconceptions.B: Yes! A hundred 37s minus ninety-nine 37s leaves one 37.
misconceptions.C: 0 would be right if the second part were 37 × 100. It is 37 × 99, so one 37 is left.
misconceptions.D: 74 is two 37s. A hundred 37s minus ninety-nine 37s leaves one.

G4A_OPERATIONS_007.questionText: A sweet shop makes 500 laddoos and packs them in boxes of 12. The laddoos left over are shared equally among 4 children. How many laddoos does each child get?
hints: Packing into equal boxes is division, and the laddoos that do not fill a box are the remainder. The children share only the remainder.
Divide 500 by 12. Find how many full boxes there are and how many laddoos are left over.
A similar one: 150 toffees in packets of 8. Eighteen packets use 144 toffees and 6 are left over. Shared between 2 children, each gets 3.

stepByStep.text: Find the full boxes.
Laddoos left over.
Share the left-over laddoos among 4 children.
Each child gets 2 laddoos.

misconceptions.A: 8 is the number of laddoos left over. They are shared among 4 children.
misconceptions.B: 41 is the number of full boxes. The children share the laddoos that are left over.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 8 laddoos are left over, and 8 ÷ 4 = 2.
misconceptions.D: 125 shares all 500 laddoos among the children. Only the left-over laddoos go to them.

hints: Start with the innermost bracket and work outwards: round brackets, then square brackets, then curly brackets.
Inside the round bracket is 18 + 12 ÷ 3. Do the division there before the addition.
A similar one: {50 − [30 − (6 + 8 ÷ 2)]} ÷ 5. The round bracket is 6 + 4 = 10, then 30 − 10 = 20, then 50 − 20 = 30, and 30 ÷ 5 = 6.

stepByStep.text: Round bracket: divide before adding.
Square bracket.
Curly bracket.
Divide by 2.
The value is 31.

misconceptions.A: 25 comes from adding 18 and 12 before dividing by 3. Inside the bracket, 12 ÷ 3 is done first.
misconceptions.B: 9 comes from taking 60 and then 22 away from 100. The square bracket means 60 − 22 is worked out first, and that result is taken from 100.
misconceptions.C: 62 is the value of the curly bracket. One more step is left: divide by 2.
misconceptions.D: Yes! The brackets give 22, then 38, then 62, and 62 ÷ 2 = 31.

G4A_OPERATIONS_009.questionText: Asha earns ₹500 a day and works 6 days every week. Each week she spends ₹1,800 and saves the rest. How many weeks will she take to save ₹18,000?
hints: Find how much she saves in one week first. Then see how many such weeks make the amount she wants.
In one week she earns 6 times ₹500. Take away what she spends in a week to get her weekly saving.
A similar one: Ravi earns ₹200 a day for 5 days, which is ₹1,000 a week. He spends ₹600 and saves ₹400. To save ₹2,000 he needs 2,000 ÷ 400 = 5 weeks.

stepByStep.text: Money earned in a week.
Money saved in a week.
Number of weeks needed.
She will take 15 weeks.

misconceptions.A: 6 weeks would be enough only if she saved all ₹3,000 each week. She spends ₹1,800 of it.
misconceptions.B: Yes! She saves ₹1,200 a week, and 18,000 ÷ 1,200 = 15.
misconceptions.C: 10 divides ₹18,000 by the ₹1,800 she spends. Divide by the amount she saves each week.
misconceptions.D: 36 divides ₹18,000 by her pay for one day. Find her saving for a whole week first.

hints: Do the bracket first. Then do every multiplication and division, going from left to right. Addition and subtraction come last, also from left to right.
The bracket 9 − 4 is 5. Now the sum has three parts joined by − and +. Work out each part before joining them.
A similar one: 5 × 6 − 2 × (7 − 3) + 12 ÷ 3 × 2. The parts are 30, then 2 × 4 = 8, then 4 × 2 = 8. So 30 − 8 + 8 = 30.

stepByStep.text: Bracket first.
First two parts.
Third part, from left to right.
Join the parts from left to right.
The value is 34.

misconceptions.B: 28 comes from doing 5 × 2 before the division. Division and multiplication go from left to right, so 20 ÷ 5 comes first.
misconceptions.C: 14 comes from working 6 × 9 − 4 without the bracket. The bracket 9 − 4 is done first, giving 6 × 5.
misconceptions.D: 18 comes from adding 30 and 8 and taking both from 56. Work from left to right: 56 − 30 first, then add 8.

G4A_OPERATIONS_011.questionText: A hall has 28 rows with 35 chairs in each row. For a function, 15 rows are taken away completely and 6 more chairs are added to each row that is left. How many chairs are in the hall now?
hints: Two things change: the number of rows and the number of chairs in a row. Find both new numbers before you multiply.
Rows left: 28 minus 15. Chairs in each of those rows: 35 plus 6.
A similar one: 10 rows of 8 chairs. Four rows are removed and 2 chairs are added to each row left. Now there are 6 rows of 10, which is 60 chairs.

stepByStep.text: Rows left.
Chairs in each row now.
Chairs in the hall.
There are 533 chairs in the hall now.

misconceptions.A: 455 is 13 rows of 35. Each row that is left gets 6 more chairs, so each has 41.
misconceptions.B: 623 adds 6 chairs to all 28 rows before taking rows away. Only the 13 rows that are left get extra chairs.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 13 rows of 41 chairs make 533.
misconceptions.D: 461 adds only 6 chairs in all. Six chairs are added to each of the 13 rows.

G4A_OPERATIONS_012.questionText: A farmer has 1,000 mangoes. He fills 25 crates with 2 dozen mangoes in each. He packs the rest in baskets of 50. How many baskets does he need?
hints: Find how many mangoes go into the crates, take them away from the total, and then pack what is left.
One dozen is 12, so 2 dozen is 24 mangoes in each crate. Multiply by 25 crates.
A similar one: 300 oranges. Ten bags hold 1 dozen each, which is 120. The 180 left go into boxes of 30, so 6 boxes are needed.

stepByStep.text: Mangoes in one crate.
Mangoes in 25 crates.
Mangoes left.
Baskets needed.
He needs 8 baskets.

misconceptions.A: 20 packs all 1,000 mangoes in baskets. The crates take 600 mangoes first.
misconceptions.B: 19 puts only 2 mangoes in each crate. Two dozen is 24 mangoes.
misconceptions.C: 12 is the number of baskets the 600 crate mangoes would fill. The baskets hold the mangoes that are left.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 600 mangoes go into crates, and the other 400 fill 8 baskets of 50.

G4A_TRIANGLES_001.questionText: A triangle has sides 5 cm, 5 cm and 8 cm. What kind of triangle is it?

options.text: These sides cannot make a triangle

hints: Triangles are named by how many of their sides are equal. Compare the three lengths.
Two of the lengths are 5 cm and the third is 8 cm. How many sides are equal?
A similar one: a triangle with sides 7 cm, 4 cm and 6 cm has three different lengths, so it is a scalene triangle.

stepByStep.text: The two shorter sides together are 10 cm, which is more than 8 cm, so the sides do make a triangle.
Exactly two sides are equal: 5 cm and 5 cm.
A triangle with exactly two equal sides is an isosceles triangle.

misconceptions.A: An equilateral triangle has all three sides equal. Here the third side is 8 cm, not 5 cm.
misconceptions.B: Yes! Two sides are 5 cm and the third is different, so it is isosceles.
misconceptions.C: A scalene triangle has three different sides. Here two of the sides are the same.
misconceptions.D: The two shorter sides add up to 10 cm, which is more than 8 cm, so they do close up into a triangle.

G4A_TRIANGLES_002.questionText: The angles of a triangle are 35°, 55° and 90°. What kind of triangle is it?
hints: Triangles can be named by their biggest angle. Is it less than 90°, exactly 90°, or more than 90°?
The biggest of the three angles is 90°. What is an angle of 90° called?
A similar one: a triangle with angles 30°, 40° and 110° has one angle bigger than 90°, so it is an obtuse-angled triangle.

stepByStep.text: The biggest angle is 90°.
An angle of 90° is a right angle.
A triangle with one right angle is a right-angled triangle.

misconceptions.A: In an acute-angled triangle all three angles are less than 90°. Here one angle is exactly 90°.
misconceptions.B: An obtuse-angled triangle has one angle more than 90°. Here the biggest angle is exactly 90°.
misconceptions.C: Yes! One angle is 90°, a right angle.
misconceptions.D: An equilateral triangle has three angles of 60° each. These three angles are all different.

G4A_TRIANGLES_003.questionText: All three sides of a triangle have different lengths. By its sides, what is the triangle called?
hints: There are three names for triangles by their sides: one for three equal sides, one for two equal sides, and one for no equal sides.
This triangle has no two sides the same. Which of the three names is for that?
A similar one: a triangle with sides 6 cm, 6 cm and 6 cm has all sides equal, so it is called an equilateral triangle.

stepByStep.text: Three equal sides make an equilateral triangle, and two equal sides make an isosceles triangle.
This triangle has no equal sides at all.
A triangle with three different sides is a scalene triangle.

misconceptions.A: Yes! Scalene means no two sides are equal.
misconceptions.B: An isosceles triangle has two equal sides. Here all three are different.
misconceptions.C: An equilateral triangle has three equal sides. Here all three are different.
misconceptions.D: Right-angled is a name that comes from the angles. The question asks for the name that comes from the sides.

G4A_TRIANGLES_004.questionText: An isosceles triangle has two equal sides of 9 cm each. Its third side is 6 cm. What is its perimeter?
hints: The perimeter is the distance all the way around, so add all three sides.
The three sides are 9 cm, 9 cm and 6 cm. Add them.
A similar one: equal sides of 5 cm each and a third side of 4 cm give a perimeter of 5 + 5 + 4 = 14 cm.

stepByStep.text: The three sides are 9 cm, 9 cm and 6 cm.
Add them.
The perimeter is 24 cm.

misconceptions.A: 15 cm adds 9 and 6 only. There are two sides of 9 cm.
misconceptions.B: 21 cm uses one side of 9 cm and two of 6 cm. It is the 9 cm side that comes twice.
misconceptions.C: 54 comes from multiplying 9 by 6. For perimeter, add the three sides.

G4A_TRIANGLES_005.questionText: A triangle has angles 100°, 40° and 40°. Which name describes it best?
hints: The name has two parts. One part comes from the biggest angle. The other part comes from how many angles, and so how many sides, are equal.
The biggest angle is 100°. Is that less than, equal to, or more than 90°? Then look at the two angles of 40°.
A similar one: a triangle with angles 90°, 45° and 45° has a right angle and two equal angles, so it is a right-angled isosceles triangle.

stepByStep.text: The biggest angle is 100°, which is more than 90°, so the triangle is obtuse-angled.
Two angles are equal, both 40°. The sides opposite equal angles are equal, so two sides are equal.
It is an obtuse-angled isosceles triangle.

misconceptions.A: Acute-angled means every angle is less than 90°. Here one angle is 100°.
misconceptions.B: Scalene means no sides are equal. Two equal angles give two equal sides.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 100° makes it obtuse-angled, and the two angles of 40° make it isosceles.
misconceptions.D: Right-angled needs an angle of exactly 90°. The biggest angle here is 100°.

G4A_TRIANGLES_006.questionText: Which of these sets of lengths cannot be the sides of a triangle?
hints: Three lengths make a triangle only when the two shorter ones together are longer than the longest one.
For each set, add the two shorter lengths and compare the total with the longest length. Watch for a total that is only equal, not greater.
A similar one: 2 cm, 3 cm and 7 cm cannot make a triangle, because 2 + 3 = 5 is less than 7 and the short sides cannot meet.

stepByStep.text: 3 + 4 = 7 is more than 5, and 6 + 6 = 12 is more than 11. These two sets make triangles.
7 + 8 = 15 is more than 14, so this set makes a triangle too.
4 + 5 = 9 is only equal to the longest side, 9. The two short sides would lie flat along the long side.
The set that cannot make a triangle is 4 cm, 5 cm, 9 cm.

misconceptions.A: 3 + 4 = 7 is more than 5, so these lengths do make a triangle.
misconceptions.B: 6 + 6 = 12 is more than 11, so these lengths do make a triangle, a rather flat one.
misconceptions.C: 7 + 8 = 15 is more than 14, so these lengths do make a triangle.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 4 + 5 is exactly 9, so the two short sides cannot rise above the long side to form a triangle.

G4A_TRIANGLES_007.questionText: In a right-angled triangle, one of the two acute angles is twice the other. What is the smallest angle of the triangle?
hints: The three angles of a triangle add up to 180°. In a right-angled triangle one angle is 90°, so think about what is left for the other two.
The two acute angles together make 90°. One is twice the other, so think of them as 1 part and 2 parts.
A similar one: in a right-angled triangle one acute angle is 4 times the other. Five equal parts make 90°, so one part is 18°. The angles are 18° and 72°, and the smallest is 18°.

stepByStep.text: The two acute angles together.
One angle is 1 part and the other is 2 parts, so 3 parts make 90°.
The acute angles are 30° and 60°.
The smallest angle is 30°.

misconceptions.A: Yes! The angles are 30°, 60° and 90°, and 60° is twice 30°.
misconceptions.B: 60° is the bigger of the two acute angles. The question asks for the smallest angle.
misconceptions.C: 45° would make the two acute angles equal. One of them must be twice the other.
misconceptions.D: 15° comes from sharing 90° into too many parts. One part and two parts make 3 parts in all.

G4A_TRIANGLES_008.questionText: The perimeter of an isosceles triangle is 40 cm. The side that is different from the other two is 12 cm. How long is each of the equal sides?
hints: The perimeter is the sum of the three sides. Take away the side you know, and what is left belongs to the two equal sides.
Take 12 cm away from 40 cm. The rest is shared equally between the two equal sides.
A similar one: perimeter 26 cm and a different side of 6 cm. The two equal sides share 26 − 6 = 20 cm, so each is 10 cm.

stepByStep.text: Take the different side away from the perimeter.
The two equal sides share this equally.
Each equal side is 14 cm.

misconceptions.A: 28 cm is the two equal sides together. Share it between the two sides.
misconceptions.C: 20 cm is half the perimeter. Take away the 12 cm side before halving.
misconceptions.D: 16 cm comes from taking 12 away twice. The 12 cm side appears only once.

G4A_TRIANGLES_009.questionText: All three angles of a triangle are equal. What is the sum of any two of its angles?
hints: The three angles of any triangle add up to 180°. If they are all equal, you can find one of them.
Share 180° equally among three angles to find each one. Then add two of them.
A similar one: a right-angled triangle has two equal angles. They share 180 − 90 = 90°, so each is 45°, and those two together make 90°.

stepByStep.text: The three equal angles add up to 180°, so find one angle.
Add two of the angles.
The sum of any two angles is 120°.

misconceptions.A: 60° is one angle. The question asks for two of them added together.
misconceptions.B: 180° is the sum of all three angles. Add only two of them.
misconceptions.C: Yes! Each angle is 60°, and 60° + 60° = 120°.
misconceptions.D: 90° would be right for the two equal angles of a right-angled triangle. Here each angle is 60°.

G4A_TRIANGLES_010.questionText: Two sides of a triangle are 7 cm and 10 cm. The third side is a whole number of centimetres. What is the greatest length the third side can have?
hints: In a triangle, any two sides together must be longer than the third side. Use this to find how long the third side is allowed to be.
Add the two sides you know. The third side must be shorter than this total, not equal to it.
A similar one: with sides 4 cm and 6 cm, the third side must be shorter than 4 + 6 = 10 cm. The greatest whole number is 9 cm.

stepByStep.text: Add the two known sides.
The third side must be shorter than 17 cm. At exactly 17 cm the two sides would lie flat along it.
The greatest whole number less than 17 is 16.
The greatest length of the third side is 16 cm.

misconceptions.A: At 17 cm the other two sides would lie flat along the third side and no triangle would form. It must be a little shorter.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 7 + 10 = 17 is more than 16, so the triangle closes, and 16 is the greatest whole number that fits.
misconceptions.C: 18 cm is longer than the other two sides put together, so they could not reach each other.
misconceptions.D: 3 cm is the difference of the two sides. That is about the shortest end, and the question asks for the greatest length.

G4A_TRIANGLES_011.questionText: Jay has four sticks of lengths 3 cm, 5 cm, 7 cm and 10 cm. He picks three sticks at a time to make a triangle. How many different triangles can he make?
hints: List every way of choosing three sticks from the four. Then test each choice: the two shorter sticks together must be longer than the longest one.
There are four ways to choose three sticks: leave out one stick each time. Begin with 3, 5 and 7, and compare 3 + 5 with 7.
A similar one: sticks of 1 cm, 2 cm, 3 cm and 4 cm. Of the four choices, only 2, 3 and 4 works, because 2 + 3 = 5 is more than 4. So 1 triangle can be made.

stepByStep.text: Sticks 3, 5, 7: 3 + 5 = 8 is more than 7, so this makes a triangle.
Sticks 3, 5, 10: 3 + 5 = 8 is less than 10, so no triangle.
Sticks 3, 7, 10: 3 + 7 = 10 is only equal to 10, so no triangle.
Sticks 5, 7, 10: 5 + 7 = 12 is more than 10, so this makes a triangle.
He can make 2 different triangles.

misconceptions.A: 4 is the number of ways to choose three sticks, but not every choice closes into a triangle. Test each one.
misconceptions.B: 3 counts the sticks 3, 7 and 10 as a triangle. But 3 + 7 is exactly 10, so those sticks would lie flat.
misconceptions.C: There is more than one. Both 3, 5, 7 and 5, 7, 10 pass the test.
misconceptions.D: Yes! Only 3, 5, 7 and 5, 7, 10 make triangles.

G4A_TRIANGLES_012.questionText: In an isosceles triangle, the angle between the two equal sides is 3 times each of the other two angles. How big is that angle?
hints: In an isosceles triangle the two angles opposite the equal sides are equal. Think of the angles as equal parts that add up to 180°.
Call each of the two equal angles 1 part. The angle between the equal sides is then 3 parts. How many parts are there altogether?
A similar one: if the top angle is twice each base angle, the angles are 2 parts, 1 part and 1 part. Four parts make 180°, so one part is 45° and the top angle is 90°.

stepByStep.text: The two equal angles are 1 part each, and the angle between the equal sides is 3 parts.
Five parts make 180°, so find one part.
The angle between the equal sides is 3 parts.
That angle is 108°.

misconceptions.A: Yes! The angles are 108°, 36° and 36°, which add up to 180°.
misconceptions.B: 36° is each of the two equal angles. The angle asked for is 3 times as big.
misconceptions.C: 135° comes from sharing 180° into 4 parts. There are 3 + 1 + 1 = 5 parts.
misconceptions.D: 60° is the angle when all three angles are equal. Here one angle is 3 times each of the others.

G4A_TRIANGLES_013.questionText: In a triangle, the second angle is 20° more than the first angle, and the third angle is 20° more than the second. What is the largest angle?
hints: The three angles add up to 180°. Describe the second and third angles by how much more they are than the first.
The second angle is the first plus 20°, and the third is the first plus 40°. So three times the first angle, plus 60°, makes 180°.
A similar one: the second angle is 10° more than the first and the third is 10° more than the second. Three times the first plus 30° is 180°, so the first is 50° and the largest is 70°.

stepByStep.text: The third angle is 20° + 20° = 40° more than the first.
Take the extra 20° and 40° away from 180°. What is left is three times the first angle.
Find the first angle.
The largest angle is the third one.
The largest angle is 80°.

misconceptions.A: 40° is the first, smallest angle. The largest is 40° more than that.
misconceptions.B: 60° is the second, middle angle. The third angle is 20° more.
misconceptions.C: Yes! The angles are 40°, 60° and 80°, which add up to 180°.
misconceptions.D: 100° would make the angles 60°, 80° and 100°, which add up to 240°. The three angles must total 180°.

G4A_TRIANGLES_014.questionText: An isosceles triangle has a perimeter of 50 cm. One of its sides is 12 cm long. Which of these can be the lengths of its other two sides?
hints: There are two things to check: two of the three sides must be equal, and the two shorter sides together must be longer than the longest side.
The 12 cm side could be one of the equal pair, or it could be the side that is different. Work out the sides in each case and test whether they can close into a triangle.
A similar one: an isosceles triangle with perimeter 20 cm and one side 4 cm. Sides 4, 4 and 12 cannot close, because 4 + 4 is less than 12. Sides 4, 8 and 8 can, so the other sides are 8 cm and 8 cm.

stepByStep.text: If 12 cm is one of the equal sides, the sides are 12, 12 and 26.
But 12 + 12 = 24 is less than 26, so those sides cannot close into a triangle.
If 12 cm is the different side, the equal sides share the rest.
Check: 12 + 19 is more than 19, so the triangle closes. The other two sides are 19 cm and 19 cm.

misconceptions.A: These add up to 50 cm with two equal sides, but 12 + 12 = 24 is less than 26, so the sides cannot meet.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 12 + 19 + 19 = 50, two sides are equal, and the triangle closes.
misconceptions.C: These add up to 50 cm, but 12, 14 and 24 are all different, so the triangle would not be isosceles.
misconceptions.D: These add up to 50 cm, but 12, 18 and 20 are all different, so the triangle would not be isosceles.

G4A_TRIANGLES_015.questionText: Which of these statements about triangles is true?

options.text: A triangle can have two obtuse angles
An equilateral triangle can be right-angled
A scalene triangle can have two equal angles
A right-angled triangle can be isosceles

hints: Test each statement with two facts: the three angles of a triangle add up to 180°, and equal sides sit opposite equal angles.
For each statement, try to write down three angles that would fit it and still add up to 180°. If you cannot, the statement is not true.
A similar test: can a triangle have two right angles? 90° + 90° is already 180°, which leaves nothing for the third angle. So it cannot.

stepByStep.text: Two obtuse angles would add up to more than 180°, so a triangle cannot have them.
An equilateral triangle has three angles of 60°, so it never has a right angle.
Two equal angles give two equal sides, and a scalene triangle has no equal sides.
Angles of 90°, 45° and 45° add up to 180° and two of them are equal. So the true statement is: A right-angled triangle can be isosceles.

misconceptions.A: Each obtuse angle is more than 90°, so two of them are already more than 180°. A triangle has room for only one.
misconceptions.B: Every angle of an equilateral triangle is 60°, so none of them can be 90°.
misconceptions.C: Equal angles always sit opposite equal sides. A scalene triangle has no equal sides, so it has no equal angles.
misconceptions.D: Yes! A triangle with angles 90°, 45° and 45° is both right-angled and isosceles.

G4A_QUADS_001.questionText: A quadrilateral has all four sides equal, but none of its angles is a right angle. What is it called?
hints: Two of these shapes have four equal sides. What makes them different from each other is their angles.
A square has four equal sides and four right angles. Which shape has four equal sides but leans over, so its angles are not right angles?
A similar one: a quadrilateral with opposite sides equal and four right angles, but with its length different from its breadth, is a rectangle.

stepByStep.text: Four equal sides are found in a square and in a rhombus.
A square always has four right angles, so it does not fit here.
A shape with four equal sides and no right angles is a rhombus.

misconceptions.A: Yes! A rhombus has four equal sides, and its angles need not be right angles.
misconceptions.B: A square does have four equal sides, but all its angles are right angles.
misconceptions.C: A rectangle has four right angles, and only its opposite sides have to be equal.
misconceptions.D: A trapezium has just one pair of parallel sides, and its four sides are not all equal.

G4A_QUADS_002.questionText: One angle of a parallelogram is 70°. What is the size of the angle next to it?
hints: In a parallelogram, opposite angles are equal, and two angles that are next to each other add up to 180°.
The angle next to the 70° angle makes 180° together with it. Take 70° away from 180°.
A similar one: if one angle of a parallelogram is 65°, the angle next to it is 180° − 65° = 115°.

stepByStep.text: Angles next to each other in a parallelogram add up to 180°.
Take the known angle away from 180°.
The angle next to it is 110°.

misconceptions.A: 70° is the angle opposite the given one. The angle next to it is different.
misconceptions.B: 20° would be right if the two angles made a right angle. Neighbouring angles of a parallelogram make 180° together.
misconceptions.D: 290° comes from taking 70° from 360°. Two neighbouring angles add up to 180°, and all four add up to 360°.

G4A_QUADS_003.questionText: The perimeter of a rhombus is 52 cm. How long is each side?
hints: Think about what is special about the sides of a rhombus. The perimeter is all the sides added together.
A rhombus has four equal sides, so the perimeter is 4 times one side. Share 52 cm into 4 equal parts.
A similar one: a rhombus with perimeter 36 cm has sides of 36 ÷ 4 = 9 cm each.

stepByStep.text: All four sides of a rhombus are equal, so the perimeter is 4 times one side.
Divide the perimeter by 4.
Each side is 13 cm.

misconceptions.A: 26 cm shares the perimeter between 2 sides. A rhombus has 4 equal sides.
misconceptions.C: 48 cm takes 4 away from 52. To share equally among 4 sides, divide by 4.
misconceptions.D: 208 comes from multiplying by 4. A side is shorter than the perimeter, so divide.

G4A_QUADS_004.questionText: A square handkerchief has sides of 25 cm. Lace is stitched all around its edge. The lace costs ₹3 for every centimetre. What does the lace cost?
hints: Lace that goes all around the edge is as long as the perimeter. Find that length first, then the cost.
A square has 4 equal sides, so the perimeter is 4 times 25 cm.
A similar one: ribbon at ₹2 a centimetre around a square of side 10 cm. The perimeter is 40 cm, so the ribbon costs 40 × 2 = ₹80.

stepByStep.text: Length of lace = perimeter of the square.
Each centimetre costs ₹3.
The lace costs ₹300.

misconceptions.A: ₹75 is the cost of lace for one side only. The lace goes around all four sides.
misconceptions.B: ₹150 is the cost for two sides. A square has four sides.
misconceptions.C: ₹1,875 uses the area, 25 × 25. Lace goes along the edge, so use the perimeter.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 100 cm of lace at ₹3 a centimetre costs ₹300.

G4A_QUADS_005.questionText: A wire is bent into a square of side 18 cm. The same wire is then bent into a rectangle whose length is twice its breadth. What is the area of the rectangle?
hints: The wire does not change length, so the square and the rectangle have the same perimeter. Use the perimeter to find the sides of the rectangle.
The wire is 4 times 18 cm long. In the rectangle, the length is 2 breadths, so going around it is 2 + 1 + 2 + 1 = 6 breadths.
A similar one: a square of side 6 cm uses 24 cm of wire. For a rectangle with length twice its breadth, 6 breadths make 24 cm, so the breadth is 4 cm, the length is 8 cm and the area is 32 cm².

stepByStep.text: Length of the wire = perimeter of the square.
Around the rectangle there are 6 breadths, because each length is 2 breadths.
The breadth is 12 cm, so the length is twice that.
Area = length times breadth.
The area of the rectangle is 288 cm².

misconceptions.A: 324 cm² is the area of the square. The rectangle has the same perimeter, but a different area.
misconceptions.B: 648 cm² keeps 18 cm as the breadth and doubles it for the length. That rectangle would need more wire than there is.
misconceptions.C: Yes! The rectangle is 24 cm by 12 cm, and 24 × 12 = 288.
misconceptions.D: 72 is the length of the wire in centimetres. Use it to find the sides, then multiply them.

G4A_QUADS_006.questionText: A rectangular garden is 20 m long and 14 m wide. A path 2 m wide runs all around it on the outside. What is the area of the path?
hints: The garden and the path together make a bigger rectangle. The path is the bigger rectangle with the garden taken out.
The path adds 2 m at both ends of the length and 2 m at both ends of the width. Find the length and width of the big rectangle.
A similar one: a lawn 10 m by 6 m with a 1 m path outside. The big rectangle is 12 m by 8 m, area 96 m². The lawn is 60 m², so the path is 36 m².

stepByStep.text: The path adds 2 m on each side, so 4 m to the length and 4 m to the width.
Area of the garden with the path.
Area of the garden alone.
Area of the path.
The area of the path is 152 m².

misconceptions.B: 72 m² adds the path only once to each measurement. The path is on both sides, so add 4 m, not 2 m.
misconceptions.C: 136 m² is the garden's perimeter times the path's width. That leaves out the four corner squares of the path.
misconceptions.D: 432 m² is the garden and the path together. Take away the garden's own area.

G4A_QUADS_007.questionText: A floor is 6 m long and 4 m wide. It is covered with square tiles of side 50 cm, with no gaps. How many tiles are needed?
hints: The floor is measured in metres and the tile in centimetres. Use the same unit for both, then count how many tiles fit along the length and along the width.
Two tiles of 50 cm make 1 metre. So how many tiles fit along 6 m, and how many along 4 m?
A similar one: a floor 5 m by 3 m with 50 cm tiles. Ten tiles fit along the length and 6 along the width, so 10 × 6 = 60 tiles are needed.

stepByStep.text: Two tiles of 50 cm make 1 m. Along the 6 m length.
Along the 4 m width.
Tiles needed = tiles in a row times number of rows.
The floor needs 96 tiles.

misconceptions.A: 24 is the area of the floor in square metres. Each square metre holds 4 of these tiles.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 12 tiles along the length and 8 along the width make 96.
misconceptions.C: 48 puts 2 tiles in each square metre. Two tiles fit each way, so 4 tiles cover one square metre.
misconceptions.D: 20 is the perimeter of the floor in metres. Tiles cover the whole floor, so think of rows of tiles.

G4A_QUADS_008.questionText: A square sheet of paper has sides of 12 cm. It is cut into two equal rectangles by one straight cut. What is the perimeter of each rectangle?
hints: Picture the cut going across the middle of the square. Work out the length and the breadth of one of the pieces.
The cut halves one pair of sides. Each rectangle is 12 cm long. How wide is it?
A similar one: a square of side 10 cm cut into two equal rectangles gives pieces 10 cm by 5 cm. Each has a perimeter of 10 + 5 + 10 + 5 = 30 cm.

stepByStep.text: The cut goes through the middle, so each rectangle is 12 cm long and half of 12 cm wide.
Add the four sides of one rectangle.
The perimeter of each rectangle is 36 cm.

misconceptions.A: 24 cm is half the square's perimeter. Cutting makes a new edge of 12 cm on each piece, so the perimeter is not simply halved.
misconceptions.B: 48 cm is the perimeter of the whole square. Each piece is smaller than that.
misconceptions.C: 72 is the area of each piece, 12 × 6. Perimeter is the distance around.
misconceptions.D: Yes! Each piece is 12 cm by 6 cm, and 12 + 6 + 12 + 6 = 36.

G4A_QUADS_009.questionText: Think about these four shapes: square, rectangle, rhombus and parallelogram. How many of them always have four right angles?
hints: Go through the shapes one by one. The word always matters: ask whether every shape of that kind must have right angles.
A square and a rectangle have right angles at every corner. Can a rhombus or a parallelogram lean over to one side?
A similar one: how many of the same four shapes always have opposite sides equal? The square, rectangle, rhombus and parallelogram all do, so the count is 4.

stepByStep.text: A square always has four right angles. So does a rectangle.
A rhombus can lean over, like a diamond, so its angles need not be right angles.
A parallelogram can lean over too, so its angles need not be right angles.
Only the square and the rectangle always have four right angles, so the count is 2.

misconceptions.A: The square is one of them, and there is one more: every rectangle has four right angles too.
misconceptions.B: Yes! The square and the rectangle always have four right angles.
misconceptions.C: A rhombus has four equal sides, but it can lean over, so its angles are not always right angles.
misconceptions.D: A rhombus and a parallelogram can both lean over, so they do not always have right angles.

G4A_QUADS_010.questionText: A rectangle is 20 cm long and 15 cm wide. Its length is made 5 cm longer and its width is made 5 cm shorter. What happens to its area?
hints: Do not guess from the fact that 5 is added and 5 is taken away. Work out the area before and the area after, and compare them.
The new rectangle is 25 cm long and 10 cm wide. Find its area, and the area of the first rectangle.
A similar one: a rectangle 10 cm by 8 cm has area 80 cm². Make it 2 cm longer and 2 cm narrower: 12 cm by 6 cm has area 72 cm². The area decreases by 8 cm².

stepByStep.text: Area at the start.
New length and width.
New area.
Compare the two areas.
The new area is smaller, so it decreases by 50 cm².

misconceptions.A: Yes! The area goes from 300 cm² down to 250 cm².
misconceptions.B: The perimeter stays the same, but the area does not. Work out 25 × 10 and compare it with 20 × 15.
misconceptions.C: The area does change by 50 cm², but the new area, 250 cm², is smaller than the old one, 300 cm².
misconceptions.D: 25 is 5 × 5. Find the two whole areas, 300 cm² and 250 cm², and subtract.

G4A_QUADS_011.questionText: A hall is 12 m long and 9 m wide. Carpet for the whole floor costs ₹150 for each square metre. A wooden strip along all four walls costs ₹40 for each metre. What is the total cost?
hints: Carpet covers the floor, so it needs the area. A strip along the walls goes around the edge, so it needs the perimeter.
Find the area of the floor with 12 times 9, and the perimeter with 12 + 9 + 12 + 9. Then find each cost separately.
A similar one: a room 5 m by 4 m. Carpet at ₹100 a square metre costs 20 × 100 = ₹2,000. A strip at ₹10 a metre costs 18 × 10 = ₹180. Together that is ₹2,180.

stepByStep.text: Area of the floor, and the cost of the carpet.
Perimeter of the floor, and the cost of the strip.
Add the two costs.
The total cost is ₹17,880.

misconceptions.A: ₹16,200 is the cost of the carpet alone. Add the cost of the wooden strip.
misconceptions.B: ₹20,520 charges both prices on the area. The strip runs along the walls, so it uses the perimeter, 42 m.
misconceptions.C: Yes! ₹16,200 for the carpet and ₹1,680 for the strip make ₹17,880.
misconceptions.D: ₹7,980 charges both prices on the perimeter. Carpet covers the floor, so it uses the area, 108 square metres.

G4A_QUADS_012.questionText: A rectangular field is 30 m long and 20 m wide. Fence posts are fixed all around it, 5 m apart, with one post at each corner. How many posts are needed?
hints: The posts go around a closed loop. On a closed loop, the number of posts is the same as the number of gaps between them.
Find the perimeter of the field. Then see how many gaps of 5 m fit into it.
A similar one: a square plot of side 10 m with posts 5 m apart. The perimeter is 40 m, so there are 40 ÷ 5 = 8 gaps and 8 posts.

stepByStep.text: Distance around the field.
Number of 5 m gaps around the field.
Around a closed loop every gap ends at a post, and the last gap ends at the first post, so posts and gaps are equal in number.
The field needs 20 posts.

misconceptions.A: 21 adds an extra post, which is right for a straight line of posts. Around a closed loop the last gap comes back to the first post.
misconceptions.B: 24 counts 7 posts on each long side and 5 on each short side, so each corner post is counted twice. Take away the 4 extra.
misconceptions.C: 10 counts the gaps along one long side and one short side only. The posts go all the way around.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 100 m around with posts every 5 m needs 20 posts.

G4A_ANGLES_001.questionText: Three angles lie side by side on a straight line. Two of them are 48° and 67°. What is the third angle?
hints: Angles that lie side by side on a straight line add up to a straight angle. Remember how many degrees that is.
A straight angle is 180°. Add the two angles you know, then see what is left.
A similar one: two angles of 50° and 70° on a straight line make 120° together, so the third angle is 180° − 120° = 60°.

stepByStep.text: Angles on a straight line add up to 180°.
Add the two known angles.
Take this away from 180°.
The third angle is 65°.

misconceptions.A: 115° is the two known angles added together. Take that away from 180° to find the third.
misconceptions.C: 245° comes from using 360°. That is for angles all the way around a point. On a straight line the total is 180°.
misconceptions.D: 75° comes from a slip in the subtraction. Check it by adding: 115 + 65 = 180.

G4A_ANGLES_002.questionText: A round pizza is cut from the centre into 8 equal slices. Ria eats 3 slices. What angle at the centre do the remaining slices make together?
hints: The angles all the way around a point add up to 360°. Equal slices share this equally.
Find the angle of one slice by sharing 360° among 8 slices. Then count the slices that are left.
A similar one: a cake cut into 6 equal slices has 360° ÷ 6 = 60° in each slice. If 2 are eaten, the 4 left make 4 × 60° = 240°.

stepByStep.text: The angle at the centre of one slice.
Slices left.
Angle made by the slices left.
The remaining slices make an angle of 225°.

misconceptions.A: 135° is the angle of the 3 slices Ria ate. The question asks about the slices that are left.
misconceptions.B: 45° is the angle of one slice. Five slices are left.
misconceptions.C: Yes! Five slices of 45° each make 225°.
misconceptions.D: 315° is what is left after only one slice is eaten. Ria ate 3 slices.

G4A_ANGLES_003.questionText: Through how many degrees does the hour hand of a clock turn between 3 p.m. and 7:30 p.m. on the same day?
hints: The hour hand goes once around the clock, 360°, in 12 hours. Find how far it turns in one hour.
In one hour the hour hand turns 360° ÷ 12 = 30°. How many hours are there from 3 p.m. to 7:30 p.m.?
A similar one: from 1 p.m. to 3:30 p.m. is 2 and a half hours. The hour hand turns 30° + 30° for the two hours and 15° for the half hour, which is 75°.

stepByStep.text: The hour hand turns 30° every hour.
From 3 p.m. to 7:30 p.m. is 4 and a half hours.
Four hours give 120°, and half an hour gives half of 30°, which is 15°.
The hour hand turns through 135°.

misconceptions.A: Yes! 120° for the four hours and 15° more for the half hour make 135°.
misconceptions.B: 120° is the turn for 4 hours. The hour hand keeps moving during the extra half hour.
misconceptions.C: 270° uses 60° for each hour. The hour hand moves only 30° in an hour.
misconceptions.D: 150° is the turn for 5 full hours. The time from 3 p.m. to 7:30 p.m. is 4 and a half hours.

G4A_ANGLES_004.questionText: Arjun is facing East. He makes a three-quarter turn anticlockwise. Which direction is he facing now?
hints: A quarter turn is 90° and takes you from one main direction to the next. Anticlockwise is the opposite way to the hands of a clock.
Starting from East, one quarter turn anticlockwise brings Arjun to North. Make two more quarter turns the same way.
A similar one: facing North, a half turn anticlockwise goes North to West to South. So that person ends up facing South.

stepByStep.text: Going anticlockwise, the directions come in the order East, North, West, South.
First quarter turn: East to North. Second quarter turn: North to West.
Third quarter turn: West to South.
Arjun is now facing South.

misconceptions.A: North is where Arjun faces after one quarter turn. He makes three quarter turns.
misconceptions.B: West is where Arjun faces after a half turn. One more quarter turn is still to come.
misconceptions.C: He would face East again only after a full turn. Three quarters is one quarter short of that.
misconceptions.D: Yes! East to North to West to South is three quarter turns anticlockwise.

G4A_ANGLES_005.questionText: A ladder leans against an upright wall on level ground. The ladder makes an angle of 58° with the ground. What angle does the ladder make with the wall?
hints: The ladder, the wall and the ground make a triangle. An upright wall meets level ground at a right angle.
One angle of the triangle is 90°, so the other two angles together make 90°. One of them is 58°.
A similar one: a ladder that makes 65° with the ground makes 90° − 65° = 25° with the wall.

stepByStep.text: The wall and the ground meet at 90°. The three angles of the triangle add up to 180°.
So the two angles at the ends of the ladder add up to 90°.
Take away the angle with the ground.
The ladder makes an angle of 32° with the wall.

misconceptions.A: 122° comes from taking 58° from 180°. The right angle between the wall and the ground uses up 90° of that.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 58° and 32° make 90° together, and the third angle is the right angle.
misconceptions.C: 42° comes from a slip in the subtraction. Check it by adding: 58 + 32 = 90.
misconceptions.D: 58° is the angle with the ground. The two angles would be equal only if each were 45°.

G4A_ANGLES_006.questionText: At 6:00 the hands of a clock make an angle of 180°. By how many degrees has the angle between the hands become smaller at 6:30?
hints: Both hands move. In half an hour the minute hand goes halfway around, and the hour hand moves a little too.
At 6:30 the minute hand points at 6. The hour hand is not at 6 any more: it is halfway between 6 and 7. How many degrees is half of one hour space?
A similar one: at 3:00 the angle is 90°. At 3:30 the minute hand is at 6 and the hour hand is halfway between 3 and 4, so the angle is 90° − 15° = 75°. The angle became smaller by 15°.

stepByStep.text: At 6:30 the minute hand points exactly at 6.
The hour hand has moved halfway from 6 to 7. One hour space is 30°, so half of it is 15°.
So the angle between the hands at 6:30 is 15°.
Compare with the angle at 6:00.
The angle has become smaller by 165°.

misconceptions.A: 180° would be right if the hands were together at 6:30. The hour hand has moved on, halfway towards 7.
misconceptions.B: 150° allows a whole hour space of 30° between the hands. In half an hour the hour hand moves only half a space, 15°.
misconceptions.C: Yes! The angle goes from 180° down to 15°, which is 165° smaller.
misconceptions.D: 15° is the angle between the hands at 6:30. The question asks how much smaller it is than 180°.

G4A_ANGLES_007.questionText: The lamp of a lighthouse turns at a steady speed and makes one full turn every 40 seconds. Through how many degrees does it turn in 15 seconds?
hints: One full turn is 360°. Find how many degrees the lamp turns in one second, then in the number of seconds asked.
Share 360° equally among 40 seconds to get the turn in one second.
A similar one: a wheel makes a full turn in 20 seconds, so it turns 360° ÷ 20 = 18° each second. In 5 seconds it turns 5 × 18° = 90°.

stepByStep.text: A full turn is 360°. Find the turn in one second.
Multiply by 15 seconds.
The lamp turns through 135°.

misconceptions.A: Yes! The lamp turns 9° each second, and 15 × 9 = 135.
misconceptions.B: 150° uses 10° for each second. Share 360° among 40 seconds: it is 9° each second.
misconceptions.C: 24° comes from dividing 360° by 15. Divide by 40 first, because the full turn takes 40 seconds.
misconceptions.D: 600 comes from multiplying 15 by 40. In 15 seconds the lamp makes less than half a turn, so the result must be less than 180°.

G4A_ANGLES_008.questionText: The supplement of an angle is 3 times its complement. What is the angle?
hints: The complement of an angle is what must be added to make 90°. The supplement is what must be added to make 180°. You can test each choice.
The supplement is always 90° more than the complement. If the supplement is 3 times the complement, then that extra 90° is 2 times the complement.
A similar one: the supplement of an angle is 7 times its complement. Try 75°: its supplement is 105° and its complement is 15°, and 105 = 7 × 15. So that angle is 75°.

stepByStep.text: The supplement is 90° more than the complement, because 180° is 90° more than 90°.
The supplement is 3 times the complement, so the extra 90° is 2 times the complement.
The complement is 45°, so find the angle.
Check: the supplement is 135°, which is 3 times 45°. The angle is 45°.

misconceptions.A: For 60° the supplement is 120° and the complement is 30°. That is 4 times, not 3 times.
misconceptions.B: For 30° the supplement is 150° and the complement is 60°. That is less than 3 times.
misconceptions.C: 135° is the supplement of the angle we want. An angle bigger than 90° has no complement at all.
misconceptions.D: Yes! The supplement of 45° is 135° and its complement is 45°, and 135 = 3 × 45.

G4A_ANGLES_009.questionText: Two straight lines cross each other. One of the angles formed is 4 times the angle beside it. What is the largest angle formed?
hints: When two straight lines cross, two angles that are beside each other lie on a straight line, so they add up to 180°.
Think of the smaller angle as 1 part and the angle beside it as 4 parts. Together the 5 parts make 180°.
A similar one: if one angle is twice the angle beside it, then 3 parts make 180°. One part is 60°, so the angles are 60° and 120°, and the largest is 120°.

stepByStep.text: Two angles beside each other on a straight line add up to 180°.
The angles are 1 part and 4 parts, which is 5 parts in all.
The larger angle is 4 parts.
The largest angle formed is 144°.

misconceptions.A: 36° is the smaller angle. The angle beside it is 4 times as big.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 36° and 144° lie on a straight line and add up to 180°.
misconceptions.C: 72° shares the whole turn of 360° into 5 parts. The two angles beside each other share 180°.
misconceptions.D: 288° uses 360° for the two angles. Two angles beside each other on a straight line add up to 180°.

G4A_ANGLES_010.questionText: Five angles meet at a point and fill the whole turn around it. One of them is 80° and the other four are equal. How big is each of the four equal angles?
hints: Angles that fill the whole turn around a point add up to 360°. Take away the angle you know, then share the rest.
Take 80° away from 360°. What is left is shared equally among the four equal angles.
A similar one: four angles fill the turn around a point. One is 60° and the other three are equal. They share 360° − 60° = 300°, so each is 100°.

stepByStep.text: Angles around a point add up to 360°. Take away the known angle.
Share the rest equally among the four angles.
Each of the four equal angles is 70°.

misconceptions.A: 25° uses 180° as the total. Angles all the way around a point add up to 360°.
misconceptions.B: 56° shares 280° among five angles. Only four angles are equal, and the 80° angle has been taken out already.
misconceptions.D: 280° is the four equal angles together. Share it among the four.
